Caveats: observational study without controlled dosing; the ASD group was younger, more male, received more midazolam (mean 0.01 mg/kg, clinically negligible) and had 9.5% epilepsy; in the burst-suppression analysis the ASD patients were older and 21.4% had epilepsy. The abstract gives p < 0.01 for burst suppression, the results section p < 0.05.
Walsh et al. Front Syst Neurosci 2018;12:23

Children 1–17 years: more power, but the same structure as in adults

  • Structure: in patients over 1 year, propofol-induced EEG is qualitatively similar regardless of age, with slow-delta and coherent frontal alpha. Under 1 year, alpha is not coherent (Lee 2017, 97 patients 0–21 years). The same applies to sevoflurane: alpha coherence is absent under 1 year (Akeju 2015, 54 patients 0–28 years; only 4 were under 1 year).
  • Power: total EEG power during sevoflurane increased from infancy to about 6 years and then declined to a level that remained stable from about 21 years (Akeju 2015). The results section in Akeju 2015 gives the peak as 5–8 years, while the abstract gives about 6 years. Reviews and later articles citing Lee 2017 and Akeju 2015 give about 6–8 years. The timing varies somewhat between sources.
  • Higher frequencies: according to Akeju 2015, power in the higher frequency bands (beta and gamma) is higher in children over 1 year than in adults at a surgical level of anaesthesia. The alpha peak and the structure were similar across ages over 1 year.
  • Caveats (Akeju 2015): retrospective study of routine recordings with SedLine (Fp1, Fp2, F7 and F8) in 54 patients, with sevoflurane as the only hypnotic. The groups were divided by visual assessment and had different treatment: end-tidal sevoflurane fell from 3.0 vol% in those under 1 year to 1.9 vol% in 22–28-year-olds (1.3 to 1.0 MAC), and neuromuscular blocking agents were used in none under 1 year and in 9–10 adults. The authors argue that the dose cannot explain an approximately threefold difference in amplitude (about 9–10 dB) in children over 1 year, and that the differing use of neuromuscular blockers may explain some of the difference at high frequency (beta and gamma) but not the power below 24 Hz. They also discuss that skull conductivity changes with age, but conclude that the findings reflect brain development. Three authors (Akeju, Brown and Purdon) have filed a provisional patent application on the use of the EEG measures.
  • Alpha frequency: the sources do not state that the alpha peak is faster in children over 1 year than in adults. In infants, an alpha/beta oscillation is described that appears around 9 months and decreases in peak frequency towards about 1 year, but that applies to infants. In older patients the alpha peak slows (ch. 36). The simulator for children therefore changes power and sevoflurane beta, but not alpha frequency.
  • Practical: the authors suggest that age must be taken into account when interpreting EEG, and that raw EEG and spectrogram are more informative than indices developed in adults. The studies are observational studies of patients who received anaesthesia at the anaesthetist's discretion.
Akeju 2015, Lee 2017

EEG-guided sevoflurane in children 1–6 years: less emergence delirium (Miyasaka 2025, RCT)

Randomised single-centre study from Tokyo (JAMA Pediatr 2025;179:704–712), 177 children aged 1 to under 6 years undergoing procedures with good regional/opioid analgesia. Control: mask induction with 5% sevoflurane and maintenance at 1.0 MAC (2.5%). Intervention: sevoflurane titrated to the lowest concentration that maintained a continuous alpha and slow-delta pattern on the spectrogram, adjusted in 0.1% steps, typically from 2% downwards. All received remifentanil 0.5 µg/kg/min plus a block.

  • Main finding: emergence delirium (PAED ≥ 10) in 21% versus 35% (difference 14%, p = 0.04). Sevoflurane during maintenance 0.9% (about 0.36 MAC) versus 2.5%; exposure 0.8 versus 2.1 MAC-hours. Emergence 21 minutes earlier and 16.5 minutes shorter in the recovery unit.
  • The most important point for EEG interpretation: PSI during surgery averaged 66 in the EEG group versus 42 in the control group, and SEF 24 versus 17 Hz. The index thus said “too light” (above 50) in children who, in the authors' assessment, were deeply unconscious with clear alpha and slow-delta. The authors explain this by the indices being calibrated against conventional practice where 1.0 MAC is regarded as adequate, so that index-guided dosing favours 1.0 MAC. Burst suppression occurred equally often in both groups (22 versus 23%, mostly seconds).
  • What they steered by: not theta, but alpha + slow-delta. At lower concentration the alpha frequency rose and alpha began to dissolve into higher frequencies while delta persisted; this was regarded as the start of a lighter state, and sevoflurane was increased again. In practice this is the same picture as “alpha without theta fill”.
  • The emergence course: all the children passed through a delta-dominated state before emergence. Children who developed delirium had a broader delta band and slightly more beta in the minute before eye opening. The authors suggest that PAED may be more related to the emergence course than to total exposure (cf. Hesse 2019 in adults).
  • The authors' own caveats: the effect on delirium was “marginal” relative to the large dose reduction; with a PAED threshold of 12 instead of 10 the difference was not significant, and an interim analysis means that p = 0.04 does not fully control the error rate (adjusted p = 0.03 with Lan-DeMets, 0.05 with O'Brien-Fleming). One anaesthetist with EEG training delivered all the anaesthetics, at Japan's largest children's hospital, so the result is not readily transferable. Awareness was not investigated with a structured interview; the maintenance concentration was about 1.4 × MAC-awake for the age group.
  • Conflicts of interest: Masimo provided Root, SedLine and paediatric sensors; Miyasaka and Nagasaka report non-financial support from Masimo, Nagasaka is a consultant for Masimo, and Brown receives royalties from Masimo. Masimo saw the manuscript without editorial rights.
  • Context in the app: supports that the indices cannot be used uncritically in children (images 1, 7 and 18 in the image quiz), and is the closest evidence for the hypothesis of dosing sevoflurane to the alpha pattern and no higher (the card on sevoflurane theta). Earlier RCTs with index-guided dosing (Frederick 2016, Long 2022, Han 2022) gave much smaller dose reductions.
Miyasaka et al. JAMA Pediatr 2025;179:704–712

Three case reports with EEG in children (Brandt 2020)

Narrative review with case reports from Purdon's group (Anesth Analg 2020;131:1043–1056). EEG was recorded observationally and not used to guide the anaesthetic.

  • 2 years, propofol for endoscopy and colonoscopy: at 100 µg/kg/min the spectrogram showed beta/gamma oscillations, as in sedated adults, and the child moved at the start of colonoscopy. After a bolus and 250 µg/kg/min the power shifted down to alpha and slow-delta, the same pattern as in unconscious adults, and the child lay still.
  • 9 months, isoflurane and nitrous oxide for ureteroureterostomy: from an unconscious state with slow-delta and a widened alpha/beta band (7–23 Hz), the 7–15 Hz power weakened and beta shifted upwards from minute 204; the child moved at minute 208, while the heart rate only changed at the movement. The EEG thus warned of emergence about 4–5 minutes before clinical signs. Propofol 40 mg and higher isoflurane then gave about 6 minutes of burst suppression with isoelectric periods and a MAP fall of 20 mmHg to 35 mmHg. The authors call this overcorrection.
  • 19 years with severe autism, propofol for sigmoidoscopy: after ketamine and midazolam as premedication, the EEG showed broad beta. Three minutes after starting propofol 350 µg/kg/min, burst suppression occurred with apnoea and SpO₂ 82%, followed by 12 minutes of isoelectric EEG despite reduction to 200 µg/kg/min, with stable haemodynamics and SpO₂ above 99%. The patient did not wake for over 2 hours. Autistic patients have twice the incidence of burst suppression at comparable doses (Walsh 2018), and valproate lowers anaesthetic requirements.
  • The authors' point: the patterns from adults (beta/gamma during sedation, alpha and slow-delta during unconsciousness, “unzipping” at emergence, burst suppression with overdosing) are also seen in children over about 1 year, with higher power. Indices are assumed to give too high values in adequately anaesthetised children, because beta and gamma are elevated, and raw EEG with spectrogram is proposed as an alternative.
  • Caveats: case reports, no control, and Purdon reports patents licensed to Masimo, speaker fees from Masimo and co-founding of PASCALL Systems.
Brandt et al. Anesth Analg 2020;131:1043–1056
This is a schematic model built on EEG signatures described in the literature, not real patient data. It shows qualitative patterns and is not suitable for clinical interpretation. Ketamine and dexmedetomidine are only described in younger adults in the sources, and for midazolam the sources do not describe age differences. Older patients, children and infants are therefore only available for propofol and sevoflurane.

Drugs: consciousness and amnesia

Different agents affect consciousness, recall, pain and movement to different degrees. The numbers below are population averages from the literature, with large individual variation. They are not dosing advice.

Basic concepts: receptors, ion channels and circuits
Miller's ch. 21 and 8 Purdon 2015 Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010

Each drug below has its own section on the micro level: which receptors the drug binds to, what happens in the nerve cell, and which circuits are affected. Much of this knowledge comes from animal experiments, cell studies and modelling, and the sources describe the mechanisms as probable, not fully mapped.

  • The GABAA receptor: a chloride channel made of five subunits. Chapter 21 states that the receptor is built from 18 or more different subunits, and that the α subunit exists in six variants (α1–α6). Many combinations occur in different parts of the brain. The binding sites lie at the interfaces between subunits, and the combination determines how well, for example, propofol, etomidate or pentobarbital binds.
  • When the channel opens: chloride flows in, the cell membrane is hyperpolarised, and the threshold for the nerve cell to fire rises. This is why the GABA system is called inhibitory (ch. 21).
  • Enhancing or activating: chapter 21 describes that propofol, barbiturates and etomidate at clinical concentrations enhance the action of GABA, so that less GABA is needed. At higher concentrations they can open the channel directly, without GABA. Benzodiazepines are described only as enhancers of the GABA response.
  • Synaptic and tonic inhibition: the hippocampus has many GABAA receptors with the α5 subunit, which is almost absent elsewhere in the cortex. They give sustained (tonic) inhibition of CA1 pyramidal cells and regulate long-term potentiation (LTP) with stimulation in the theta range (ch. 8). This is linked to amnesia, see etomidate and inhaled agents.
  • The NMDA receptor: a glutamate-gated ion channel. Ketamine is a channel blocker and works only when the channel is open (Purdon 2015).
  • α2 adrenoceptors: G-protein-coupled receptors. They inhibit adenylate cyclase and affect calcium and potassium channels (ch. 21).
  • The arousal centres: wakefulness is maintained by nuclei in the brainstem, hypothalamus and basal forebrain: locus coeruleus (noradrenaline), raphe (serotonin), tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine), ventral tegmental area (dopamine), basal forebrain and the laterodorsal and pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei (acetylcholine), and lateral hypothalamus (orexin). The preoptic area of the hypothalamus sends inhibitory GABA and galanin pathways to these centres. Purdon 2015 writes that activation of these pathways is thought to be a key part of how NREM sleep begins (Brown 2010, Purdon 2015).
  • From receptor to EEG: Purdon 2015 builds on the idea that EEG signatures arise because the drugs act on specific receptors in specific circuits. For propofol, thalamus and cortex, which are tightly connected, are described as not switching off when inhibited, but instead oscillating in rhythms such as alpha and beta.
  • Interactions as clues: Hendrickx 2008 uses interactions as hints about the site of action: additivity suggests a shared site, synergy different sites. See the card «Synergy between agents and isoelectric EEG».
Propofol
EEG signature (Purdon 2015) Miller's ch. 21
  • Consciousness: The concentration at which half do not respond to verbal command is given as 2.3–3.5 µg/ml when no other agents are given. In a volunteer study, half were unresponsive at BIS 63 and 95% at BIS 51.
  • Amnesia: 95% had no recall at BIS 77 in the same type of study (Glass 1997). Amnesia thus sets in at a lighter level of hypnosis than loss of response. Chapter 21 states that unstimulated volunteers needed an infusion of at least 2 mg/kg/h for amnesia.
  • Movement: The concentration that prevented movement at incision in half was 16 µg/ml without other agents, and markedly lower with opioid (ch. 21; ch. 36 gives at least 15). Aitkenhead (ch. 3) writes that muscle tone is reduced but movement in response to surgical stimulation may occur, and gives lower figures (see Discrepancies).
  • Awareness at induction: rapid redistribution and metabolism of propofol may increase the risk of awareness during intubation after a non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agent, or at the start of surgery, unless an inhaled agent or more propofol is given (Aitkenhead ch. 3).
  • EEG: Alpha-delta during maintenance. See the Spectrogram tab.
  • Time course: The half-time for equilibration between blood and EEG effect is about 2.5 minutes, and about 7 minutes for haemodynamic depression. Hypotension may increase some minutes after loss of consciousness.
  • Age: Chapter 21 states that patients aged 80 years or more need about half the dose of 20-year-olds. Chapter 16 states that the dose for 80-year-olds should be reduced by 65% (Schnider 1999). The numbers differ.

The BIS values are from healthy volunteers. Chapter 36 states that individual patients can become conscious at BIS values from 40 to 90.

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Binding site: the hypnotic effect is mainly mediated by the GABAA receptor, where propofol binds to the β subunit. Sites on β1, β2 and β3 in the part of the receptor that crosses the cell membrane are crucial, and the α and γ2 subunits also seem to contribute (ch. 21).
  • Two modes of action: indirectly, by enhancing GABA and shifting the concentration–response curve to the left, and at higher concentrations by direct activation of the channel (ch. 21).
  • Other targets: chapter 21 mentions widespread inhibition of NMDA receptors through modulation of sodium channel gating, action on GABAA and glycine receptors in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, increased dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (well-being), reduced serotonin in the area postrema (antiemetic) and inhibited release of acetylcholine in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. The α2 system seems to play an indirect role in sedation.
  • Circuits: in the cortex, propofol enhances the inhibition of pyramidal cells by inhibitory interneurons. In the thalamus, propofol enhances GABA inhibition in the reticular nucleus, which controls what the thalamus passes on to the cortex. Because thalamus and cortex are tightly connected, this produces oscillations in beta and alpha. Propofol also enhances the inhibitory GABA pathways from the preoptic area to the arousal centres. Less excitatory input from thalamus and brainstem hyperpolarises the cortex and gives slow-delta (Purdon 2015). Brown 2010 adds inhibited release of histamine from the tuberomammillary nucleus.
  • Bolus: after a bolus, slow-delta appears within seconds, together with loss of response, loss of the oculocephalic reflex, apnoea and atonia. Purdon interprets this as rapid action in the brainstem: cranial nerve nuclei III, IV and VI (eye movements), the respiratory centres in the medulla and pons (apnoea) and reticular nuclei in the pons and medulla (atonia).
  • Coherent alpha, incoherent slow waves: frontal alpha is highly coherent and may arise in circuits between thalamus and frontal cortex. The slow waves are not coherent, and recordings with electrodes in the cortex show that they bracket brief periods of firing. Purdon proposes that alpha prevents normal communication between thalamus and cortex, and that the slow waves prevent communication within the cortex.
  • Paradoxical excitation: Purdon 2015 describes two proposed mechanisms: GABAA-mediated inhibition of the inhibitory pathways from the globus pallidus to the thalamus, so that the thalamus drives the cortex more, and (from simulation studies) transient blockade of slow potassium currents in cortical nerve cells.
  • Memory (ch. 8): when we learn something new, the connections between nerve cells in the hippocampus become stronger and stay strong. This is called long-term potentiation (LTP) and is regarded as a cellular mechanism of learning. Propofol prevents such strengthening from getting started, but does not weaken strengthening that has already taken place. The opposite, connections becoming weaker (long-term depression, LTD), is not affected. The effect acts via the GABAA receptor, because it disappears when the receptor is blocked with picrotoxin. One study found that LTP was inhibited only at doses that produce anaesthesia, not at the lower doses that only cause memory loss. In addition, the cortex and hippocampus stop oscillating together in the theta rhythm (4–8 Hz), and this happens via one particular part of the GABAA receptor (the β3 subunit). In short: propofol prevents new connections from being strengthened, but does not weaken connections that were already strengthened. This fits with words learned before propofol being remembered normally in Veselis 2004, while words learned while propofol was acting were lost faster (interpretation based on the sources, see the card on Veselis 2004).
  • Physostigmine: Brown 2010 writes that propofol-induced unconsciousness has been reversed with physostigmine in clinical studies, which increases cholinergic activity throughout the cortex.
  • Seizures: chapter 21 describes that propofol can suppress seizures through GABA, NMDA inhibition and slow calcium channels, but that GABA agonism and glycine antagonism can also produce epileptiform changes, especially at induction and emergence.
Propofol and involuntary movements: dyskinesia and seizure-like phenomena
Walder 2002 San-juan 2010 Lee 2020 Bilotta 2006 Reddy 1993
  • What it is: Walder 2002 divided seizure-like phenomena with propofol into five groups: generalised tonic-clonic seizures, focal motor seizures, increased tone with twitching and rhythmic movements, opisthotonus (arched back) and involuntary movements. The first three most resemble epilepsy (as reported in San-juan 2010).
  • When it happens: Walder found 81 published cases. In 70 without known epilepsy, the phenomena came at induction (34%), at emergence (40%), delayed after anaesthesia (23%) and in only 2 during maintenance. Patients with epilepsy had them mostly at emergence (San-juan 2010). That it is rare during maintenance may be because neuromuscular blockade hides the movements (Kumar 2021).
  • How often: rare as a serious event. Movements at induction are more common: 5.5% in adults with propofol, versus 86.6% with etomidate (Reddy 1993). In children, 3 mg/kg gave spontaneous movements in 90%, versus 20% at 4 mg/kg (Borgeat 1997).
  • Bolus or infusion for sedation: during ERCP, 21% had involuntary movements with repeated boluses, versus 3.5% with continuous infusion. The authors link this to the peaks and troughs in concentration that boluses produce (Lee 2020).
  • Possible mechanisms: glycine antagonism in structures below the cortex, or enhanced GABA inhibition giving uncoordinated oscillations (San-juan 2010). Another explanation is an imbalance between acetylcholine and dopamine in the basal ganglia, triggered by a rapid change in propofol concentration (Jeon 2007). In the laboratory, propofol is mainly anticonvulsant but also has a weaker pro-convulsant effect (Voss 2015).
  • Parkinson's disease: patients operated on off levodopa developed dyskinesias resembling their levodopa dyskinesias (Krauss 1996). One patient had severe dyskinesia about 20 minutes after a small propofol dose (Nakajima 2022).
  • Prevention: lidocaine 2 mg/kg before propofol in 358 children gave movements in 2.5% versus 29% with saline, but more coughing (62.5 versus 17.5%) (Bilotta 2006). Fentanyl 1.5 µg/kg gave fewer excitatory events (1 of 32 versus 13 of 32) (Middle East J Anesthesiol 1996). Continuous infusion instead of boluses for sedation (Lee 2020).
  • Treatment: in the case reports it most often resolves on its own, over a few hours to 21 days (Tam 2009). Benzodiazepines have had variable effect.
  • EEG: of 24 patients who had an EEG after the episode, 5 were abnormal (Walder, as reported in San-juan 2010). Reddy 1993 found no seizure activity with propofol. But a normal scalp EEG does not exclude epileptic activity deeper in the brain (Voss 2015), and in one patient polyspike-and-wave complexes coincided with the jerks (Jeon 2007).
  • For monitoring (interpretation based on the sources): the movements cause muscle artefact that raises the index and can look as if the patient is light. Look at the raw EEG and the patient. For prolonged, recurrent or delayed episodes, or known epilepsy, a full EEG should be considered.
Midazolam (benzodiazepines)
Miller's ch. 21 and 8
  • Concentration: Plasma levels for hypnosis and amnesia during surgery are given as 100–200 ng/ml, and awakening usually occurs below 50 ng/ml.
  • Amnesia: Anterograde. Retrograde memory is not affected. Amnesia after an anaesthetic dose lasts about 1–2 hours.
  • Sedation without recall: Patients can appear awake and coherent during benzodiazepine sedation and still not remember the procedure. This is scenario 1 in the Components tab.
  • Reversal: Flumazenil usually reverses the hypnotic and respiratory effects more than the amnestic ones. This is a pharmacological example of how amnesia and sedation can be separated.
  • Mechanism: Chapter 21 links sedation and anterograde amnesia to GABA-A receptors with the α1 subunit. Chapter 8 describes that amnesia for etomidate in mice is linked to α5 subunits. These concern different agents and are not necessarily contradictions.
  • Age: Older patients need less (Jacobs 1995).
  • High dose or poisoning: Sutter and Kaplan 2012 describe “beta coma” (12–16 Hz, mostly frontal, mixed with spindle-like activity, alpha or delta) in poisoning with and withdrawal from benzodiazepines and barbiturates. It is largely reversible with a good prognosis. Alpha coma and spindle coma can also be seen in poisoning. See the simulator in the Spectrogram tab and the alpha coma case in the Intensive care tab.
  • EEG: midazolam at sedative doses is associated with beta oscillations (Brandt 2020), so the beta picture can resemble ketamine. Brandt describes a child who received ketamine and midazolam as premedication and had beta and gamma at the start, and the authors think this probably reflects both drugs together. What the EEG looks like at higher doses of midazolam is not described in the sources in the app.

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Binding site: benzodiazepines act selectively at the GABAA receptor and enhance the response to GABA by facilitating opening of the chloride channel, resulting in hyperpolarisation (ch. 21). Hendrickx 2008 distinguishes the benzodiazepine site from the site where propofol, barbiturates and etomidate act.
  • Subunits and effects: α1 is linked to sedation, anterograde amnesia and anticonvulsant effect, α2 to anxiolysis and muscle relaxation. α2 and α3 are linked to the rewarding effects and thus addiction (ch. 21).
  • Where the receptors are: highest density in the olfactory bulb, cerebral cortex, cerebellum, hippocampus, substantia nigra and inferior colliculus, lower in the striatum, lower brainstem and spinal cord (ch. 21).
  • Potency: affinity is lorazepam > midazolam > diazepam. Midazolam is about 3–6 and lorazepam 5–10 times as potent as diazepam (ch. 21).
  • Ceiling: midazolam alone cannot fully abolish movement to noxious stimuli, whereas propofol alone can. Hendrickx 2008 uses this as one argument that propofol and midazolam act differently, even though both act through GABAA, and that the combination is therefore synergistic.
  • Flumazenil and receptor occupancy: flumazenil is a competitive antagonist with high affinity and almost no intrinsic effect. Its effect depends on what fraction of the receptors the agonist occupies. After a very high agonist dose, a small dose of flumazenil attenuates the deep CNS depression (unconsciousness, respiratory depression) without reducing the effects that need only low receptor occupancy (drowsiness, amnesia). Large doses of flumazenil with little agonist reverse everything. Flumazenil is cleared rapidly, so sedation can return (ch. 21).
  • Remimazolam: resembles midazolam and binds selectively to the benzodiazepine site. A carboxylic ester side chain is rapidly broken down by tissue esterases to an inactive metabolite (CNS7054), not via CYP. Clearance is about 70 l/h, and chapter 21 states that long infusions do not cause accumulation. Pharmacokinetics were unchanged in end-stage renal failure, but caution is advised in hepatic failure, and lower doses should be considered in the frail elderly. Flumazenil reverses it in about 1 minute (10.5 minutes with placebo) without resedation. For endoscopy, sedation success was comparable to propofol and better than midazolam (ch. 21).
  • Remimazolam and EEG (Kim 2024): randomised substudy, 52 patients over 65, induction with remimazolam 6 mg/kg/h or propofol TCI 3.5 µg/ml, both with remifentanil. Remimazolam produced alpha and delta during induction, and there were no significant differences in spectral power or BIS between the drugs. Both produced alpha anteriorisation and reduced frontal-to-parietal feedback connectivity. Maintenance and emergence were not measured, and no patient had burst suppression. The study was partly funded by the pharmaceutical company Hana Pharmaceutical, which according to the article had no role in the analysis. Interpretation based on the sources: that remimazolam produced alpha and delta, whereas Brandt 2020 links midazolam to beta, may reflect dose (anaesthesia vs sedation) and is not necessarily a difference between the drugs.
Propofol and midazolam: alone, together and in withdrawal
Miller's ch. 21 and 16 Hendrickx 2008 Olsen and Liang 2017 Lorentzen 2014 Shah 2018 Zhou 2014
  • Midazolam alone: binds the benzodiazepine site on the GABAA receptor and enhances the response to GABA by facilitating chloride channel opening (ch. 21). It therefore needs GABA to work, and its effect has a ceiling: midazolam alone cannot fully abolish movement to noxious stimuli (Hendrickx 2008).
  • Propofol alone: binds the β subunit, a different site. At clinical concentrations propofol enhances GABA; at higher concentrations it can open the channel directly, without GABA. Chapter 21 also describes inhibition of NMDA receptors.
  • Together, at the receptor: because the drugs bind different sites, the studies in Hendrickx 2008 found synergy for hypnosis (Short and Chui 1991, McClune 1992, Short 1992), and chapter 21 states that midazolam often acts synergistically with other hypnotics. Chapter 16 instead calls the interaction «primarily additive», see Discrepancies.
  • Together, in the blood: a sedative midazolam concentration (200 ng/ml) raises propofol concentration by about 25 %, probably via altered circulation and hepatic perfusion. Propofol raises midazolam concentration by 27 %. Propofol also inhibits CYP3A4 (about 37 % lower activity at 3 µg/ml), which metabolises midazolam (ch. 21). Interpretation based on the sources: both synergy and higher concentrations point towards lower dose requirements when the drugs are given together.
  • Why combine in the ICU: chapter 21 lists amnesia and haemodynamic stability as advantages of benzodiazepines, and accumulation (active metabolite, especially in renal failure) and more delirium than with dexmedetomidine as drawbacks. Propofol gives fast awakening but more hypotension. In Zhou 2014 (randomised, open-label, single centre, n=124 ventilated patients) time to extubation was 45 hours with midazolam alone, 3 hours with propofol alone and 2 hours when midazolam was switched to propofol before waking. Hypotension: 23 %, 52 % and 21 %. Agitation after stopping: 49 % with midazolam alone vs 19 % after switching. The authors suggest propofol may mask midazolam withdrawal. Note that this was switching, not simultaneous use, and that patients with alcoholism were excluded.

Micro level: why benzodiazepines can fail in alcohol withdrawal

  • Alcohol acts on two systems: it enhances GABAA and inhibits NMDA. With chronic use GABAA function weakens, and when alcohol is withdrawn the NMDA system is left unopposed (Lorentzen 2014, Shah 2018).
  • The receptors are remodelled (rat): Olsen and Liang 2017 describe a «subunit switch» after repeated alcohol exposure: extrasynaptic δ-containing receptors (tonic inhibition) and α1 are down-regulated, while α4, γ2 and α2 are up-regulated. The rats became tolerant to the sedative effect of alcohol, benzodiazepines and neurosteroids, while anticonvulsant and anxiolytic effects showed little tolerance. After repeated cycles the changes lasted at least 120 days. The authors extend this to humans as a hypothesis.
  • The clinicians' explanation: Lorentzen 2014 and Shah 2018 explain benzodiazepine resistance by «saturation» of GABAA receptors and by benzodiazepines having no effect on the overactive NMDA system.
  • What propofol adds: Lorentzen 2014 writes that propofol has a «dual effect»: GABAA via a different site and NMDA inhibition. Interpretation based on the sources: since propofol at higher concentrations can open the channel without GABA, it is biologically plausible that it works where benzodiazepines have reached their ceiling. This is not tested in the sources.
  • Lorentzen 2014: retrospective, n=15 with delirium tremens refractory to up to 2000 mg benzodiazepines. Propofol a mean 4.22 mg/kg/h over 48 hours (max 5.65), RASS −4 to −5, ventilated. 12 of 15 were treated successfully, 7 of 15 developed pneumonia, none developed propofol infusion syndrome, and mean ICU stay was 4.67 days.
  • Ketamine as an alternative (Shah 2018): retrospective, n=30 with benzodiazepine-resistant withdrawal (more than 40 mg diazepam per hour). Ketamine blocks NMDA directly. Lorazepam requirement fell by 4 mg/h at 24 hours, but 73 % were intubated.
  • Caveats: the studies are small, retrospective and uncontrolled. Deep sedation with propofol requires a secured airway. The sources in the app concern alcohol withdrawal; other poisonings (mixed overdose, stimulants, GHB) are not covered. EEG in benzodiazepine poisoning and withdrawal (beta coma) is described in the midazolam card.
Ketamine in refractory status epilepticus: when GABAergic drugs lose their grip
Espinosa 2023 Gaspard 2013
  • What happens at the receptor: after a few minutes of continuous seizures, GABAA receptors move from the cell surface into the cell («internalisation»), while more glutamate and NMDA receptors move out to the surface («externalisation»). Inhibition weakens and excitation increases. This has been shown in animal models (Espinosa 2023).
  • The consequence: resistance to benzodiazepines rises quickly the longer the seizure lasts. It is not GABA that is missing, but the receptors the drugs act on. Gaspard 2013 writes that sensitivity to GABA agonists declines with prolonged seizures, whereas sensitivity to NMDA antagonists does not.
  • Why ketamine: ketamine blocks the NMDA receptor and so targets the part of the system that is up-regulated. It causes little respiratory or cardiovascular depression (Gaspard 2013).
  • Gaspard 2013: retrospective study from ten centres, 58 patients (60 episodes, median age 24, seven after anoxic brain injury), almost all with continuous video-EEG. Loading dose median 1.5 mg/kg, infusion median 2.75 mg/kg/h (up to 10), started a median 9 days after onset and always with other drugs. Permanent seizure control in 57 %, likely ketamine response in 12 % and possible response in 20 %. Likely responses required at least 0.9 mg/kg/h and were not seen when ketamine was started 8 days or more after onset, or after 7 or more failed drugs. Mortality was 43 %, but 16 % when seizures were controlled within 24 hours of ketamine vs 56 % otherwise. ICP did not rise in monitored patients, except two with anoxic cerebral oedema.
  • Espinosa 2023 (scoping review): about 20 publications, mostly case reports and small series. Loading doses 0.5–5 mg/kg and infusions 0.05–10.5 mg/kg/h. Of 19 case reports, 63 % achieved complete seizure control, usually within 12 hours, but seizures recurred in 10–60 % after withdrawal. Adverse effects were arrhythmias, cardiovascular collapse and metabolic acidosis, with unclear causality in patients on many drugs. The authors consider the evidence insufficient for ketamine as first choice or monotherapy.
  • Link to withdrawal: interpretation based on the sources: the pattern resembles that described in alcohol withdrawal (the propofol and midazolam card above), where GABAA function is weakened and the NMDA system overactive, and where ketamine and propofol are used when benzodiazepines fail.
  • EEG: continuous EEG is used to guide treatment and to detect non-convulsive seizures (Intensive care tab). Ketamine produces a more activated EEG with beta and gamma and does not cause classic burst suppression at clinical doses (see the ketamine card). Interpretation based on the sources: the treatment target should therefore be judged on the raw EEG.
  • Caveats: no randomised trials. Gaspard 2013 is retrospective and biased towards only the most severe cases receiving ketamine. Several authors disclose ties to the pharmaceutical industry (including UCB, GSK and Pfizer). Espinosa 2023 reports no conflicts of interest.
Ketamine
EEG “gamma burst” (Akeju, 12 patients) Miller's ch. 21 and 10
  • State: Dissociative anaesthesia, not sleep-like. The patient may have open eyes and some protective reflexes. The chapter warns against assuming that the reflexes are protective.
  • Concentration: Minimum 0.6–2 µg/ml for general anaesthesia. The pain threshold is raised at 0.1 µg/ml or more, that is, far below the level for unconsciousness.
  • Amnesia: No recall of surgery, but the amnesia is less pronounced than with benzodiazepines.
  • Brain metabolism: Increases CMRO₂ and blood flow (ch. 10 and 21).
  • EEG: Chapter 21 describes generalised theta activity in the EEG and seizure-like (petit mal) activity in the hippocampus, and does not mention gamma or slow-delta. Akeju describes alternating slow-delta and gamma, together with increased theta. Theta appears in both, so the descriptions differ in scope rather than conflict.

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Main target: blockade of the NMDA receptor. Ketamine is a channel blocker, so the channel has to be open for ketamine to act (Purdon 2015).
  • Interneurons first: NMDA channels on inhibitory interneurons are generally more active than those on pyramidal cells. At low to moderate doses ketamine therefore mainly affects the interneurons, and the pyramidal cells become less inhibited. Purdon 2015 uses this to explain increased metabolism, and that cortex, hippocampus and amygdala keep communicating but without coordination in time and space: hallucinations, dissociation, euphoria and dysphoria. At higher doses the NMDA receptors on the excitatory nerve cells are also blocked, and consciousness is lost. Brown 2010 describes the same.
  • Dopamine: the hallucinations are probably enhanced by disrupted dopamine transmission in the prefrontal cortex, partly due to increased glutamate activity at glutamate receptors other than NMDA (Purdon 2015).
  • Other receptors: opioid receptors and monoaminergic receptors. At high concentrations sigma receptors are also affected, muscarinic receptors are blocked and GABA transmission is facilitated. S(+)-ketamine has some μ-opioid activity, and experiments in μ-knockout mice suggest that the μ system contributes to respiratory depression and supraspinal antinociception (ch. 21). Chapter 8 describes increased activity in the locus coeruleus, which appears to contribute to the anaesthetic effect.
  • Analgesia: chapter 21 links the spinal analgesia to inhibition of wide dynamic range neurons in the dorsal horn, and describes that ketamine inhibits central sensitisation and opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Purdon 2015 places the analgesia at «the dorsal root ganglia, the first synapse of the pain pathway in the spinal cord».
  • Circuits: chapter 21 describes that ketamine depresses parts of the cortex (especially association areas) and thalamus, but stimulates limbic areas including the hippocampus, and calls this a functional disorganisation. Chapter 8 writes that many anaesthetics reduce metabolism in the thalamus, with ketamine as the exception.
  • To the EEG: the active EEG fits with the disinhibition. At a low dose given alone, Purdon describes beta–gamma at about 25–32 Hz. No specific antagonist reverses all the effects of ketamine (ch. 21).
  • The HCN1 channel (Tian 2023): ketamine also inhibits HCN1, a channel activated by hyperpolarisation that is important for rhythmic activity. Mice lacking HCN1 do not lose the righting reflex with ketamine, and propofol also inhibits HCN1. Tian proposes that frontal gamma results from NMDA-mediated disinhibition (counteracted by the GABA effect of propofol), while the shared HCN1 inhibition may explain why occipital alpha falls further when propofol is added. See the card in the Components tab.
  • Communication in the cortex (Schroeder 2016): in monkeys under ketamine, sensory information reached the primary somatosensory cortex but did not pass on to the motor cortex, and the directed coupling between neurons in the two areas fell.
Dexmedetomidine
EEG (Akeju 2016, 8 volunteers) Miller's ch. 21 and 8
  • State: Patients can be roused and follow commands, and fall asleep when not stimulated. The pattern resembles natural NREM sleep.
  • Concentration: Rousable sedation at about 0.2–0.3 ng/ml and unrousable deep sedation above about 1.9 ng/ml (Ebert 2000).
  • Recall: Chapter 21 cites an ICU study in which patients on dexmedetomidine remembered more of their stay than patients on propofol. Chapter 8 describes failure of encoding in an experimental low-dose study. The findings are not directly comparable.
  • Hysteresis: Chapter 36 says that dexmedetomidine increases neural inertia.

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Receptor: α2 agonist at G-protein-coupled α2 adrenoceptors. Inside the cell, adenylate cyclase is inhibited, L- and P-type calcium channels are inhibited, and calcium-activated potassium channels conduct more easily (ch. 21).
  • Subtypes: α2A, α2B and α2C. Chapter 21 writes that α2A is mainly peripheral and α2B and α2C are in the brain and spinal cord, and links analgesia in the dorsal horn to α2C and α2A. Chapter 8 cites that removing α2A receptors from the locus coeruleus in rodents prevents dexmedetomidine-induced loss of righting reflex (see Discrepancies in the Sources tab).
  • Circuit: dexmedetomidine binds presynaptically on nerve cells from the locus coeruleus and hyperpolarises them, so that less noradrenaline is released. This removes the inhibition of the preoptic area, and the preoptic area inhibits the arousal centres with GABA and galanin, including histamine release from the tuberomammillary nucleus. In addition, the noradrenaline supply to the basal forebrain, the intralaminar thalamic nuclei and the cortex is lost (Purdon 2015, ch. 21).
  • Animal experiments: microinjection of dexmedetomidine into the locus coeruleus lowers the level of consciousness, and this is prevented by the α2 antagonist atipamezole. Mice that cannot make noradrenaline are hypersensitive to dexmedetomidine, suggesting that other mechanisms also exist (ch. 8).
  • To the EEG: the spindles (9–15 Hz) probably arise, like propofol frontal alpha and sleep spindles, in loops between thalamus and cortex, but they are brief and episodic. Slow-delta arises because the cortex receives less excitatory input. Both spindles and slow waves are smaller than under propofol. Purdon interprets this as less disruption of nerve cell activity, and as a possible explanation for why the patient can be roused.
  • Cognition: chapter 21 mentions data suggesting that reduced expression of α5-GABAA receptors after anaesthesia may contribute to better preserved cognition with dexmedetomidine.
  • Reversal: the α2 antagonist atipamezole reverses the effect, but is not approved for humans (ch. 21).
  • α2A in the locus coeruleus (Mizobe 1996): in rats, antisense against α2A in the locus coeruleus delayed and shortened loss of righting reflex after dexmedetomidine, while antisense against α2C had no effect. See the card below and Discrepancies.
  • Thalamus (Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014): during dexmedetomidine-induced loss of consciousness, coupling between cortical areas was preserved, while coupling between the thalamus and the default mode network was disrupted. See the card below.
  • Spindles (Huupponen 2008): spindles during deep dexmedetomidine sedation had the same density, amplitude and frequency as spindles in normal NREM 2 sleep, but lasted longer. See the card below.
Clonidine
Miller's ch. 21, 10 and 22 Hendrickx 2008 Hight 2020 Giovannitti 2015 Zhang 2021
  • What it is: an α2 agonist like dexmedetomidine, but less selective. The ratio of α2 to α1 binding is about 220:1, versus 1600:1 for dexmedetomidine (ch. 21). Chapter 10 describes clonidine as significantly less specific and less potent.
  • Background: experience with patients taking clonidine showed that α2 agonists could be used in anaesthesia, and one study found lower halothane MAC in such patients. This led to the development of dexmedetomidine (ch. 21).
  • MAC: clonidine reduced the MAC of isoflurane by about 30% and of sevoflurane by 17–34%, and MAC-awake by 30% (isoflurane) and 17–21% (sevoflurane) in humans. In children, doubling the dose did not further reduce sevoflurane MAC-awake. Clonidine alone does not produce immobility at clinically used doses, so the effect has a ceiling (Hendrickx 2008).
  • Interactions: propofol and clonidine were additive for hypnosis in humans. Midazolam and clonidine were synergistic in rats, and fentanyl and clonidine produced hypnosis together in animals even though neither did alone (Hendrickx 2008). Chapter 21 writes that the infusion dose of clonidine, among others, should be reduced when combined with propofol.
  • Respiration and opioids: clonidine does not enhance the respiratory depression from fentanyl and other opioids. Intravenous clonidine abolished the sympathetic activation from μ blockade in opioid-dependent patients, and α2 agonists can suppress fentanyl cough (ch. 22).
  • EEG: dexmedetomidine and other α2 agonists such as clonidine produce a slow-wave-dominant EEG with intermittent spindles, sharing features with sleep stages 2 and 3 (Hight 2020). Hight also lists clonidine among the conditions in which hysteresis is more marked, and urges caution when lowering the inhaled agent concentration below that needed for unconsciousness.
  • EEG when clonidine is added to propofol or a volatile agent: more hypnosis or just a different EEG? The question was raised by the author of the app. The sources give a split answer.
    • Part of the effect is real hypnosis: propofol and clonidine were additive for hypnosis in humans, and clonidine lowered MAC-awake for sevoflurane by 17–21 % (Hendrickx 2008). Chapter 21 recommends a lower infusion dose when clonidine is combined with propofol.
    • The EEG change in combination: no study of clonidine plus propofol or volatile agent with spectral analysis was found. For dexmedetomidine, Zhang 2021 (21 patients under propofol) found that the alpha peak fell (about 3 to 1.5 dB, but the confidence interval crossed zero), delta–theta rose from 4.5 to 7.7 dB, and PSI fell from 30 to 23. The authors interpret this as deeper anaesthesia, but consciousness was not tested, because the patients were already unconscious.
    • Slow waves from α2 agonists do not mean the same as from propofol: under dexmedetomidine alone the patient can be roused even though the EEG is dominated by slow waves and spindles (Purdon 2015 Part I; see dexmedetomidine).
    • Ceiling: doubling the clonidine dose gave no further fall in MAC-awake for sevoflurane in children (Hendrickx 2008).
    • Interpretation based on the sources: the answer is probably both. Part of the alpha loss and delta increase reflects a real, additive hypnotic effect, and the propofol or volatile dose can then be reduced somewhat. But increased delta after clonidine should not be read as just as much deeper hypnosis as the same change after more propofol, and the hypnotic should not be reduced just because the index falls. Hight 2020 warns against lowering the volatile agent below what is needed for unconsciousness when clonidine has been given. Remember also that alpha loss can have other causes, such as nociception (García 2021).
  • Clinical use and pharmacokinetics (Giovannitti 2015): clonidine is the original α2 agonist and is used mostly for hypertension, but also for anxiety, ADHD, chronic pain, withdrawal and postoperative shivering. The half-life is 12–16 hours. About 50% is metabolised in the liver, and 40–60% is excreted unchanged in the urine.
  • Blood pressure: at initiation, blood pressure may rise transiently because peripheral postjunctional α1 receptors are stimulated. Abrupt withdrawal after long-term use can cause rebound hypertension up to 20 hours after the last dose, and an early case report described a hypertensive crisis when one dose was withheld before anaesthesia (Giovannitti 2015).
  • Premedication: the review writes that clonidine improves mask acceptance at induction in children and reduces anaesthetic requirements by 40–60% (see Discrepancies). In a study of 45 children (2–8 years), oral clonidine gave better sedation, separation and mask acceptance and less shivering than midazolam, but onset was slower (60 vs 30 minutes).

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Receptor: clonidine acts at α2 adrenoceptors, which are G-protein-coupled and inhibit adenylate cyclase (see dexmedetomidine). The sources here describe the circuit mechanism (locus coeruleus and preoptic area) for dexmedetomidine, not specifically for clonidine.
  • Imidazoline receptors: clonidine and dexmedetomidine both belong to the imidazole subclass (ch. 21). Mizobe 1996 writes that the clinically available α2 agonists have an imidazole ring that also activates imidazoline binding sites, that they do not discriminate between α2 subtypes, and that bradycardia may partly be due to imidazoline receptors in the brainstem.
  • Neuroprotection in animals: clonidine lowered plasma catecholamines and improved outcome after incomplete ischaemia in rats (ch. 10).
  • Signalling pathway (Giovannitti 2015): all three α2 subtypes inhibit adenylate cyclase. In the locus coeruleus, lower cAMP leads to potassium efflux through calcium-activated channels, calcium cannot enter the nerve terminal, and firing is suppressed. Less noradrenaline and less activity in the ascending noradrenergic pathways give hypnosis and sedation. The same negative feedback lowers heart rate and blood pressure and dampens the stress response.
  • Subtypes: α2A and α2C are found mainly in the central nervous system and probably account for sedation, analgesia and sympatholysis, while α2B is found mostly on vascular smooth muscle and causes vasoconstriction (Giovannitti 2015).
  • Analgesia: α2 receptors in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord inhibit nociceptive neurons and reduce substance P release. The review writes that the spinal mechanism accounts for most of the analgesia, although there is also evidence for supraspinal and peripheral sites.
Dexmedetomidine and clonidine compared
Miller's ch. 8, 10 and 21 Giovannitti 2015 Hendrickx 2008 Walsh 2025 (A2B)

Both are α2 agonists (they stimulate the receptor); atipamezole is an example of an α2 antagonist. Even so, they are quite different.

  • Selectivity: dexmedetomidine binds α2 over α1 in a ratio of about 1600:1, clonidine about 220:1 (ch. 21). Chapter 10 describes clonidine as considerably less specific and less potent. Clonidine's α1 effect can cause a transient rise in blood pressure at the start (Giovannitti 2015).
  • Locus coeruleus: both act via α2 receptors, including in the locus coeruleus. Dexmedetomidine being “more specific” refers to the receptor type (α2 over α1), not the brain region. The animal studies linking loss of consciousness to α2A receptors in the locus coeruleus were done with dexmedetomidine (ch. 8, Mizobe 1996). The sources do not describe a separate circuit mechanism for clonidine.
  • Imidazoline: both have an imidazole ring and can also activate imidazoline binding sites, which may contribute to bradycardia (ch. 21, Mizobe 1996).
  • Duration: clonidine has a half-life of 12–16 hours (Giovannitti 2015). The A2B protocol gives about 13 hours for clonidine and about 2 hours for dexmedetomidine. Clonidine is therefore harder to titrate and takes longer to wear off.
  • Hypnosis and MAC: clonidine lowers MAC-awake for sevoflurane by 17–21 % and has a ceiling, while dexmedetomidine gives rousable sedation at 0.2–0.3 ng/ml and non-rousable sedation above about 1.9 ng/ml (Hendrickx 2008, Ebert 2000).
  • EEG: both give a sleep-like pattern with slow waves and spindles (Hight 2020). Spectral studies exist for dexmedetomidine (Akeju, Purdon, Huupponen), but not for clonidine in the sources the app has.
  • In intensive care (A2B, Walsh 2025): neither gave faster extubation than propofol. Both caused more agitation (RR 1.54 and 1.55) and more severe bradycardia (RR 1.62 and 1.58). Clonidine is not licensed for ICU sedation in the UK, but is much cheaper.
Dexmedetomidine in children: maturation, circulation and pallor
Chrysostomou 2014 Morse 2020 Janse van Rensburg 2025 Potts 2010 Yuen 2008, 2010
  • Newborns break down dexmedetomidine more slowly: preterm infants had a clearance of 0.3 L/h/kg and a half-life of 7.6 hours, term infants 0.9 L/h/kg and 3.2 hours (Chrysostomou 2014). Term newborns have about 42% of adult clearance, and by 3 years it is about 80% (Morse 2020). The half-life is about 2.3 hours under 2 years and 1.6 hours at 2–11 years (Janse van Rensburg 2025).
  • Why: dexmedetomidine is broken down in the liver, partly via CYP2A6 and partly by direct glucuronidation (Precedex prescribing information; Janse van Rensburg 2025 names UGT1A4 and UGT2B10). These enzyme systems are not fully developed at birth. On cardiopulmonary bypass, clearance falls by about 95% (Janse van Rensburg 2025).
  • Intranasal premedication: 2–3 µg/kg, with onset after 20–30 minutes (Janse van Rensburg 2025). Yuen 2010 found onset after about 25 minutes and a duration of about 85 minutes. In Yuen 2008, 0.5 and 1 µg/kg gave more sedation at separation from the parents than midazolam.
  • Blood pressure and heart rate: a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found that intranasal dexmedetomidine lowered systolic blood pressure by 6.7 mmHg and heart rate by 6.8 beats/min compared with control (Can J Anesth 2017). A review reports hypotension and bradycardia in 10–20% and transient hypertension via peripheral α2B receptors (JPPT 2010).
  • Two opposite effects on the vessels: in children, Potts 2010 found a blood-pressure-lowering effect at low concentrations (half effect at 0.10 µg/L, maximum −12.3 mmHg) and a blood-pressure-raising effect at higher ones (half effect at 1.1 µg/L, maximum +50.3 mmHg). Above about 1 µg/L, mean arterial pressure rose about 20%. The raising effect comes from peripheral vasoconstriction.
  • Pallor: no peer-reviewed source was found that describes pallor as a side effect of intranasal dexmedetomidine in children. The closest is a case report of local vasoconstriction in a newborn after a block with dexmedetomidine (Guensch 2023, only the title was read). A possible explanation is that α2B receptors in skin vessels constrict, while a lower heart rate gives a lower cardiac output. This is an interpretation based on the sources, not a documented explanation. In practice: check heart rate, blood pressure and capillary refill. If the circulation is otherwise good, the pallor is probably harmless, but that is not documented either.
  • Noradrenaline and the developing brain: no studies were found that link the maturation of the locus coeruleus or the noradrenaline system in children to how sensitive they are to dexmedetomidine. The experiment with mice lacking noradrenaline concerns genetically modified animals and cannot be transferred directly. In 7-day-old rats, dexmedetomidine was not neurotoxic and reduced cell death from isoflurane (Sanders 2009), but long-term outcome data in children are lacking.
  • EEG in children: Mason 2012 recorded EEG in 107 children given intramuscular dexmedetomidine: 55 reached N3 and 51 N2, a sleep-like pattern. Spindles are not synchronous in infants: at 3 months it is normal to lack spindles, and they become synchronous around 2 years of age (Yune 2026). Missing spindles under dexmedetomidine in an infant are therefore not a sign that the drug acts differently (interpretation based on the sources).
Thiopental and etomidate
Miller's ch. 21 and 10
  • Thiopental: The amnesia is less pronounced than with benzodiazepines. When the EEG becomes isoelectric, brain metabolism is according to chapter 21 about 50% of baseline.
  • Etomidate: At 0.2–0.3 mg/kg, CBF falls by 34% and CMRO₂ by 45% without change in mean arterial pressure.

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Barbiturates: the GABAA receptor is the only proven site of barbiturate anaesthesia. At low concentrations barbiturates slow the dissociation of GABA from the receptor and prolong channel openings, which probably gives sedation and hypnosis. At higher concentrations they open the channel without GABA, which may explain the anaesthesia itself. They also inhibit excitatory transmission (glutamate, acetylcholine), and thiopental reduced glutamate levels and NMDA currents in rat prefrontal cortex (ch. 21).
  • Metabolism and function: CMRO₂ falls to about 50% when the EEG becomes isoelectric, and no further. Barbiturates reduce the energy used for signalling, not the energy used to keep cells alive. Only hypothermia can reduce that (ch. 21).
  • Etomidate: acts almost exclusively through GABAA: positive modulation at clinical concentrations and direct activation at higher concentrations. Chapter 21 describes two independent binding sites on the α1β2γ2 receptor that contribute equally.
  • Etomidate and amnesia: in mice, etomidate blocks LTP in CA1, but not in mice lacking the α5 subunit. These mice are resistant to the amnesia but not to the anaesthesia, and the effect is reversed by an α5-selective drug with the opposite action (inverse agonist, L-655,708). The β3 subunit does not appear to be involved in the amnesia from etomidate (ch. 8). Amnesia and hypnosis can thus run through different receptor variants.
  • Seizure foci: etomidate increases EEG activity in epileptogenic foci and has been used for mapping before epilepsy surgery (ch. 21).
Inhaled agents (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane)
Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 Purdon 2015 Miller's ch. 8 and 22 Hendrickx 2008
  • MAC: the alveolar concentration that prevents movement at surgical incision in half of patients. MAC is only one point on the concentration–response curve (equivalent to the EC50). About 1.3 MAC prevents movement in about 95% (Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8).
  • MAC values: for 30–55-year-olds, Morgan and Mikhail give about 2.0% for sevoflurane, 1.2% for isoflurane and 6.0% for desflurane.
  • Emergence: 0.3–0.4 MAC is associated with awakening (MAC-awake) when the inhaled agent is the only anaesthetic (Morgan and Mikhail).
  • Combinations: MAC values for combinations are roughly additive, for example 0.5 MAC nitrous oxide and 0.5 MAC isoflurane give the same effect as 1.0 MAC isoflurane (Morgan and Mikhail). Hendrickx 2008 found no synergy between two inhaled agents, but usually synergy with intravenous agents. Opioids reduce MAC, but with a ceiling (ch. 22).
  • Age: MAC falls about 6% per decade, regardless of agent (Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8). Chapter 43 of the same book gives a different figure (see Discrepancies).
  • Uptake and elimination: the effect depends on the brain concentration reaching a therapeutic level, and it follows the alveolar concentration. Low solubility in blood and tissues makes desflurane give very rapid induction and emergence (Morgan and Mikhail).
  • EEG: below MAC, sevoflurane gives strong alpha and slow-delta resembling propofol. At MAC and above, a theta oscillation fills in between slow-delta and alpha, and when the concentration is lowered, theta disappears first. At emergence, alpha gives way to lower-amplitude beta and gamma, like a zipper opening. Isoflurane and desflurane give the same pattern, and high doses give burst suppression (Purdon 2015). See the Spectrogram tab.

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Many targets: Purdon 2015 lists enhanced GABAA inhibition, blockade of two-pore potassium channels and HCN channels, and inhibited glutamate release via NMDA receptors. Morgan and Mikhail also mention the glycine receptor α1 subunit, which the inhaled agents enhance, and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. They write that no obligatory site of action has been identified.
  • Meyer–Overton: potency correlates with lipid solubility, which once supported a shared mechanism for all inhaled agents. The correlation is only approximate (Morgan and Mikhail).
  • Immobility in the spinal cord: MAC is unchanged after spinal cord transection in rats (Morgan and Mikhail; see Discrepancies and the Jinks 2010 card in the Components tab), and Purdon writes that the muscle-relaxing effect results from action on receptors and channels in the spinal cord. Hendrickx 2008 found no synergy between any two inhaled agents for MAC and interprets this as a shared site for immobility despite different receptor effects.
  • Circuits: noradrenergic nerve cells in the locus coeruleus modulate isoflurane anaesthesia and emergence from it. In the pontine reticular formation, lower GABA levels are linked to isoflurane-induced unconsciousness, an example that GABA does not always inhibit wakefulness (ch. 8).
  • Memory: isoflurane and sevoflurane inhibit LTP in the hippocampus, and the effect is abolished by GABAA antagonists. For isoflurane, the α4β2 nicotinic receptor is also implicated. Low, amnestic concentrations enhance tonic inhibition through α5 receptors. Mice lacking α4, or lacking β3 in the forebrain, are resistant to the amnesia from isoflurane, while α1 and α2 do not appear to be involved. Mice lacking HCN1 channels are resistant to the amnesia from sevoflurane. In rodents, impaired memory 24–48 hours after isoflurane appears to be mediated by α5 (ch. 8).
  • To the EEG: below MAC, sevoflurane gives alpha and slow-delta resembling propofol, which Purdon interprets as GABA enhancement being the main mechanism. Theta at MAC and above may, according to Purdon, reflect one of the other mechanisms. Chapter 8 mentions that the effect of sevoflurane on hippocampal theta may involve TASK-3 channels. Both are hypotheses.
Nitrous oxide
Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 Purdon 2015 Miller's ch. 8 and 22 Hendrickx 2008
  • Role: nitrous oxide is used as an adjunct because it is not potent enough on its own for general anaesthesia. Attempts to give enough nitrous oxide alone for unconsciousness cause nausea and vomiting (Purdon 2015). MAC is given as 105%, i.e. above one atmosphere (Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8).
  • Elimination: nitrous oxide is eliminated so rapidly that alveolar oxygen and CO₂ are diluted. Diffusion hypoxia is prevented with 100% oxygen for 5–10 minutes after nitrous oxide is turned off (Morgan and Mikhail).
  • Side effects with prolonged exposure: bone marrow depression (megaloblastic anaemia) and peripheral neuropathies (Morgan and Mikhail).
  • EEG: nitrous oxide typically gives beta and gamma, and BIS can rise even though the patient is unconscious (Liu 2023). When switching from an ether agent to more than 70% nitrous oxide, a transient strong slow-delta can appear (Purdon 2015).

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Site of action: Purdon 2015 links the EEG patterns of nitrous oxide to NMDA receptors. Hendrickx 2008 counts nitrous oxide among the inhaled agents with a less clear site of action. Nitrous oxide is not potent enough on its own for general anaesthesia.
  • EEG and possible mechanisms: nitrous oxide typically gives beta–gamma. When switching from an ether agent to a high concentration of nitrous oxide (above 70%), strong transient slow-delta can appear with loss of power above about 10 Hz. The mechanism is unknown. Purdon proposes blockade of NMDA-mediated excitatory signals from the parabrachial nucleus and the medial pontine reticular formation to the basal forebrain and thalamus, and that the beta–gamma may share its mechanism with ketamine.
  • Memory: amnestic concentrations of nitrous oxide, isoflurane and halothane suppress hippocampus-dependent fear learning in animals, in proportion to how much the theta peak frequency is slowed (ch. 8).
  • Interaction: nitrous oxide and isoflurane are possibly infra-additive (Hendrickx 2008).
  • Analgesia (ch. 22): in mice, the analgesia from nitrous oxide is not mediated by the μ receptor, but by the κ receptor and descending inhibitory pathways in the spinal cord. The hypnotic effect does not depend on κ. Chapter 22 describes 70% nitrous oxide as an effective NMDA antagonist that reduced opioid-induced hyperalgesia.
Opioids
Miller's ch. 22 Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010 Hendrickx 2008 Balanza 2022

Chapter 22 (Fukuda) describes opioid action from receptor to clinic. Much of the mechanistic knowledge comes from cell studies and animal experiments.

  • Not complete anaesthetics: opioids reduce MAC, but with a ceiling, and must be combined with other drugs. Analgesia is not usually accompanied by loss of consciousness. High doses can abolish spontaneous breathing without unconsciousness, and the patient may breathe on command (ch. 22). Brown 2010 uses this to explain awareness in cardiac surgery with high-dose opioids. Hendrickx 2008 describes that fentanyl alone does not give full hypnosis.
  • EEG: fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanil and remifentanil give the same pattern. Small doses of fentanyl (2–5 µg/kg) give minimal EEG changes, while high doses (30–70 µg/kg) give high-amplitude slow delta waves, with a ceiling. Isolated transient sharp waves (usually frontotemporal) can be seen after large doses. In children and adolescents, morphine reduced alpha and beta, while delta and theta were unchanged (Montandon 2016). The spectral edge frequency follows remifentanil concentration with almost no delay, while it lags for fentanyl and sufentanil (ch. 22). Balanza 2022 found frontal theta with fentanyl (see the card below and Discrepancies).
  • Respiratory depression: results from direct μ-receptor action on the brainstem respiratory centres. The preBötzinger complex mediates only part of the effect (timing, not the fall in rate). G-protein-gated potassium channels contribute. Mice lacking the μ receptor do not get respiratory depression from morphine. The A118G gene variant alters analgesia but not respiratory depression from morphine-6-glucuronide, suggesting different signalling pathways. In monkeys, tolerance developed to analgesia but not to respiratory depression (ch. 22).
  • Hyperalgesia and tolerance: opioid-induced hyperalgesia is linked in animal experiments to sensitisation to glutamate and substance P, NMDA plasticity and AMPA receptors in the dorsal horn. Ketamine, nitrous oxide, magnesium and buprenorphine reduced it in studies cited in the chapter. With long-term use the cAMP system in the locus coeruleus is upregulated (ch. 22).
  • Muscle rigidity: is not caused by action on the muscle. The nucleus raphe pontis, caudate nucleus and fentanyl action in the locus coeruleus on spinal motor neurons have been proposed. Naloxone reverses the rigidity (ch. 22).

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • The receptor family: μ, δ, κ and the nociceptin receptor share about 50% amino acid sequence. All are G-protein-coupled receptors with seven segments crossing the cell membrane, and the ligand binds deep within a large pocket. Endogenous ligands are β-endorphin and endomorphins (μ), enkephalins (δ), dynorphins (κ) and nociceptin. The sigma receptor is no longer regarded as an opioid receptor. Morphine, fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil and remifentanil are μ agonists (ch. 22).
  • Inside the nerve cell: the receptor activates Gi/o proteins. Adenylate cyclase is inhibited (less cAMP), voltage-gated calcium channels are inhibited and inwardly rectifying potassium channels are activated. The result is lower excitability of the nerve cell (ch. 22).
  • In the spinal cord: opioid receptors are abundant in the substantia gelatinosa. Presynaptically, inhibited calcium channels reduce release of glutamate and substance P from primary sensory neurons. Postsynaptically, open potassium channels hyperpolarise the dorsal horn projection neuron, so glutamate excites it less easily (ch. 22). Brown 2010 describes the same.
  • In the brainstem: in the periaqueductal grey (PAG), opioids inhibit GABA release from tonically active interneurons. This releases descending pathways via the medulla, which release noradrenaline and serotonin that dampen pain signals in the dorsal horn. Opioids thus act partly by inhibiting the inhibition (ch. 22).
  • In the cortex: PET with remifentanil showed activation in the anterior cingulate, insula, orbitofrontal cortex and brainstem. Action in the amygdala contributes to analgesia in rats (ch. 22).
  • Arousal: morphine reduced acetylcholine release in the prefrontal cortex of rats, given both intravenously and directly into the basal forebrain. Chapter 22 calls this a possible neurochemical basis for altered consciousness. Brown 2010 describes that fentanyl reduces acetylcholine in the medial pontine reticular formation.
  • Biased agonism: the theory is that Gi/o signalling gives analgesia, while β-arrestin gives side effects such as respiratory depression, constipation and euphoria. Mice lacking β-arrestin-2 had less respiratory depression from morphine in one study, but not in a newer one. Chapter 22 concludes that it is unresolved whether G-protein-biased opioids have fewer side effects.
  • Reward: μ and δ agonists are rewarding, κ agonists aversive. Opioids inhibit GABA neurons in the ventral tegmental area and nucleus accumbens, so that more dopamine is released in the nucleus accumbens. Activity in the locus coeruleus is inhibited (ch. 22).
  • Other targets: buprenorphine blocks sodium channels, d-methadone is an NMDA antagonist, pethidine acts at the α2B adrenoceptor (a possible explanation for its anti-shivering effect), and morphine and hydromorphone inhibit the 5-HT3A receptor. In mice lacking the μ receptor, ketamine-induced respiratory depression and antinociception were reduced, and the MAC of sevoflurane was higher (ch. 22).

What another textbook says: Morgan and Mikhail 2022 (ch. 8, 9 and 43)

Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 7th edition (Butterworth, Mackey, Wasnick, McGraw Hill 2022). The chapters on volatile agents, intravenous agents and geriatric anaesthesia contain little on EEG, but three things are worth keeping alongside Miller's.

  • MAC-awake (ch. 8): 0.3–0.4 MAC is associated with awakening when the volatile agent is the only thing maintaining the anaesthetic, versus 1.3 MAC to prevent movement in about 95%. It is the distance between “no movement” and “awake” that allows the EEG pattern to look adequate close to emergence (see neural inertia in Hight 2020, Fundamentals tab).
  • MAC and age: ch. 8 gives a 6% fall in MAC per decade “regardless of agent”, ch. 43 gives 4% per decade over 40 years (see discrepancies). Miller's ch. 61 gives 6% per decade after 30 years (Mapleson 1996).
  • Barbiturates and EEG (ch. 9): the EEG goes from low-voltage fast activity at small doses to high-voltage slow activity, burst suppression and electrical silence at large doses, in parallel with the fall in cerebral metabolism (up to 50%). Thiopental doses that maintain burst suppression or a flat line give prolonged emergence, delayed extubation and a need for inotropes. Ketamine “dissociates” sensory impulses from the limbic cortex, and the patient can look awake (eye opening, swallowing) without being so.
  • Older patients (ch. 43): the chapter says that “some have suggested” that BIS monitoring may reduce cognitive impairment, and that the mechanism of perioperative neurocognitive disorder is unclear. This is more weakly worded than Miller's ch. 61, which proposes pEEG to avoid burst suppression.
Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 7th ed. 2022, ch. 8, 9 and 43

Dexmedetomidine and sleep spindles: like NREM 2 sleep (Huupponen 2008)

Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2008;52:289–294. Eleven healthy young men (20–28 years) received dexmedetomidine as a target-controlled infusion, first 0.5 ng/ml for 25 minutes and then 3.2 ng/ml for 30 minutes. Measured plasma concentration during deep sedation was 5.1 ng/ml (SD 1.0). EEG was recorded from a single frontal channel with the Entropy Module. The control group was ten other healthy people (seven men, 21–43 years) during normal night sleep, with the first sleep cycle analysed.

  • Visual: the EEG during deep dexmedetomidine sedation resembled NREM sleep stage 2, with slight to moderate slow activity and abundant spindles. The low dose (0.5 ng/ml) did not induce sleep in everyone and was excluded from analysis.
  • Quantitative: spindle density (1.17 vs 1.26 per minute), amplitude and frequency (11.5 vs 12.0 Hz) did not differ between groups. Spindles lasted longer under dexmedetomidine (1.11 vs 0.88 seconds, p = 0.0014). The authors mention that longer spindles might mean stronger sleep protection, but call this only one possible explanation.
  • Frequency and origin: frontal spindles are slower than central ones (11–12 Hz frontally vs 13–14 Hz centrally in normal sleep). The authors believe the frontal spindles are probably generated in the mediodorsal thalamic nucleus, and that the same pathway is active under dexmedetomidine.
  • Arousal: in an earlier study by the same group, participants could be roused with verbal commands and possibly light shaking, even at 5.1 ng/ml (see Discrepancies).
  • Caveats: different people in the two groups, morning versus night recording, a single channel and small groups. The number of spindles per person ranged from 1 to 174. Three of the authors are from GE Healthcare, which makes the Entropy Module, and one author does contract research and consulting for Orion Pharma, which manufactures dexmedetomidine.
Huupponen et al. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2008;52:289–294

Dexmedetomidine and the thalamus: cortical coupling preserved, thalamocortical disrupted (Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014)

eLife 2014;3:e04499. Healthy volunteers (18–36 years, ASA I) received dexmedetomidine 1 µg/kg over 10 minutes followed by 0.7 µg/kg/h. Loss of consciousness was defined as sustained eye closure and no response to a request to open the eyes. Glucose metabolism was measured with FDG-PET (ten participants, two visits each), and blood flow (ASL) and functional connectivity (BOLD) were measured simultaneously with MRI (17 participants, complete BOLD data in 15). Not the same study as «Akeju 2014» on sevoflurane elsewhere in the app.

  • Metabolism and blood flow: glucose metabolism and blood flow fell most in the thalamus, the default mode network (DMN) and both frontoparietal networks. Blood flow and metabolism fell together, so the coupling between them was preserved.
  • Connectivity: coupling between cortical areas within the DMN and frontoparietal networks was preserved. Coupling between the thalamus and the DMN was disrupted, especially towards the posterior cingulate, precuneus and inferior parietal lobule. The thalamic region corresponded to intralaminar, midline, mediodorsal and ventral anterior nuclei, but the method could not resolve the nuclei precisely.
  • Recovery: coupling between the thalamus and the DMN, especially the posterior cingulate, returned when participants again responded to commands, while blood flow did not rise. The authors interpret this as coupling being restored before metabolism normalises, and recovery happening gradually.
  • A hierarchy of unconsciousness: the authors propose that lighter states (NREM 2 sleep, dexmedetomidine) involve disrupted thalamocortical coupling with preserved cortical coupling, while deeper states (propofol anaesthesia, some disorders of consciousness) also disrupt cortical coupling. Preserved cortical coupling may explain why the patient is easily roused.
  • Caveats: loss of consciousness was defined by failure to open the eyes on request. Functional connectivity in fMRI is co-variation in slow BOLD fluctuations, not directly measured communication between nerve cells. No conflicts of interest declared. Funded by the NIH and FAER.
Akeju, Loggia et al. eLife 2014;3:e04499

Which α2 receptor produces hypnosis? α2A in the locus coeruleus (Mizobe 1996)

J Clin Invest 1996;98:1076–1080, from the Maze group. Rats received antisense oligonucleotides (short DNA strands that prevent a specific receptor from being made) against α2A or α2C directly into the locus coeruleus, followed by dexmedetomidine 7 µg into the same area.

  • Cell studies: antisense against α2A reduced α2A receptors by about 30%, and antisense against α2C reduced α2C by nearly 40%, without affecting the other subtype.
  • Rats: after α2A antisense, loss of righting reflex came later and lasted shorter, and the effect was gone eight days after the last dose. α2C antisense, scrambled control sequences and saline had no effect.
  • Conclusion: α2A is the subtype mediating the hypnotic effect in the locus coeruleus. The authors write that α2A and α2C predominate in the central nervous system, while α2B is sparsely represented.
  • Side effects: the authors write that the rise in blood pressure after a rapid bolus is probably due to α2B (knockout mouse experiments), and that the bradycardia may partly be due to imidazoline receptors in the brainstem.
  • Caveats: 4–5 rats per group, and receptor reduction was measured only in cell cultures, not in the locus coeruleus itself. Funded by Veterans Affairs, the NIH and the Uehara Foundation.
Mizobe et al. J Clin Invest 1996;98:1076–1080

Several effects, different concentrations

Chapter 16 describes that each drug has a dynamic range: the concentration at which the effect changes. Below the range little happens, and above it more drug does not give more effect. Different effects of the same agent have different C50 values.

Chapter 16 also describes that hypnotics and opioids interact. Analgesic effects are markedly synergistic, and hypnotic effects moderately synergistic. Combinations of two GABAergic hypnotics are largely additive. The chapter recommends aiming for a 95–99% probability of effect, not 50% as MAC does. Drug displays show predicted effect, but are based on population models that do not fit everyone.

Miller's ch. 16 (Hendrickx 2008, Bouillon 2004, Egan 2001)

Fentanyl and EEG: frontal theta (Balanza 2022)

  • Design: 25 patients (31–64 years, ASA I–III, BMI below 30) received fentanyl 2 µg/kg of ideal body weight every 2 minutes, two or three doses, before induction of general anaesthesia, while performing an auditory task and being monitored with four-channel frontal EEG, chest belts for respiration and pulse oximetry. The effect-site concentration is model-derived (PK/PD in stanpumpR), not measured. 31 consented, and recruitment stopped early because of covid-19.
  • EEG: increasing fentanyl concentration gave increased power in theta (4–8 Hz) and in slow-delta (below 4 Hz). The theta power is difficult to see in the raw EEG, but clear in the spectrum and spectrogram. Theta power was related to concentration (model slope 0.55, 95% CI 0.25–0.80), but the proportion explained by the fixed effect was low (marginal R² 0.15) while the whole model explained 0.74 because individuals differed a great deal.
  • Respiration: the minute ventilation index fell by 30% after the first dose, 55% after the second and 60% after the third, while SpO₂ stayed between 95 and 100% (with preoxygenation). Increased theta power was related to lower ventilation (slope −1.62, marginal R² 0.054).
  • Behaviour: reaction time increased on average 277 seconds (95% CI 220–333) after ventilation began to fall. The concentration that gave a 10% fall in minute ventilation was about 1750 times lower (CI 839–2854) than the concentration when reaction time increased. 16 of 25 lost responsiveness (three consecutive missed responses, about 12 seconds). All could be roused, and four needed a jaw thrust. Slow-delta was more informative than theta for loss of response.
  • What it may mean: the authors suggest that it may be possible to predict respiratory depression with processed EEG. This is a hypothesis that has not been tested, and the study is small and did not measure during anaesthesia.
  • Relation to chapter 16: the chapter gives fentanyl C50 of about 2 ng/ml for analgesia, 4 for ventilatory depression and 20 for EEG changes (Egan 2001). Balanza found EEG changes (theta) that increased with concentration within the range 0–15 ng/ml in figure 1, but gives no threshold. The numbers are not directly comparable, since the endpoints and methods differ.
  • Caveats: Purdon reports patents, a licence to Masimo and co-founding of a company developing closed-loop systems.
Balanza et al. PNAS Nexus 2022;1:pgac158

Synergy between agents and isoelectric EEG

A clinical picture many will recognise: when several agents are given at the same time in large doses, for example at induction, or in response to the patient moving during the procedure (more volatile agent, opioid, clonidine and esketamine all at once), the EEG abruptly becomes completely flat, without bursts, and only returns when the bolus effect has worn off. Older patients are most at risk. This is not a separate phenomenon, but the extreme end of burst suppression.

  • Terms: suppression is amplitude below 10 µV, and electrocerebral inactivity (“isoelectric EEG”) is 2 µV or lower (Guay 2025). Ching 2012 describes burst suppression as a continuum, not a separate state: the suppression ratio increases with dose until the EEG is finally completely isoelectric. The monitor shows this as SR near 100, not as a separate pattern.
