It is easily confused with a technical fault: a loose electrode or a cable break gives noise, an impedance alarm or a high artefact proportion, whereas isoelectric EEG is a clean flat line in all channels with normal impedance, and it appears in temporal relation to the doses.
  • What is synergistic (Hendrickx, Eger, Sonner og Shafer, Anesth Analg 2008;107:494–506): a systematic review of all interaction studies for hypnosis and immobility, with reanalysis of raw data where available. Definition: a sum of normalised doses below 0.9 is synergy, 0.9–1.1 additive, above 1.1 infra-additive. Main finding: between drug classes, most interactions are synergistic. Opioids are synergistic with both intravenous and inhaled hypnotics (11 of 13 studies for propofol + opioid), and because opioids alone can never produce full hypnosis or immobility (ceiling effect), any reduction of more than 10% is “synergy by definition”. Propofol + midazolam is synergistic for hypnosis (Short and Chui 1991, McClune 1992, Short 1992), probably because they bind to different sites on the GABAA receptor. Volatile agents are synergistic with intravenous agents, but additive with each other, and propofol + sevoflurane is additive.
  • The exception is ketamine: ketamine showed no synergy with GABAergic agents in any study; propofol + ketamine was additive, and on reanalysis infra-additive for immobility (Hui 1995). Midazolam + ketamine was infra-additive for hypnosis on reanalysis. Clonidine + propofol was additive for hypnosis (Higuchi 2002), but clonidine lowers MACawake for sevoflurane by 17–21% and MAC by 17–34% with a ceiling effect, which counts as synergy by definition. In the example above it is therefore sevoflurane + fentanyl (+ clonidine) that produces the synergy, not the esketamine. The authors stress that the review concerns only hypnosis and immobility: synergy for side effects (respiratory depression, hypotension) is little studied. The same is seen in dogs: Mair 2009 (Vet Anaesth Analg, 90 dogs, blinded and randomised) found that ketamine 0.25 or 0.5 mg/kg before propofol TCI did not change the propofol target for intubation (median 3.0 µg/ml in all groups) and did not change blood pressure or heart rate, but gave more apnoea after induction at the highest dose (4 of 30 versus 0). The authors conclude that ketamine is not a useful co-induction agent with propofol in dogs.
  • The numbers from Short and Chui 1991 (BJA 67:539–545): 200 women aged 18–40 years, not premedicated. ED50 for hypnosis was 1.01 mg/kg propofol and 0.14 mg/kg midazolam; for “anaesthesia” (no response to a 5 s tetanic stimulus) 1.93 mg/kg propofol, while midazolam alone never achieved it. In combination, 85% achieved hypnosis on a combined dose that gave hypnosis in 50% with each agent alone, and midazolam 0.13 mg/kg halved the propofol dose for anaesthesia (1.93 to 0.93 mg/kg, 52%). The fall in blood pressure was the same for the combination as for each agent at equipotent dose, that is, synergy for the hypotension too.
  • How interactions are measured: isobologram (lines through equieffective dose combinations; straight line = Loewe additivity, curved towards the origin = synergy) and response surface models such as Minto 2000, where the effect is shown as a surface over two dose dimensions. Lee 2010 (Korean J Anaesthesiol) reviews the models and points out that the classification depends on the reference model, and that a single interaction parameter cannot capture synergy in one dose range and antagonism in another.
  • Age and pressure amplify: older patients are more sensitive to propofol (Schnider 1999, Purdon 2015 BJA), MAC falls with age, and hypotension after a bolus can in itself produce suppression (Georgii 2022, Burst suppression tab). Ching 2012 (Burst suppression tab) links suppression to reduced cerebral metabolism, and notes that ketamine, which increases CMRO₂, does not produce classic burst suppression at clinical doses.
  • The return: when the effect wears off, activity returns, often as high-amplitude slow activity before the alpha band is re-established. Sepúlveda 2026 (Burst suppression tab) shows that the EEG after burst suppression does not go straight back to the baseline pattern at the same calculated concentration.
  • What has not been shown: that a brief isoelectric period gives a worse outcome. Suppression is associated with delirium (Fritz 2016, Burst suppression tab), but ENGAGES (Wildes 2019) reduced suppression time without reducing delirium. “Cortical collapse” is an image, not a technical term. “Reboot”, on the other hand, is used by Huang 2021 (Neuroimage) for the abrupt jump in subcortico-cortical connectivity at emergence; see the card on hysteresis and neural inertia in the Fundamentals tab.
  • Practical: movement is a spinal response to nociception and does not mean that the hypnosis is too light (see the Fundamentals tab: nociception). Titrate one agent at a time, slowly in older patients (Obert 2024, Sepúlveda 2020), and look at the raw EEG and SR after each bolus, not only at the index. See image 16 in the image quiz.
Hendrickx 2008, Short & Chui 1991, Minto 2000, Lee 2010, Ching 2012, Guay 2025

Multimodal anaesthesia: lidocaine and magnesium in the EEG

Lidocaine and magnesium are used as adjuvants to spare opioid and hypnotic. The question is whether they have an EEG signature of their own, whether they take part in the synergy between agents, and whether they affect the coupling between brain regions. The literature is thin and deals almost exclusively with dose sparing measured with BIS.

  • Lidocaine, hypnosis and BIS: Hans 2010 (BJA, 40 patients plus two dose–response series, bolus 1.5 mg/kg and 2 mg/kg/h) found that lidocaine reduced BIS-guided propofol requirements only during surgical stimulation; without stimulation neither BIS nor haemodynamics changed. The authors interpret the effect as antinociceptive, not hypnotic. Lidocaine thus does not “lower” the EEG in itself at clinical doses; it dampens the arousal response to surgery.
  • Lidocaine and interaction type: Hendrickx 2008 has a separate section on sodium channel blockers. Lidocaine lowers MAC for halothane, enflurane and isoflurane in animals, usually described as additive, but with a ceiling of about 50% MAC reduction at 12–20 µg/mL in dogs, which by their definition is synergy. Propofol–lidocaine: one animal study, synergy for hypnosis. Thiopental–lidocaine in rats: infra-additive. Lidocaine potentiates midazolam in humans, interaction type unknown. No human isobolograms exist, and the studies stopped below 10 µg/mL because of the risk of seizures.
  • Lidocaine on the spectrogram: the only thing that exists is Firdaus 2026, two craniotomy patients with TIVA and lidocaine 1.5–2 mg/kg/h: one maintained an alpha–delta pattern down to propofol 1.8 µg/mL, the other developed delta dominance with attenuated alpha and intermittent burst suppression. The authors themselves say that no dose–response or causal relationship can be drawn. Remember that lidocaine at high plasma levels is proconvulsant, so the EEG effect is not monotonic.
  • Magnesium and BIS: Walia 2018 (RCT, 120 patients) found that MgSO4 30 mg/kg before induction reduced the propofol requirement for BIS 40–50 (114 ± 15 versus 160 ± 25, unit not given in the abstract) and gave lower BIS than control for the first 40 minutes, less than dexmedetomidine 1 µg/kg. Mg also spared vecuronium. Memiş 2003 (Crit Care, 30 intensive care patients) found that Mg 2 g/h for 6 hours reduced sufentanil requirements without a difference in BIS, and writes that Mg does not produce sedation at serum levels below 8 mmol/L when ventilation is adequate.
  • Why “propofol sparing” is not the same as an EEG effect: magnesium crosses the blood–brain barrier poorly. A reasonable reading (an interpretation, not from a source) is that the saving in BIS studies is a mixture of reduced nociceptive response, haemodynamics and less muscle activity, since Mg potentiates neuromuscular blockade and thus the EMG contribution to the index. This is a hypothesis and should be labelled as such.
  • Coupling between brain regions: no human studies on lidocaine or magnesium and EEG connectivity during anaesthesia were found. What exists on connectivity concerns propofol and sevoflurane (Fundamentals tab), ketamine (Vlisides 2017, above) and dexmedetomidine.
  • In summary: neither of the two agents has a known EEG signature of its own at clinical doses, as propofol, sevoflurane, ketamine and dexmedetomidine have. The literature supports that they reduce the need for hypnotic, mostly via antinociception, and that the EEG change you see is therefore most often indirect: less arousal response to surgery, or the hypnotic being dosed lower. In the synergy accounting (the card above) they should be counted as opioid-sparing, not as an additional hypnotic. The evidence base is small, and without spectrogram studies of adequate size.
Hans 2010 · Hendrickx 2008 · Firdaus 2026 · Walia 2018 · Memiş 2003

Propofol and memory: loss over time (Veselis 2004)

  • Design: 83 healthy volunteers (mean 31 years) were randomised to propofol (n = 30), thiopental (n = 31), dexmedetomidine (n = 10) or placebo (n = 12) at a constant target concentration for about 90 minutes (propofol 0.3, 1.2 or 2.5 µg/ml, thiopental 2, 5 or 7 µg/ml, dexmedetomidine 0.25 or 0.5–0.8 ng/ml). They heard words in a continuous recognition task with repetition after 1, 5 or 10 words (about 6, 15–21 and 33 seconds). Recognition of the words was tested again after about 225 minutes.
  • Grouping: since the effects of the doses overlapped, the authors divided the participants into “high” and “low” performance based on a median split of recognition after 33 seconds under the drug. The 23 who did not respond to voice or firm touch (BIS 72 ± 16) were excluded, and 9 others were excluded for other reasons.
  • High performance (lightly sedated): the words entered long-term memory as well as with placebo (BIS about 94). The loss of these words after 3.5–4 hours was 38.8 ± 23.0 percentage points with propofol, versus 17.2 with thiopental, 22.9 with dexmedetomidine and 11.9 with placebo (propofol versus placebo p = 0.008, and versus thiopental p = 0.037). Recognition of the words from the drug period was 31% with propofol, 39% with thiopental, 34% with dexmedetomidine and 61% with placebo.
  • Low performance (more sedated): they responded to 54% of the words versus 87% in high performance, had 225 ms (18%) longer reaction time and BIS about 89. Recognition after 15–33 seconds was no better than chance, regardless of agent, and the words were remembered very poorly later. The authors interpret this as failure of encoding.
  • Before the drug: recognition of words presented before the drug was equal to placebo, so the effect applies only to material presented while the drug was acting.
  • In brief: those who were lightly sedated took in the words and stored them, but with propofol they had forgotten more of them a few hours later than with the other drugs. Those who were more sedated did not store the words at all, whatever the drug. Words from before the drug were remembered as well as with placebo.
  • The authors' interpretation: sedation prevents anything from being stored in long-term memory at all (failure of encoding), while propofol additionally makes what was actually stored disappear faster afterwards (“drug-induced amnesia”). The mechanism is speculative (interplay between hippocampus and neocortex, interference from new words). Dexmedetomidine had the same profile as thiopental and a smaller loss than propofol. Midazolam was not tested here, and the claim about midazolam rests on earlier studies the authors refer to.
  • The authors' own caveats: the finding for propofol is not conclusive, partly because the high-performance group with propofol had a slightly better baseline (borderline, omnibus test not significant). Recognition after the drug was below 40%, so there may be a floor effect, the lists were built differently, and dexmedetomidine was given to few (4 per group).
  • What it means: these are laboratory data from healthy volunteers at low to moderate doses and without surgical stimulation. They say nothing directly about memory in surgical patients, and the BIS values in the article (89–94 with preserved response, 72 with unresponsiveness) are not the same as in other sources.
Veselis et al. Anesthesiology 2004;101:831–841

Memory loss over time for different agents (Pryor 2010)

  • Design: 61 healthy volunteers (analysed of 67 randomised) received propofol, thiopental, midazolam, dexmedetomidine or placebo, each at two concentrations (propofol 0.45 and 0.90 µg/ml, thiopental 1.5 and 3.0, midazolam 20 and 35 ng/ml, dexmedetomidine 0.20 and 0.40 ng/ml, model-derived). They viewed 375 pictures with repetition after 6, 27 and 63 seconds, and were tested on recognition 15, 45, 105 and 225 minutes after the infusion stopped.
  • Model: memory strength over time was described with a power function, m = λ·t−ψ, where λ is the strength of the initial memory trace and ψ is how fast it decays (R² on average 0.85). The model predicted that the loss became visible 1.7–8 minutes after encoding.
  • What was related to what: λ followed self-reported alertness (r = 0.83, p = 0.005), while ψ followed reaction time (r = 0.95, p < 0.0001) and attenuation of the P2-N2 complex in the EEG at encoding (P2 amplitude r = −0.82, p = 0.007). The correlations are based on group values (nine points) and do not show causation.
  • The profiles: dexmedetomidine lowered the initial trace in step with reduced alertness and barely affected the decay (pure sedation). Propofol gave strong encoding (a paradoxically higher λ at the highest dose) and a marked, dose-dependent faster loss. Midazolam was a mixture: faster loss dominated at low dose and reduced alertness at high dose. Thiopental resembled dexmedetomidine, but the comparison was not significant (the authors point to many comparisons).
  • No retrograde effect: a visual word test, learned just before the drug, showed no difference between the agents and placebo. The difference between 6, 27 and 63 seconds was not affected either.
  • The authors' hypothesis: failing consolidation is due to the drug disrupting synchrony between regions at encoding, which may affect plasticity. They stress that P2-N2 is an indirect and preliminary measure, and that the results only provide a framework for further studies.
  • Limitations: model-derived concentrations without measurement, not entirely equal levels of amnesia between the agents, residual drug at recognition testing, and small groups (12 per agent).
Pryor et al. Anesthesiology 2010;113:313–326

Midazolam and retrograde amnesia (Bulach 2005)

  • Design: 40 adult ASA I–II patients randomised and blinded to midazolam 2, 5 or 10 mg or saline 8 minutes before induction (10 per group). Pictures (posters) and events were shown and tested at fixed time points before and after the dose, and memory was tested again at least 4 hours after the patient left the recovery unit.
  • Retrograde: recognition of posters shown 4, 2 and 1 minute before the dose was equal between groups (9–10 of 10 throughout), and there was no difference either in events such as venous cannulation, transfer to the operating table and sticking out the tongue.
  • Anterograde: after the dose, the midazolam groups remembered less well than control. The poster 4 minutes after the dose was recognised by 8 of 10 in the control group versus 2, 0 and 1 in the midazolam groups, and 8 minutes after by 8 versus 4, 1 and 0 (dose–response p = 0.002). BIS was median 97 in the control group and 71 after 10 mg at 4 minutes.
  • The time point at the dose: only 4 and 3 of 10 remembered mask preoxygenation that started at the same time as the dose after 5 and 10 mg respectively, versus 10 of 10 in the control group. The authors suggest this may indicate a near-immediate retrograde effect, but that it must in that case be very short-lived since memories from the minutes before the dose were intact. One patient in the 10 mg group had a tourniquet inflated to 300 mmHg without remembering it.
  • Conclusion: midazolam 2–10 mg does not give reliable retrograde amnesia, but gives dose-dependent anterograde amnesia, clear at 5 and 10 mg. The authors say that midazolam therefore cannot be used to erase the memory of what has already happened.
  • Limitations: small groups, only explicit visual and event-based memory (no implicit tests and no auditory test, even though awareness often concerns sounds), and all received propofol at induction, which may itself contribute to amnesia close to induction.
  • Relation to chapter 8: the chapter says there is little support for retrograde amnesia in humans and that some controlled studies show improved memory for material presented just before the dose (retrograde facilitation). Bulach supports the first, but found no facilitation (the difference for the poster at the time of the dose was not significant (p = 0.10) and went in different directions between groups).
  • Control for false memories: no patient “recalled” any of the six control posters shown only after surgery, or the fictitious finger-prick test. The authors take this as a sign that the memory tests did not produce false positives. A few controls still failed to recall everything, which they attribute to inattention in the operating room.
  • BIS and sedation: BIS fell dose-dependently after the dose (p < 0.001). BIS four minutes after the dose correlated with how many events the patient recalled from the time of the dose onwards (r = 0.51–0.56), but not with the event two minutes before (r = 0.02). Patients rated their own sedation higher than the investigators did. The authors think some of the anterograde amnesia may come from the sedation itself, and that propofol just before induction may have contributed.
  • Sample and power: excluded for age over 60 years, weight under 50 or over 100 kg, and no sedative premedication. The authors write themselves that 15 patients per group are needed for 80% power to detect a halving of recall (from 95% to below 50%), that they have only 10, and that a small retrograde effect may have been missed.
  • Funding: Alfred Trust Research Grant 2002. The BIS equipment was from Aspect Medical Systems. The article has no separate declaration of interests.
Bulach, Myles and Russnak. Br J Anaesth 2005;94:300–305

Dreaming and EEG during propofol and desflurane (Leslie 2009)

Randomised, double-blind study (Anesthesiology 2009;111:547–555) with 300 patients aged 18–50 years undergoing non-cardiac surgery with neuromuscular blockers, maintenance with propofol (TCI) or desflurane titrated to BIS 40–55. Patients were interviewed (the Brice questions) as soon as they were orientated. Raw EEG was recorded from induction until after the interview.

  • Dreams equally common: 27% (propofol) and 28% (desflurane) reported dreams. None reported awareness, and no dreams suggested memory of the operation. The dreams were simple (family, friends, work, leisure).
  • When the dreams occur: dreamers had more high-frequency power (30 Hz) and fewer spindles (10.7 Hz) than non-dreamers in the last 5 minutes before the interview, a REM-like pattern. During the operation itself there were no definite differences. The authors conclude that anaesthesia-related dreaming appears to occur just before emergence. The hypothesis that the dreamers were in deep sleep was refuted.
  • Predictors of dreams: dream frequency at home above one per week (OR 3.0), anaesthesia duration up to 100 minutes (OR 2.0) and BIS above 90 at interview (OR 1.9).
  • Propofol versus desflurane in the raw EEG: propofol gave more and faster spindle-like oscillations (peak 11 versus 10 Hz, 8–16 Hz range), desflurane fewer spindles and more delta (delta peak 3 versus 2 Hz). BIS values during maintenance were equal. At eye opening BIS was lower with propofol (75 versus 80) and at interview 85 versus 92, so the relationship between BIS and clinical level of consciousness differs for the two agents. Propofol patients moved more often (31% versus 10% with signs consistent with awareness) and received more fentanyl.
  • What the study says about chapters 8 and 36: it supports that dreaming is a disconnected experience that most often belongs to emergence, and that patients' own timing (“during the anaesthetic”) cannot be taken literally. It says nothing about recall without conscious experience, and therefore cannot settle the disagreement between chapter 8 and figure 36.1.
  • Caveats: usable raw EEG from only 150 of 300 patients, young patients (18–50 years), the propofol group received more opioid, and whether the findings are due to more dreaming or less amnesia for the dreams is unknown. Funded by ANZCA.
Leslie et al. Anesthesiology 2009;111:547–555

Dreams as a target: EEG-guided emergence with propofol (Sikka 2026)

Prospective quality-improvement study from Stanford (Anesthesiology 2026;145:21–36), 474 patients 2020–2023, no control group. The question was whether a standardised “emergence bundle” can make dreaming under anaesthesia common and safe. The bundle has five elements: (1) verbal priming before induction that one may dream, (2) propofol as the emergence agent, (3) EEG guidance with SedLine towards a “preemergence” state, (4) at least 10 undisturbed (“hands-off”) minutes before emergence, and (5) a modified Brice interview immediately after extubation.

  • The preemergence state in the spectrogram: the infusion is reduced to a minimum at least 10 minutes before planned emergence; the alpha band fades gradually and high-frequency activity (beta) increases, with PSI about 40–70. At signs of premature emergence (PSI above 70 or movement) small propofol boluses of 5–10 mg were given. During surgery itself PSI was 25–50, and just before emergence 80–90 (fig. 2 in the article). EEG is used here not to measure depth but to steer towards a specific brain state.
  • Who read the EEG: a small group of about ten anaesthesiologists and nurse anaesthetists (CRNAs) was trained in the operating room by the physician who developed the protocol, with emphasis on recognising alpha reduction and beta increase in the DSA, and supervised until proficient, typically at least five cases. The team was deliberately kept small for consistency.
  • Results: 452 patients were interviewed; 69% reported dreams. Among the 57 in whom all five elements were delivered, 93% dreamed. 86% of dreams were positive, none very negative. Dreamers rated sleep quality during anaesthesia higher than non-dreamers (9.16 versus 7.65, p < 0.001). In a breast-surgery subset (106 patients) dreaming was unrelated to recovery time, analgesic or antiemetic use in the PACU.
  • Awareness: no patient reported intraoperative awareness. One was uncertain and described people in blue scrubs removing the tumour, without recognising voices or staff; the first definite memory was waking up. This was classified as a surgery-related dream, not awareness.
  • The weakest link: the 10-minute hands-off period was achieved in only 14% of cases. The authors attribute this to operating-room workflow, where calm at emergence “is often not considered a clinical priority”, and call for institutional recognition of emergence quality as a valued clinical outcome. The 93% figure therefore comes from a small, self-selected subset.
  • Caveats: no control group, so the effect of each element cannot be separated; EEG was interpreted retrospectively without real-time documentation of the state's duration; interviewers were clinicians (possible interviewer bias); the PACU analyses were exploratory and underpowered. The editorial in the same issue is Palanca and Sleigh, “Protocolizing Propofol Emergence: Turning ‘Milk of Amnesia’ into Designer Dreams?” (Anesthesiology 2026, PMID 42262384). Doyal, Wanderer and Ende, “Dream Weaving: How Anesthesiologists Can Encourage Dreaming under Anesthesia” (Anesthesiology 2026;145(1):A16), is a one-page infographic based on the Sikka bundle. The same group’s scoping review (Sikka, Hu and Heifets, Br J Anaesth 2026;137:506–524) has its own card below.
  • Read together with Leslie 2009: both find that dreams belong to emergence and that none are awareness; Sikka shows that the proportion who dream can be steered up from Leslie's 27–28% by prolonging and quietening the last phase with propofol and asking immediately. This app is built around exactly that: it is the preemergence pattern in the spectrogram (alpha fading, beta arriving) that staff must be able to see in order to do it.
Sikka, Ngo, Hu, … Heifets. Anesthesiology 2026;145:21–36

Dreaming during anaesthesia: scoping review of 157 studies (Sikka, Hu and Heifets 2026)

Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, pre-registered on OSF. Searches in Medline/PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO up to 26 February 2024: 2,958 hits and 20 from reference lists, 1,721 after removing duplicates, 324 assessed in full text and 157 studies (1921–2024) with 87,866 participants. Of these, 130 were clinical studies in adults (84,945 participants), 11 in children and adolescents (2,301, aged 2 months–17 years) and 16 experimental studies in healthy volunteers (620, but overlapping datasets give only 10 unique samples, n = 356, so the total counts some volunteers more than once). This is a mapping exercise, not a meta-analysis.

  • Definition: only 13 of 141 clinical studies (9.2%) defined “dreaming”. Most build on Brice 1970: an experience (excluding awareness) that the patient recalls and thinks occurred between induction and the first consciousness after anaesthesia. 12 of 16 experimental studies (75%) used a theoretical definition: dreaming as disconnected consciousness, that is internally generated experience without sensory input and without response, as opposed to connected consciousness (awareness of the surroundings). The boundary is not always sharp: dreams containing elements from the operating room may be memories from before anaesthesia or processing of stimuli during it. In two experimental studies, dream-like content and incorporated memories occurred together in more than half of the reports.
  • How many recall: adult clinical studies from 0% (16% of the studies) to 94.6%, and all studies with 65% or more used ketamine (or etoxadrol). Propofol 0–64%, volatile agents (often with nitrous oxide) 0–60% but mostly 3–8%, dexmedetomidine 3–41%. The largest studies were at 3–8%, the largest double-blind RCTs at 3–7%. Children 0–50%, most 5–20%. Experimental studies 0–100%: ketamine 44–100%, dexmedetomidine 35.7–92.5%, propofol 0–77.3%, sevoflurane 11.4–60%, xenon 0–70%. High recall often went together with high awareness (experimentally up to 44.3%, ketamine 25%, dexmedetomidine 22.6%), suggesting lighter sedation. Awareness: among 89 studies reporting it, half reported 0%, and the largest studies 0.1–0.4%.
  • Why the figures differ: the authors think the difference between 3–8% in large clinical studies and often 40–80% in experimental ones “likely” reflects fragile memory and method, not that fewer actually dream: multiple agents, delayed interviews and interference at emergence in clinical settings, against single agents, immediate interviews, controlled emergence and priming through consent in the experiments. They stress themselves that heterogeneity prevents firm causal attribution to individual agents. This is an interpretation, not proof.
  • Content: of 130 adult studies, 90 (69%) reported valence or content. Pleasant dreams predominated, and only nine studies had more unpleasant ones (ether, thiopentone with volatile, ketamine, propofol, volatile). Typical content was everyday life: family, friends, work, holidays, beach. Propofol and dexmedetomidine dreams were mostly static and “not particularly strange” (resembling NREM sleep), while ketamine and sevoflurane dreams were more dynamic. Ketamine gave vivid, surreal, disembodied experiences (flying, colour distortion, altered time and space, death). Nightmares occurred in only five studies, more often with ketamine, and two of them may have been awareness.
  • Predictors of recall (71 adult studies): two were clearly the most consistent: higher home dream recall frequency and preoperative suggestion or priming (for example imagining a favourite place before induction). Interview timing was the most important methodological factor: an immediate interview after emergence gives clearly higher recall than a delayed one. Age, sex, ASA, anxiety: mixed, mostly not significant. Duration of surgery and anaesthesia: no association. Propofol and ketamine tended towards higher recall and volatile agents and dexmedetomidine towards lower in clinical studies, whereas dexmedetomidine gave higher recall in experimental studies. Benzodiazepines gave lower recall in 4 of 11 studies and opioids in 5 of 17. BIS during anaesthesia: mixed (lower BIS gave more recall in 4 studies, no difference in 7); higher BIS at emergence gave more in 2 studies.
  • Outcomes: only 14.6% of the studies examined them. Satisfaction, quality of recovery and postoperative anxiety or depression generally did not differ between dreamers and non-dreamers. The exception: unpleasant dreams gave lower willingness to have the same anaesthetic again (4 studies). Five studies that examined it found no difference in awareness between dreamers and non-dreamers, so dreaming should not be read as a sign of too light anaesthesia. Abuse potential rose in two studies; otherwise too little data. Children: too little data for conclusions.
  • Neural correlates (only 7 studies, 6 experimental): disconnected consciousness (dreaming) versus connected had more slow wave and delta frontomedially, more theta in the right cuneus/precuneus, less beta and gamma temporally and frontally and less information flow from front to back. Versus unconsciousness, dreaming had relatively preserved high-frequency activity and complexity (higher beta/delta, flatter spectral exponent, higher permutation entropy in mid bands). In the TMS-EEG studies (Sarasso 2015, Colombo 2019, Darracq 2018), ketamine with dreams gave high PCI and a wake-like spectral exponent, whereas propofol and xenon without dreams gave low PCI and a steep exponent; since dreaming occurred only with ketamine, agent and dreaming cannot be separated. Leslie 2009 (clinical, propofol): dreaming went with more 30 Hz activity 13–17 and 1–2 minutes before emergence and fewer spindles (10.68 Hz) 1–5 minutes before.
  • Monitoring in the studies: processed EEG (mostly BIS) in 24.6% of the adult studies, SedLine in one, none in the paediatric studies. In the experimental ones EEG was used to analyse brain dynamics, not to monitor depth, and only one used BIS to titrate.
  • The way forward and possible therapeutic use: the authors call for standardised definitions, validated instruments (an expanded Brice interview), an immediate interview within 5–15 minutes, serial awakenings with continuous EEG, and more studies in children, older people and psychiatric patients. They point to possible therapeutic benefit of pleasant, suggestible dreams (a small study found fewer trauma symptoms after dreaming under anaesthesia, Hack 2024) and highlight the Sikka 2026 bundle (93% recall), while calling for ethical guidelines on deliberately influencing subjective states.
  • Caveats and conflicts of interest: everything rests on self-report, so absence of a dream cannot be told apart from failure of encoding, storage or retrieval, and the timing of the dream cannot be established. Only English-language peer-reviewed empirical studies, the search stopped in February 2024, and reviews and editorials were left out. Heifets is an adviser or consultant to Osmind Mental Health, Journey Clinical, Arcadia Medicine, Vida Ventures and Tactogen. The authors state they used ChatGPT 5.3 and Claude to improve readability.
Sikka, Hu and Heifets. Br J Anaesth 2026;137:506–524

Awareness and choice of agent

Chapter 21 cites a Cochrane review (Messina 2016). It found that benzodiazepines reduced awareness compared with thiopental, ketamine and placebo, and that ketamine and etomidate reduced wakefulness compared with thiopental. The chapter points out that the evidence is weak, because of risk of bias, very few events and differing definitions of awareness.

Miller's ch. 21

Metabolism and CYP: what breaks down what, and what happens when the system is disturbed

Most anaesthetic drugs are broken down in the liver, many by cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP). Another drug, food, recreational drugs, disease or genes can inhibit or increase this breakdown. Inhibition gives a higher concentration and longer effect, induction a lower one. The table is based on the prescribing information and two guidelines from CPIC (Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium).

DrugMain routeWhat can change the effect
PropofolUGT1A9 (about 70%), CYP2B6 and CYP2C9 (about 29%), also outside the liverClearance exceeds hepatic blood flow. Pharmacokinetics are not altered by chronic cirrhosis (prescribing information). Gene variants give conflicting findings and are not used for dosing (Budic 2022).
MidazolamCYP3A4Ketoconazole ×5, itraconazole and fluconazole ×2–3, erythromycin ×1.6–2, clarithromycin up to ×2.5, ritonavir-boosted lopinavir ×5.4, grapefruit juice increases the effect. Rifampicin −60%, St John's wort −20–40%.
RemimazolamCarboxylesterases in the liverDoes not inhibit CYP. In hepatic impairment the effect may be stronger and last longer.
Ketamine and esketamineCYP2B6 and CYP3A4, less CYP2C9Clarithromycin ×2.6 exposure, grapefruit juice about ×3 and ticlopidine over ×2 with oral ketamine. St John's wort −58% (Andrade 2017). Longer half-life in moderate hepatic impairment.
DexmedetomidineGlucuronidation and CYP2A6Clearance 74, 64 and 53% of normal in mild, moderate and severe hepatic impairment, so the dose should be reduced.
ClonidineAbout 50% in the liver, 40–60% excreted unchanged in urineThe half-life can rise to 41 hours in severe renal failure.
Thiopental, etomidateLiverThiopental: 10–15% metabolised per hour, half-life 9–11 hours, lower dose in hepatic impairment. Etomidate: half-life roughly doubles in cirrhosis.
Sevoflurane, desfluraneSevoflurane about 5% via CYP2E1, desflurane under 0.02%CYP2E1 can be induced by chronic alcohol use and isoniazid. Barbiturates do not induce sevoflurane metabolism.
Fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanilCYP3A4Ritonavir reduced fentanyl clearance by about two-thirds. Fluconazole, voriconazole, erythromycin, diltiazem and cimetidine inhibit alfentanil and can cause prolonged respiratory depression. Stopping an inducer (e.g. rifampicin) can make sufentanil concentrations rise.
RemifentanilNon-specific esterases in blood and tissueNot affected by hepatic or renal failure, nor by atypical cholinesterase.
MorphineGlucuronidation to M3G (about 50%) and M6G (5–15%)M6G is active. In renal failure M3G and M6G accumulate.
OxycodoneCYP3A4, less CYP2D6Voriconazole ×3.6 exposure, rifampicin −86%. CYP2D6 inhibition has not been shown to matter clinically.
Codeine, tramadolCYP2D6 makes the active substance (morphine, O-desmethyltramadol)Ultrarapid metabolisers get more active substance and risk toxicity, poor metabolisers get poor analgesia. CPIC recommends avoiding both in both groups. Deaths in children, and advised against under 12 years.
MethadoneMainly CYP2B6, little CYP3A4CPIC 2024: genotyping should not change dosing.
LidocaineLiver, to active metabolites (MEGX, GX)The half-life may double in hepatic failure, with a risk of toxic levels.
  • The main point for EEG monitoring (interpretation based on the sources): when breakdown is inhibited, the same dose gives more effect over time. The spectrogram and the index show the combined effect in the brain, whether the cause is the dose, an interaction or organ failure. That is one reason to titrate to effect and not only to weight or habit.
  • Little affected: propofol, remifentanil and remimazolam depend little on CYP. They are therefore suitable when interactions or hepatic failure are a problem, although remimazolam may last longer in hepatic failure.
  • Most exposed: midazolam, fentanyl, alfentanil and oxycodone (CYP3A4) with concurrent antifungals, macrolides, HIV drugs or diltiazem. Induction from rifampicin or St John's wort lowers the effect, and when the inducer is stopped, levels rise again.
  • Children: the enzyme systems mature after birth, see the card on dexmedetomidine in children.
  • Uncertain: the exact CYP routes for lidocaine, thiopental and clonidine are not given in the prescribing information that was read, so they are not in the table.
Prescribing information (eMC, FDA) Budic 2022 Andrade 2017 CPIC: Crews 2021, Robinson 2024

Why do some patients tolerate more? Smoking, alcohol, cannabis and red hair

Tolerance can have two explanations: the drug is broken down faster (pharmacokinetics), or the brain responds less to the same concentration (pharmacodynamics). In smokers both seem to contribute.

  • Smokers needed more propofol and remifentanil: in 90 women with TIVA and BIS 45–60, the propofol induction dose was 102.8 mg in smokers, 84.5 mg in passive smokers and 63.2 mg in non-smokers. Total remifentanil was 1315, 1241 and 1010 µg (Öztürk 2019). The study is small and single-centre, so it is a signal and not proof.
  • It is the smoke, not the nicotine, that increases breakdown: polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke induce CYP1A1, CYP1A2 and possibly CYP2E1. Smoking also reduces sedation from benzodiazepines and analgesia from some opioids (Zevin and Benowitz 1999). Nicotine patches or snus therefore do not give the same enzyme induction (interpretation based on the sources).
  • The liver does not explain everything: remifentanil is broken down by esterases in the blood, not in the liver, and the smokers still needed more. The authors therefore also point to changes in the brain (Öztürk 2019). Nicotine withdrawal lowers pain threshold and pain tolerance, and in all six postoperative studies in a review, abstinent smokers needed more analgesia (Vega Palma 2023). This may relate to more nicotinic receptors (α4β2) during withdrawal.
  • After surgery: smokers used 13.9 mg morphine equivalents more via PCA than never-smokers, while former smokers did not differ (Wang 2023, 1162 patients). A meta-analysis found about 34% more opioids in the first 24 hours, but all studies were non-randomised, so certainty is low (Szilagyi 2026).
  • Local anaesthesia: ropivacaine is partly broken down by CYP1A2. Ciprofloxacin, which inhibits CYP1A2, reduced ropivacaine clearance by 31% (Jokinen 2003). Smoking, which induces CYP1A2, could then be expected to speed up breakdown (interpretation based on the sources).
  • Sevoflurane: no study was found that measures MAC in smokers. Washout after 1 MAC was the same in smokers and non-smokers (Adanir 2010).
  • Chronic alcohol: higher propofol concentration for loss of consciousness (EC50 3.15 versus 2.21 µg/ml), but no difference for remifentanil (Liang 2011), see the poisoning section in Intensive care.
  • Cannabis: the propofol requirement for BIS below 60 was the same, but users needed more propofol for laryngeal mask insertion (314 versus 263 mg) (Flisberg 2009). A retrospective endoscopy study with only 25 users found more fentanyl, midazolam and propofol, but without control for other factors (Twardowski 2019).
  • Red hair: red-haired women needed 6.2 vol% desflurane versus 5.2 vol% in dark-haired women. Nine of ten redheads had mutations in the MC1R gene (Liem 2004, 10 + 10 women).
  • For EEG monitoring (interpretation based on the sources): none of these factors gives a fixed dose adjustment. That is a reason to titrate to the spectrogram and the clinical response, not to a standard dose.
Öztürk 2019 Zevin and Benowitz 1999 Vega Palma 2023 Wang 2023 Szilagyi 2026 Liem 2004 Flisberg 2009

Anxiety, calm and drug requirement: is there evidence that safety lowers the need?

The idea is that an anxious patient has more excitation in the brain and therefore needs more inhibitory drugs, and that calm, safety and little stimulation mean less is needed. The literature supports parts of this, but the findings are mixed, and the mechanism has not been shown in humans.

  • Anxiety as a personality trait increases the propofol requirement: women with high trait anxiety needed 2.1 versus 1.8 mg/kg propofol for induction and 170 versus 110 µg/kg/min for maintenance, guided by BIS. Anxiety in the moment (state anxiety) had no significant effect (Maranets and Kain 1999).
  • Anxiety and pain sensitivity: in 100 women before thyroidectomy, both state and trait anxiety predicted the propofol requirement at BIS 85 and 75. The sevoflurane requirement was related only to pain sensitivity (Kil 2012).
  • But several studies found no relationship: in 197 patients, anxiety did not affect the propofol dose independently of other factors (Morley 2008). Kim and Choi 2013 also found no relationship with dose, but more anxious patients had a higher entropy value when they lost consciousness. Anxiety may therefore affect what the monitor shows without changing the dose.
  • Music in intensive care: in an RCT of 373 ventilated patients, patient-directed music gave 19.5 mm lower anxiety and somewhat lower sedation intensity and frequency than usual care (Chlan 2013). Anxiety was not lower than with noise-cancelling headphones.
  • Music during surgery: a meta-analysis found a lower propofol requirement with music (SMD 0.72, 9 RCTs) and somewhat fewer opioids, but the three fully blinded studies showed no effect on opioids (Fu 2020). The Dutch guideline rates the evidence on drug use as very low.
  • Is it the music or less noise? patient-controlled propofol was 0.004 mg/kg/min with music, 0.014 with white noise and 0.012 with operating-room noise (Ayoub 2005), so the music did more than just remove noise. Noise of about 80 dB from the saw gave a higher BIS (76.9 versus 68.5) than when the noise was blocked out (Kang 2008).
  • Parents present for children: a Cochrane review (28 RCTs) found that parental presence did not reduce the child's anxiety and worked less well than midazolam. The evidence is very uncertain. Small studies with low sensory stimulation, clowns and video games were promising, but none measured drug requirement (Manyande 2015).
  • The mechanism: in mice, activating the locus coeruleus shortened emergence from isoflurane but did not change induction (Ao 2021). No human studies were found showing that increased noradrenergic activity raises the induction dose.
  • Conclusion (interpretation based on the sources): there is evidence that calm and less stimulation can reduce anxiety and, in some studies, the need for sedatives and propofol. That this is due to “more natural inhibition in the brain” is a reasonable hypothesis that fits what is known about excitation and inhibition, but it is not proven. The effect is small to moderate, and the studies diverge.
Maranets and Kain 1999 Kil 2012 Morley 2008 Kim and Choi 2013 Chlan 2013 Fu 2020 Ayoub 2005 Kang 2008 Manyande 2015

Intensive care: sedation for days and weeks

Most of what is in the other tabs also applies to the intensive care patient, but three things are different: the sedation lasts for days to weeks, the patients often have encephalopathy, organ failure or brain injury that itself alters the EEG, and the goal is seldom unconsciousness, but calm, safe ventilator treatment and as little drug as possible. This tab collects what the sources say about EEG and processed EEG in the critically ill. Brief notes on perfusion, ICP and EEG in ischaemia are in the Perfusion tab (van Putten and Hofmeijer, Foreman and Claassen, Lenstra, Guay, Nycz).

What the EEG can give you in intensive care: seven situations

Intensive care uses EEG little compared with the operating room. Here are the situations where the sources in the app show that a frontal EEG monitor can change what you do. The details are on the cards further down the tab.

The cardiologist who examines the brain. Mashour 2013 (editorial in Anesthesiology) describes a cardiologist who performs only a neurological examination and assesses the heart with EEG and brain scanning after a run on the treadmill. Cardiology does not work this way, he writes, but anaesthesiology does: we make inferences about the nervous system from cardiovascular data, even though the target organ of general anaesthesia is the brain. Guay 2025 builds its framework on the ECG: periodic discharges resemble extrasystoles, seizures resemble ventricular tachycardia, and signs of too little oxygen to the brain resemble ST changes. Gruenbaum 2026 compares burst suppression with myocardial ischaemia on the ECG. Reflection from the author of the app: even when we are worried about the brain, we often do not look at it until any injury has already happened. The EEG detects reduced blood flow within seconds, whereas diffusion-weighted MRI needs about 30 minutes (Foreman and Claassen 2012, Perfusion tab).
  • 1. Delirium: What you can see: hypoactive delirium is often accompanied by a slow EEG dominated by slow-delta, and as the delirium resolves, power shifts towards faster frequencies (Guay 2025). The EEG can therefore show the direction over time. What the EEG cannot do: make the diagnosis on its own. In Eskioglou 2021, general slowing was just as common in patients without delirium. What distinguished delirious patients from others was burst suppression, rhythmic or periodic patterns and seizures (see Discrepancies). Use the EEG together with CAM-ICU, not instead of it. How many are quiet: in a review of 131 studies, 50 % of ICU delirium was hypoactive, 28 % mixed and 23 % hyperactive. In studies that distinguished only two types, 61 % were hypoactive. Hyperactive patients more often received drugs targeted at the delirium (64 % vs 39 %) (la Cour 2022). Clinical experience suggests that hypoactive patients are the hardest to detect, because they are simply quiet.
  • 2. Seizures without convulsions (nonconvulsive seizures): What it is: the patient lies still, but the brain is seizing. This is common in critical illness and cannot be seen without EEG (Guay 2025). What to look for: rhythmic or periodic sharp discharges on the raw EEG. Guay 2025 gives two limits: more than 25 discharges per 10 seconds suggests a seizure or status epilepticus, and 11–25 per 10 seconds (or 5–10 sharp ones) lies in a grey zone between seizure and non-seizure, called the ictal–interictal continuum. Both findings should prompt a full EEG and a neurologist's assessment. Limitation: a frontal monitor sees only the forehead and can miss seizures in the temporal and occipital lobes. In Eskioglou 2021, 7 % of delirious patients had seizures or status epilepticus. Sepsis: Lobo and Lamperti ch. 1 write that sepsis can cause electrographic seizures and periodic discharges, and that the EEG can show changes even when the neurological examination is normal. In a medical ICU, 32 % of patients with sepsis had seizures or periodic discharges, vs 9 % of others, and 67 % of seizures were purely electrographic (Oddo 2009, abstract). In children in intensive care, 58 % of those with sepsis had electrographic seizures (Abend 2013, card below). See the simulator for epileptiform patterns below.
  • 3. Neuromuscular blockade: when the patient is paralysed, the EEG is the only way to see the brain. Rasulo 2023 recommends processed EEG as the main method of assessing sedation during neuromuscular blockade. Unexpected beta and gamma during blockade should prompt more sedation. Awareness with recall has been reported in 1.8–7.4% of patients intubated in the emergency department or ICU, versus 0.07–0.9% in the operating room (Guay 2025).
  • 4. Reactivity: What it is: the EEG changes when the patient is spoken to, touched or given a painful stimulus. Typically abrupt beta and gamma appear on top of slow-delta (Guay 2025). Why it matters: Sutter and Kaplan 2012 write that reactivity distinguishes coma states better than the pattern itself, and Miller's ch. 80 states that preserved reactivity favours a good outcome after anoxic brain injury. Two patients with the same EEG may therefore have different prognoses, depending on whether the EEG responds to stimulation. Limitation: there is no standardised way to stimulate, and raters agree only moderately (Taccone 2026, van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016). See the case where the EEG changed during visits from relatives.
  • 5. The drugs in intensive care: propofol gives alpha–delta and burst suppression at high doses, dexmedetomidine a sleep-like pattern with spindles, ketamine beta and gamma, midazolam beta at sedative doses, and inhaled agents propofol-like alpha (Purdon 2015, Brandt 2020, Taccone 2026). See the simulator in the Spectrogram tab and the Drugs tab.
  • 6. Burst suppression as a goal or as a warning: burst suppression should be avoided, except to control raised intracranial pressure, and if it is used therapeutically, Rasulo 2023 recommends a suppression ratio below 5%. Other sources describe much deeper targets, with pauses of about 10 seconds (see the Burst suppression tab). Unexpected burst suppression should first prompt questions about oxygen delivery, temperature and glucose, and then a reduction of sedation (Guay 2025). Watson 2008 found burst suppression in 39% of sedated ventilated patients, and it was associated with higher 6-month mortality. See the Burst suppression tab.
  • 7. Physiological sleep, and documenting it: What you can see: when the patient is not sedated, natural sleep may appear and is readily recognisable on a frontal monitor (Guay 2025). N2 sleep has spindles and K-complexes, and N3 has slow waves (Miller's ch. 9). The spectrogram together with the raw EEG can distinguish sleep stages (Rasulo 2023). Why it matters: propofol and benzodiazepines do not produce physiological sleep, and sleep in the ICU is fragmented, with little deep NREM and REM (cards below). Guay 2025 links the slow waves of sleep to the brain clearing waste products, and points to sleep disruption as a possible contributor to cognitive sequelae after intensive care. Eskioglou 2021 cites the hypothesis that sleep elements, especially K-complexes, are associated with better outcome in encephalopathy. Documentation: RASS and CAM-ICU cannot show whether the patient has slept. Interpretation based on the sources: an EEG can document that the patient has had periods of physiological sleep, and when. Limitation: PADIS 2018 advises against routine sleep monitoring with actigraphy, BIS, EEG or polysomnography (conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence). In up to 70 % of sedated or ventilated patients the EEG does not fit standard sleep criteria, and only polysomnography determines sleep stage precisely (Miller's ch. 9). See Discrepancies.
Guay 2025 Part 2 Rasulo 2023 Taccone 2026 Eskioglou 2021 Sutter and Kaplan 2012 Watson 2008

Expect a pattern: EEG-guided management of the critically ill (Guay 2025 Part 2)

Part 2 of the review from the Brown group (Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618) gives a framework for frontal EEG in intensive care, built on the comparison with the ECG: periodic discharges resemble extrasystoles, seizures resemble ventricular tachycardia, and signs of too little oxygen to the brain resemble ST changes.

  • Step 1, expect a pattern: based on age, vital signs, disease, sedatives and neurological examination. A healthy 40-year-old on propofol 50 µg/kg/min who opens her eyes to voice is expected to show alpha–delta with bursts of beta and gamma when spoken to. A 78-year-old in septic shock on propofol 20 µg/kg/min who does not respond is expected to show slow-delta, burst suppression or suppression.
  • RASS and EEG: RASS −5 without neurological disease is expected to give alpha–delta, slow-delta or burst suppression. RASS −4 to −1 typically gives abrupt beta and gamma on top of slow-delta when the patient is stimulated. RASS 0 to +1 gives sustained beta and gamma, and RASS +2 to +4 gives a lot of movement and EMG artefact. Natural sleep may also be seen.
  • Step 2, signal quality: low impedance, good gel contact, no leads touching other electrical equipment, and electrodes replaced every 24 hours or as recommended by the manufacturer. The amplitude scale is set as low (sensitive) as possible without clipping the peaks, and the power scale is adapted to what you are looking for. Which scales are available varies between monitors. Clinical experience suggests that a very sensitive scale, for example 1 µV/mm, magnifies the trace so much that ordinary activity can look sharp and epileptiform and the peaks are clipped. Choose the most sensitive scale at which the waves are still shown in full, and change the scale before interpreting anything as epileptiform activity. The raw EEG shows the current state, the spectrogram shows the trend.
  • Step 3, when the pattern does not fit: suspected seizures prompt a full EEG, a neurologist and consideration of antiseizure drugs and more sedation. Unexpected beta and gamma during deep sedation or paralysis prompt more sedation and/or antinociception. Unexpected low activity (shift to lower frequencies, broadband power loss, burst suppression) should first be assessed as an imbalance between oxygen delivery and consumption: hypoxaemia, anaemia and low blood flow, as well as hypothermia, hypoglycaemia and severe hypercapnia. Only then is sedation reduced. If the pattern persists without sedation, primary neurological disease should be investigated.
  • How often: there is no guideline. As with blood pressure and SpO₂, the EEG can be assessed every time you enter the patient's room, more often the more unstable the patient.
  • Case 1: a 39-year-old with respiratory failure in burst suppression on propofol 50 µg/kg/min without signs of oxygen deficit. Reduction to 40 and then 20 µg/kg/min gave alpha–delta. Two days later, burst suppression appeared every time MAP was below 70 mmHg, with right heart failure and rising CVP, and disappeared with adrenaline.
  • Case 2: an elderly patient after mitral valve surgery with falling amplitude (from 30–40 to 10–20 µV) before burst suppression, at a cardiac index of 1.3. After mechanical circulatory support (cardiac index 2.7) the activity returned. The next day, during a sedation hold, she was still unresponsive after 4 hours, and the frontal EEG showed triphasic periodic discharges (10–15 per 10 seconds). A full EEG confirmed nonconvulsive seizures, which were treated, and she woke without deficits.
  • Caveats: a review with cases from a single institution, not an outcome study. Frontal EEG has limited sensitivity for seizures and ischaemia outside the frontal lobe. Brown reports patents, royalties from Masimo and co-founding a company developing control of physiological states during anaesthesia. Brown and Guay hold a joint patent, and Guay has received travel support from Masimo.
Guay et al. Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618

The cards on burst suppression are collected in the tab.

Consensus on processed EEG during sedation of the critically ill (Rasulo 2023)

International expert panel (Neurocrit Care 2023;38:296–311), 21 clinicians in neurointensive care and neuroanaesthesia, Delphi method without a systematic literature review. 59 statements: 47 rated appropriate with strong consensus, 2 inappropriate, 3 with weak consensus, 2 uncertain and 5 without consensus. The document is to be revised after 5 years.

  • Technique: pEEG is suitable for monitoring sedation level; four to five channels are sufficient, a frontal montage is sufficient, and the monitor should display raw EEG with adjustable speed and amplitude scale as well as a continuous colour spectrogram with adjustable power scale (all strong consensus). Whether two channels are enough reached no consensus.
  • The index number: the panel could not recommend dimensionless indices as sufficient for monitoring sedation depth in the critically ill (uncertain, but with strong consensus about the uncertainty). If they are used, the manufacturer's target range should be followed, and the number should be checked against the raw EEG rhythm.
  • Burst suppression: should be avoided in all situations except to control raised intracranial pressure (strong consensus). Suppression ratio (SR) is a good measure, and if burst suppression is used therapeutically, SR should be kept below 5% (strong consensus). The article does not justify the figure, and other sources describe much deeper targets (see Discrepancies and the Burst suppression tab). The background notes that age and comorbidity lower the amplitude and weaken alpha, which increases the propensity for burst suppression.
  • Who: all sedated patients where clinical assessment is not possible, all who need deep sedation (RASS ≤ −3), patients on ECMO, patients receiving brief deep sedation for procedures, and separate criteria for older patients (all strong consensus). After cardiac arrest, continuous EEG is recommended during cooling and rewarming or in the event of seizures. During neuromuscular blockade, pEEG should be the main method for sedation assessment (strong consensus).
  • Who not: patients with only light sedation (RASS 0 to −2) do not benefit from it. RASS and SAS remain the most valid tools, and pEEG should supplement, not replace, the scales. In non-comatose, non-paralysed patients the panel could not recommend indices as the main method. Start as early as possible and measure continuously.
  • Interpretation: pEEG values vary between patients at the same clinical sedation level, and are affected by blood flow, hypothermia, age and brain injury. During light sedation, EMG can artificially raise the values.
  • Training: structured training with certification, in the frequency, time and power domains, rapid recognition of typical patterns, and access to a neurointensivist or neurophysiologist when needed (strong consensus).
  • Barriers and caveats: the panel itself mentions lack of knowledge, lack of validation in prolonged sedation, lack of standardisation between monitors with different algorithms, and cost. No systematic literature review, and the panel selection may have introduced bias: nine of the authors report speaker fees or positions with Masimo, Medtronic, Edwards or Nihon Kohden, and one is a medical director at Masimo.
Rasulo et al. Neurocrit Care 2023;38:296–311

EEG as a bedside monitor in intensive care: the intensivist's perspective (Taccone 2026)

Perspective article in Critical Care 2026;30:195 (Taccone, Ozkaya, Baggiani, Rasulo). No original data; an argument for how EEG can become a genuine bedside monitoring tool in intensive care.

  • The problem: EEG is non-invasive, cheap and meaningful, but does not meet the requirements of a bedside monitor (immediately available, continuously interpretable, directly actionable). Electrode placement requires technicians, continuous EEG cannot be offered to everyone, visual interpretation of raw EEG by experts remains the reference standard, and even experts have only moderate agreement on patterns on the ictal-interictal continuum (Jing 2023). For many intensive care teams the EEG machine is “a foreign body” at the bedside.
  • Four things the intensivist needs: background activity (continuous, discontinuous or suppressed), asymmetry, burst suppression (spontaneous or drug-induced) and ictal or highly epileptiform activity (ACNS 2021 terminology). Brief, structured training improves classification by intensivists and nurses (Citerio, Taran). The parallel is echocardiography and lung ultrasound, which intensivists use without being cardiologists.
  • Montage according to the question: continuous EEG is superior for seizure detection and DCI after SAH, whereas brief intermittent recordings may suffice for prognosis after cardiac arrest. A full 10–20 is needed for localisation, whereas simplified montages may be adequate to detect burst suppression from oversedation or highly malignant patterns after hypoxia. Continuous and intermittent EEG are not interchangeable even though outcome studies have not shown a difference.
  • Four levels of interpretation: (1) a binary “red” alarm signal on the patient monitor for nurses without EEG training, for example a brain icon indicating the side; (2) type of abnormality for doctors without formal EEG training; (3) quantitative trends (spectrogram, SEF, amplitude trend, alpha/delta ratio, burst suppression ratio, seizure probability) for EEG-trained intensive care clinicians; (4) raw EEG with montages and filters for the neurophysiologist. No treatment decision should be made by untrained staff on the basis of the alarm alone.
  • Spectrogram and SEF: the spectrogram is suited to seeing progressive background slowing (oversedation or raised ICP) and burst suppression (black bars). Low SEF means deeper suppression, whereas apparently increased high-frequency power may be EMG. Seizures appear as focal “hot spots” that build up and fade gradually, in contrast to artefacts, which are abrupt and do not evolve.
  • Drug signatures: the article reproduces Purdon 2015: propofol gives increasing delta and alpha and burst suppression at high doses, dexmedetomidine a sleep-like delta pattern, ketamine an activated picture with high beta and low gamma, and volatile agents propofol-like alpha at low concentrations, “but higher doses add theta activity and a broader spectral distribution”. This agrees with the theta fill-in in the simulator in the Spectrogram tab.
  • EEG reactivity: has shown diagnostic and prognostic value, but reproducibility varies and there is no standardised stimulation protocol, so for now it belongs at the expert level.
  • Caveats: a perspective without data, with proposals (alarm levels, AI detection) that have not been validated in multicentre studies; alarm fatigue and costs are unresolved. Taccone is a scientific adviser for Neuroptics and Nihon Kohden, and Rasulo reports speaker fees from Masimo. No funding.
Taccone et al. Crit Care 2026;30:195

PADIS 2018: what the guideline says about sedation depth and EEG monitoring (Devlin 2018)

The Society of Critical Care Medicine guideline for pain, agitation/sedation, delirium, immobility and sleep in adult intensive care patients (Crit Care Med 2018;46:e825–e873). GRADE methodology, with patient representatives on the panel.

  • Light sedation: recommends light rather than deep sedation in ventilated patients (conditional recommendation, low quality). Light sedation was defined as RASS −2 to +1 in the studies. Eight RCTs: shorter time to extubation (−0.77 days) and fewer tracheostomies (RR 0.57), but no difference in 90-day mortality (RR 1.01), delirium (RR 0.96), PTSD or self-extubation. The panel considers the old definition (RASS ≥ −2 with eye opening for 10 minutes) probably deeper than necessary.
  • Daily sedation interruption or nurse-driven protocol: both can achieve and maintain light sedation (ungraded). A brief sedation interruption should not be used as an excuse for deep sedation for the rest of the day.
  • Choice of agent: propofol or dexmedetomidine rather than benzodiazepines (conditional, low quality). Dexmedetomidine should not be used when deep sedation (with or without neuromuscular blockade) is required. Dexmedetomidine is suggested in delirium where agitation prevents weaning.
  • Objective sedation monitoring (ungraded): BIS “appears best suited for titration during deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade”, and can improve titration when a sedation scale cannot be used. 32 intensive care studies of BIS against scales were reviewed. Three studies of BIS-guided sedation showed lower sedative use and faster awakening, fewer procedure-related events, and lower midazolam and fentanyl doses, less agitation, fewer tracheostomies and shorter length of stay.
  • Why scale and EEG do not track each other: the scales bottom out at RASS −5, while the EEG can continue down to an isoelectric line; during agitation BIS tops out at 100 while the scales continue upwards. The scales also require stimulation, which in itself raises the index, so the timing of the EEG reading relative to the stimulation determines the agreement. Studies that did not account for this had the poorest agreement.
  • Sleep: advises against routine physiological sleep monitoring (actigraphy, BIS, EEG, polysomnography) clinically (conditional, very low quality).
  • Caveats: most of the recommendations are conditional with low quality of evidence. Several panel members report conflicts of interest, including an EEG-based delirium monitor under development.
Devlin et al. Crit Care Med 2018;46:e825–e873

Simulator: epileptiform patterns in the raw EEG

Schematic, synthetic traces with four frontal channels (L1, R1, L2, R2) on a sedated alpha–delta background. The shapes are drawn from the descriptions in Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4, Guay 2025 and Sutter and Kaplan 2012. They are not patient data, and a frontal trace can never replace a full EEG and a neurologist. Amplitudes and scale are approximate: the sources give duration and frequency, not amplitude, and 1 mm on screen is not necessarily 1 mm on the monitor.

Time window
Scale

ACNS 2021 (Hirsch et al.) Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4 Guay 2025 Part 2 Sutter and Kaplan 2012 Schematic, not patient data

Electrographic seizures in children in intensive care (Abend 2013)

Retrospective cohort from 11 centres in the USA and Canada (Neurology 2013;81:383–391): 550 children aged 1 month to 21 years with continuous EEG in the paediatric ICU, ordered on clinical indication and at least 6 hours long.

  • How common: 162 of 550 (30 %) had electrographic seizures, and 61 of these (38 %) had electrographic status epilepticus. In 59 of 162 (36 %) all seizures were without clinical signs.
  • By diagnosis: sepsis had the highest proportion (58 % of 19), followed by epilepsy (48 % of 159), brain malformation (38 %), CNS inflammation or autoimmune disease (33 %), stroke and traumatic brain injury (30 %), metabolic causes and CNS infection (29 %) and hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy (18 % of 73). Children only pharmacologically sedated with no known neurological problem: 13 % of 15. After neuromuscular blockade: 8 % of 26. A child could have several diagnoses.
  • The seizures: 38 % lasted 10–59 seconds, 40 % 1–5 minutes, 16 % 6–30 minutes and 6 % more than 30 minutes. Onset was focal in 53 %, multifocal in 19 % and generalised in 24 %.
  • Risk and outcome: younger age, clinical seizures before EEG, abnormal background and interictal epileptiform discharges increased risk. Electrographic status epilepticus was associated with higher mortality (OR 2.42, 95 % CI 1.08–5.40), whereas seizures without status were not.
  • Caveats: retrospective, EEGs read locally without central review, and practice varied between centres. Small groups per diagnosis (sepsis: 19 children). Several authors report fees and research funding; there was no targeted funding for the study.
Abend et al. Neurology 2013;81:383–391

When the index does not see the seizure: published examples

Nonconvulsive seizures can look like deep sedation on a frontal monitor. Three published papers show how, and what revealed the seizures.

  • Ntahe 2018 (case report): a 75-year-old woman, comatose after cardiac arrest, with nonconvulsive status epilepticus diagnosed with conventional EEG. During treatment BIS lay between 25 and 35 and SR between 20 and 35. When hypnotics were weaned on day 3, the raw EEG from the BIS monitor showed high-amplitude, irregular waves with spikes, spike-and-wave and polyspikes, alternating with a flat signal, while BIS and SR did not change significantly. Conventional EEG confirmed recurrence with continuous, generalised rhythmic spikes and spike-and-wave at 1–1.5 Hz. The conclusion is that the BIS monitor cannot replace conventional EEG, and that the raw EEG must be read together with the numbers.
  • Haesen 2018 (validation study): 32 comatose patients after cardiac arrest in whom the raw EEG from the BIS monitor was compared with full EEG. For status epilepticus, sensitivity was 86 % and specificity 100 % by consensus between two neurophysiologists. Two inexperienced investigators identified status epilepticus with sensitivity 70–90 % and specificity 92–96 %. Periodic epileptiform discharges were picked up in only 25 % of cases, probably because only frontotemporal leads were recorded.
  • Hernández-Hernández 2016 (two children): bilateral BIS spectrogram during status epilepticus in a 5-month-old infant and a 7-year-old child. In the infant the seizure activity appeared as the colours in the low frequencies shifting from orange, yellow and green to dark red, without clinical convulsions. The pattern disappeared after thiopental.
  • Sepsis: sepsis can cause electrographic seizures and periodic discharges (Lobo and Lamperti ch. 1), most seizures in the medical ICU are purely electrographic (Oddo 2009), and among children in intensive care, sepsis had the highest proportion of seizures (Abend 2013, above).
  • Interpretation based on the sources: the index tells you where the power lies in frequency, not whether the activity is epileptiform. Low-frequency periodic discharges can therefore give a low index and low SEF that resemble deep sedation, while broadband discharges can give higher numbers (Gimson 2021). It is the raw EEG that reveals the pattern. See the simulator above and images 19 and 20 in the image quiz.
  • Caveats: case reports and a small retrospective single-centre study, all with BIS. None of them tells how often the index misses. In Ntahe 2018 the sensor was changed from four to two channels on day 3. Ntahe 2018 and Haesen 2018 report no conflicts of interest.
Ntahe 2018, Haesen 2018, Hernández-Hernández 2016, Gimson 2021

The balance between excitation and inhibition: why ICU patients without brain disease can have seizures

The brain is kept stable by a balance between excitation (mostly glutamate) and inhibition (mostly GABA). If the balance shifts towards excitation, the seizure threshold falls: less is needed to trigger a seizure. (A higher seizure threshold means the opposite, that more is needed.) Fritschy 2008 points out that the model is simplified: GABA can be excitatory in some situations, and the balance depends among other things on the chloride transporters NKCC1 and KCC2 and on sustained (tonic) inhibition outside the synapses.

  • How common: of 201 patients in a medical ICU with continuous EEG, 10% had electrographic seizures and 22% seizures or periodic discharges. With sepsis the proportion was 32% versus 9% without, and sepsis was the only independent risk factor (OR 4.6) (Oddo 2009). Most seizures were non-convulsive and would not have been seen without EEG.
  • Sepsis: inflammatory mediators (including TNF-α) and bacterial toxins damage the blood–brain barrier and cause septic encephalopathy with a slow EEG (Kuperberg and Wadgaonkar 2017). Exactly how this shifts the balance towards excitation is not described in the source.
  • Electrolytes: hyponatraemia most often causes seizures when sodium falls rapidly below 115 mmol/L. Hypocalcaemia causes seizures in 20–25% of acute cases. Hypomagnesaemia causes seizures mostly below about 1 mEq/L, and magnesium normally blocks the NMDA receptor, one of the glutamate receptors. Potassium disorders do not cause seizures (Nardone 2016).
  • Low blood glucose: symptoms from the brain appear at about 3.0 mmol/L, cognitive dysfunction at about 2.8 mmol/L, and then seizures and coma at about 2.3–2.7 mmol/L (Cryer 2007).
  • Antibiotics: of 135 cases of cefepime neurotoxicity, 80% had renal impairment, and 25% of those who had an EEG had non-convulsive status epilepticus. 26% developed neurotoxicity despite correct dosing (Payne 2017). Beta-lactams, especially imipenem, are thought to inhibit the GABAA receptor. Carbapenems lower valproate levels by 50–88% (Radkowski 2025).
  • Withdrawal: alcohol withdrawal seizures usually occur 6–48 hours after the last drink and involve NMDA and GABA receptors (Hillbom 2003). GHB withdrawal starts 1–6 hours after the last dose (Karila 2024). Seizure-like phenomena with propofol occur mostly at induction and emergence, rarely during maintenance (Kumar 2021).
  • Why withdrawal causes seizures (interpretation based on the sources): with long-term use of substances that enhance GABA (alcohol, benzodiazepines, GHB, propofol), the brain adapts with less inhibition or more excitation. When the substance disappears suddenly, the adapted excitation is left without a counterweight.
  • What it means for sedation (interpretation based on the sources): GABA-enhancing sedatives raise the seizure threshold and can hide clinical convulsions without stopping electrical seizures. In patients with sepsis, renal failure, electrolyte disorders, cefepime or a carbapenem, or possible withdrawal, the threshold for EEG should therefore be low.
Fritschy 2008 Oddo 2009 Nardone 2016 Cryer 2007 Payne 2017 Radkowski 2025 Hillbom 2003

Invasive neuromonitoring in intensive care: ICP, PRx, PbtO2 and microdialysis (Lobo and Lamperti, ch. 12)

The chapter (Pusateri and Robba) deals with the brain-injured patient and supplements the EEG material in the Perfusion tab.

  • ICP: normally 5–15 mmHg when supine. The Brain Trauma Foundation has changed the treatment threshold across four editions (20, 20–25, 20 and most recently 22 mmHg), and the chapter stresses that the optimal threshold is uncertain: below 20 may be harmful for some, above the threshold may be tolerated by others. Indication for invasive measurement in severe TBI (GCS 3–8) with abnormal CT, or normal CT with two of: age over 40, motor posturing, systolic BP below 90.
  • PRx: the correlation coefficient between ICP and MAP over time, as a measure of pressure autoregulation. Negative PRx means good cerebrovascular reserve, around 0 a compensated phase, positive PRx poor reserve. Used to find the patient's optimal CPP (CPPopt) instead of a single common target (BTF recommends 60–70 mmHg).
  • PbtO2: tissue oxygen measured with a probe in white matter; normally 20–35 mmHg, below 20 compromised, below 15 brain hypoxia. Below 20 mmHg is seen in over 70% of TBI patients in the first days even with normal ICP and CPP. Focal measurement, so the placement determines what is measured.
  • Microdialysis: glucose, lactate, pyruvate, glycerol and glutamate from the interstitium. The lactate/pyruvate ratio (normally 15–20) rises with anaerobic metabolism; low glucose, high LPR, high glutamate and glycerol suggest ischaemia or secondary injury.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 12

Neurointensive care: CBF thresholds, CPP, ICP and EEG as prognosis (Miller's ch. 80)

The chapter “Neurocritical Care” (Ko and Engelhard) deals with the brain-injured intensive care patient. What concerns EEG, sedation and perfusion is collected here; the rest (SAH, stroke, neuromuscular disease, brain death) is omitted.

  • Functional CBF thresholds (table 80.5): normal CBF 50 ml/100 g/min, EEG slowing at 20, isoelectric EEG at 15, ischaemic penumbra 6–15, neuronal death below 6. The table has no separate reference in the chapter. This is the background for using EEG as an ischaemia monitor (see van Putten and Hofmeijer and Foreman and Claassen in the Perfusion tab).
  • CPP: MAP minus ICP, with the zero point for MAP at the external auditory meatus (the same reference Kalmar 2010 used). Recommended 60–70 mmHg after TBI; both higher and lower worsen outcome, and CPP above 90 mmHg with fluids and pressors increases the risk of respiratory failure. The chapter points out that measures that lower ICP, such as head elevation and barbiturate coma, also lower MAP and can thereby lower CPP. Individual CPPopt (Aries 2012, Petkus 2020) is mentioned as an alternative to a single common target.
  • ICP: threshold 22 mmHg (BTF 2017, Carney), but the chapter states outright that both indication and threshold are more expert- than evidence-based. The only randomised trial (Chesnut 2012, BEST-TRIP) found no effect of ICP measurement on long-term outcome, while an observational study from 146 ICUs suggested lower 6-month mortality. Time above threshold counts: ICP 20 mmHg for over 37 minutes worsened outcome, shorter episodes did not (Güiza 2015), and impaired autoregulation or CPP below 50 makes the patient less tolerant of high ICP.
  • Autoregulation: PRx (correlation of ICP against arterial pressure, −1 to +1) is the established continuous measure, but TCD velocity, PbtO2 or NIRS can be used instead of ICP to calculate an autoregulation index. Absent autoregulation is more often associated with poor outcome.
  • Oxygenation: SjvO2 normally 55–75%, both below 50 and above 75 are associated with poor outcome, but the method is on its way out. PbtO2 normally 20–45 mmHg, below 15–20 is regarded as ischaemia, below 10 severe ischaemia; treatment guided by ICP, CPP and PbtO2 above 20 was better than ICP and CPP alone (Lin 2015, Spiotta 2010, Nangunoori 2012). NIRS normally 60–75%, but low sensitivity for isolated cerebral hypoperfusion in TBI and SAH, good as a trend monitor during systemic changes (cardiac surgery).
  • Continuous EEG in neurointensive care: in unconscious patients EEG should be used continuously to detect non-convulsive seizures, which are frequent and cause ICP rises and metabolic crisis (Vespa 2007; ESICM consensus, Claassen 2013). Automatic seizure detection has many false positives and negatives and cannot replace an EEG-trained neurologist (Schramm 2017). The chapter mentions that pEEG monitors for depth of anaesthesia use the same frequencies.
  • EEG as prognosis after anoxia: burst suppression, alpha coma and low-voltage delta are called malignant patterns associated with poor outcome, while preserved EEG reactivity favours good outcome. The sentence stands without a reference in the chapter. Bilateral absence of N20 (SSEP after median nerve stimulation) is the most reliable predictor of not waking after anoxic coma (Zandbergen 2006, Sandroni 2020). Note that Forgacs 2020 and Jegarl 2026 (Burst suppression tab) describe burst suppression after cardiac arrest as a pattern that can progress to good consciousness; the chapter uses the term without distinguishing between spontaneous and drug-induced burst suppression.
  • Sedation in TBI: agents with a short context-sensitive half-time (propofol) to allow daily neurological examination, with a warning about propofol infusion syndrome at high doses over several days (Cremer 2001). Barbiturates and benzodiazepines have long half-lives and are less suitable; barbiturate treatment for refractory ICP “under EEG monitoring” appears as item 8 in the checklist (box 80.2), after sedation, CSF drainage and osmotherapy. High-dose propofol, prophylactic hyperventilation (PaCO2 below 30), steroids and therapeutic hypothermia are on the list of measures that are not recommended. Ketamine is no longer regarded as contraindicated in intubated and ventilated TBI patients (Kolenda 1997). Targets: PaO2 80–120 and PaCO2 35–38 mmHg.
  • Status epilepticus: third line is midazolam or propofol infusion, possibly thiopental or pentobarbital; in super-refractory status, volatile anaesthetics and ketamine are mentioned. Continuous EEG is recommended to guide treatment and to detect non-convulsive seizures in comatose patients, and prolonged neuromuscular blockade should be avoided because it masks seizures.
