The authors call the numbers “contradictory” and point out that ke0 in Schnider and modified Marsh is derived from time to peak effect after a rapid bolus, while Schnider's own Emax model gives an EC50 of 2.35 µg/ml for loss of consciousness with slow infusion.
  • Caveats: 16 patients (8 + 8) in Sepúlveda 2020 and 2021, while Obert 2020 reports 18 included (see discrepancies). Only healthy subjects under 65, only frontal EEG, Marsh model (not Schnider or Eleveld), and consciousness measured as response (FOUR score), not as experience. No conflicts of interest in Sepúlveda 2020; none in Obert 2020.
Sepúlveda et al. Anaesthesia 2020;75:196–201; Obert et al. Sci Rep 2020;10:19444; Sepúlveda et al. Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim 2021;68:245–251

Why Ce at loss of consciousness after a bolus cannot be used as a maintenance target (Sepúlveda 2010, Coppens 2010)

Two studies from 2010 that form the basis for most of the criticism above.

  • Sepúlveda 2010 (Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2010;54:447–452): 16 healthy volunteers aged 21–45 received, in randomised order, both a bolus of 1.8 mg/kg (1,200 ml/h) and an infusion of 12 mg/kg/h, with the Cerebral State Index as monitor. Loss of consciousness after 0.97 minutes (bolus) versus 6.8 minutes (infusion). Calculated Ce at loss of consciousness, bolus versus infusion: Schnider (ke0 0.45) 4.40 versus 2.81 µg/ml; modified Marsh (ke0 1.21) 3.55 versus 2.50; original Marsh (ke0 0.26) 1.28 versus 1.72. CSI at loss of consciousness was the same (70 versus 71). Conclusion: “Ce predicted at loss of consciousness after a TCI induction dose should not be used as a reference value for titrating hypnosis during maintenance.” The authors believe the error lies in the “front-end” kinetics: the models describe the early distribution after a bolus poorly. No plasma measurements. No conflicts of interest, departmentally funded.
  • Coppens 2010 (Br J Anaesth 2010;104:452–458, Ghent, with Schnider as co-author): 60 patients received propofol at 300 ml/h until they stopped responding to their name, and the calculated Ce at that moment was set as the effect-site target for 20 minutes with one of three models. Ce at loss of response was 1.96 (Marsh, ke0 0.26), 5.54 (Schnider, fixed ke0 0.456) and 5.08 µg/ml (Schnider, ke0 adjusted to time to peak effect 1.6 min). With Marsh, all patients woke up (after an average of 401 seconds, because the pump stood still for 233 seconds); with the two Schnider variants, BIS kept falling for 11 minutes to a deeper level than intended, and one patient woke up. Conclusion: targeting Ce at loss of consciousness does not give an immediately constant effect with any of the models, and surrogate measures such as BIS are needed to see when steady state is reached. The authors write that the strength of effect-site TCI is not to predict the effect in the individual, but to keep the state stable once a clinical endpoint has been reached.
  • What the two show together: the number the pump displays at loss of consciousness depends on model and speed, and the same number gives a different effect over time. That is why EEG (or an index) is necessary to find the patient's own level, and why the Sepúlveda group proposes slow induction, in which Ce and effect have time to follow each other. Mehler 2024 (Spectrogram tab) draws the consequence and reduces Ce by 15% below the level at loss of response when Schnider is used after slow induction.
Sepúlveda et al. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2010;54:447–452; Coppens et al. Br J Anaesth 2010;104:452–458

The cards on burst suppression are collected in the tab.

A critical look at the effect-site model for propofol (Sepúlveda and Demaría 2019)

Review article in Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim 2019;66:425–433.

  • The questions the article raises: do the EEG indices represent the effect? Are the indices used to build the models comparable, and what is the real response time of the monitors? Is ke0 affected by infusion rate and by age? Are induction and emergence mirror images, as the Emax models assume?
  • ke0: a first-order transfer constant in a linear, proportional model, tied to one specific PK model. The models are useful as a titration reference, but incomplete for induction, changes of plan and emergence, because they assume a linear relationship between plasma concentration and effect.
  • Clinical observation: fast induction towards an arbitrary EC95 requires a Ce of around 5 µg/ml (equivalent to about a 2 mg/kg bolus), while stepwise slow induction gives loss of consciousness at around 2.5 µg/ml.
  • Age and ke0: for remifentanil, equilibration is about three times slower in older patients (Minto), and similar is seen for fentanyl, cisatracurium and sevoflurane, but ke0 is not age-adjusted in the propofol models in clinical use.
  • Neural inertia: different concentrations for losing and regaining response (Friedman 2010, fruit flies and rats) do not fit a single concentration–effect curve. See Proekt and Kelz 2021 and Warnaby 2017 in the Spectrogram tab.
  • Caveats: narrative review; some of the arguments rest on unpublished data (EuroSIVA 2009). No conflicts of interest declared.
Sepúlveda and Demaría. Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim 2019;66:425–433

Emergence is not induction in reverse: hysteresis, neural inertia and “reboot”

Traditionally, emergence has been seen as induction in reverse: the agent disappears, and the brain returns along the same path. Several lines of evidence say that this is not correct. The phenomenon is called anaesthetic hysteresis (loss of consciousness requires a higher concentration than the one that keeps the patient unconscious during emergence) and is explained by neural inertia (Friedman 2010): the brain resists changing state in both directions.

  • Human data with fMRI (Huang 2021, Neuroimage): 26 healthy volunteers (18 analysed), propofol TCI (Marsh) stepped up by 0.4 µg/ml every 5 minutes to loss of response, then free emergence. Loss of response occurred at a higher calculated effect-site concentration than return of response (p < 0.0001), a hysteresis loop. Induction was gradual: the time scale of neural processing (autocorrelation) increased across the whole brain and connectivity fell. Emergence was abrupt: the cortical time scale normalised suddenly, and connectivity between thalamus, pallidum, brainstem and cortex jumped. The authors themselves use the word reboot: “a rapid increase in the speed of cortical processing and subcortico-cortical interactions may be a mechanism that reboots consciousness”. Pharmacokinetics alone did not explain the asymmetry. Limitation: the concentration is model-calculated, not measured, and only propofol.
  • Animal studies, nuclei (Zhang and Wei 2025, review): orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus control emergence, but not induction (Kelz 2008: removal of orexin delayed emergence without altering the EC50 for loss of righting). The same applies to serotonergic neurons in the dorsal raphe, dopaminergic neurons in the VTA, orexinergic terminals in the basal forebrain and locus coeruleus, PVT, lateral habenula and prefrontal cortex. Other nuclei (PnO) control only induction. In patients, plasma orexin-A rises during emergence, not during induction. Caveats: almost exclusively male mice and rats, mostly isoflurane, and only 3 of the studies report EC50; the patterns vary between agents.
  • Emergence can be actively induced (Solt 2011, Anesthesiology): methylphenidate (dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor) in rats halved the time to emergence (median 280 to 91 s) and restored righting in 11 of 12 animals during ongoing isoflurane, with an EEG shift from delta to theta within 30 seconds and increased ventilation; droperidol (D2/α1 antagonist) blocked everything. The point for EEG: emergence is an active arousal process from the brainstem and hypothalamus, not merely the absence of agent. Methylphenidate is not approved for this in humans.
  • The concepts (Mashour 2022, Anesth Analg): wakefulness (arousal) and consciousness (awareness) are different things; response is not the same as consciousness, and lack of response is not the same as unconsciousness (“unresponsiveness ≠ unconsciousness”, Sanders 2012). Mashour lists animal experiments in which stimulation of the thalamus, parabrachial nucleus, VTA, locus coeruleus, basal forebrain or prefrontal cortex reverses anaesthesia, and notes that recovery probably proceeds from caudal to rostral structures. Conflict of interest: consultant for TRYP Therapeutics.
  • What it means clinically: (1) that the EEG does not return to the baseline pattern at the same calculated concentration after burst suppression (Sepúlveda 2026, Burst suppression tab) is hysteresis seen in the EEG; (2) that emergence from sevoflurane often passes through a delta-dominated stage (Hesse 2019, Miyasaka 2025) and that the course, not just the dose, may matter for delirium; (3) that “alpha without theta” or a low dose does not guarantee rapid emergence, because the inertia resides in the network, not only in the concentration. Hysteresis in humans is nevertheless debated: Kuizenga 2018 and Warnaby 2017 did not find it for propofol, while Ferreira 2020, Nir 2019, Sepúlveda 2019 and Huang 2021 did.
Huang 2021, Zhang and Wei 2025, Solt 2011, Mashour 2022

How the brain wakes up: the neurotransmitters behind emergence (Kelz 2019)

Narrative review (Anesth Analg 2019;128:726–736; Kelz, García, Mashour and Solt). Emergence was long seen as a passive process occurring when concentration falls below a critical value. The authors describe it as an active, controllable process that can be driven by mechanisms distinct from induction. Much rests on animal studies, but the authors include only signalling systems for which there are also human data.

  • Two reasons to think emergence is not induction in reverse: some neuronal groups for sleep and wakefulness take part differently in the two transitions, and there is hysteresis: the concentration at which consciousness is lost is higher than that at which it returns. This has traditionally been explained by pharmacokinetics, but the authors argue newer data suggest hysteresis is a general property of the nervous system.
  • Acetylcholine: propofol and volatile agents lower cortical acetylcholine, ketamine and nitrous oxide raise it. A nicotinic agonist in the central thalamus reversed sevoflurane and desflurane during ongoing administration, whereas a nicotinic antagonist did not change induction. A cholinergic agonist (carbachol) in prefrontal cortex produced full arousal in rats at about 1 MAC sevoflurane, but not in parietal cortex. Physostigmine has reversed sevoflurane and propofol in humans, but not consistently. Low-dose ketamine during isoflurane produced burst suppression but faster emergence (about 45 %), called «paradoxical emergence».
  • Physostigmine for agitation on emergence: Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010 call physostigmine «a standard treatment for emergence delirium». Physostigmine crosses the blood–brain barrier and increases cholinergic activity in the cortex. Miller's ch. 61 advises against atropine, scopolamine, first-generation antihistamines and phenothiazine antiemetics in older patients perioperatively because of central anticholinergic effects. Clinical experience from the author of the app: on a cardiac intensive care unit many years ago, physostigmine was given when patients woke agitated after cardiac surgery. The indication was agitation; whether central anticholinergic syndrome was suspected, for example after atropine, is not known.
  • Norepinephrine: mice without norepinephrine were 10–20 % more sensitive at induction, but the largest difference was that they woke much later. Norepinephrine in the central thalamus hastened emergence from propofol without changing induction. The authors conclude that norepinephrine primes the brain for emergence but is not strong enough on its own to keep it awake.
  • Orexin: blocking orexin did not change induction but delayed emergence from isoflurane and sevoflurane in rodents. This was the first sign that emergence is not a mirror image of induction. Some patients with narcolepsy wake later after anaesthesia. High CO₂ hastens emergence, perhaps because orexin neurones are activated by CO₂.
  • Dopamine: methylphenidate (Ritalin) and dextroamphetamine restored wake-like behaviour in animals during ongoing isoflurane, sevoflurane and propofol. The effect is mainly via dopamine, because the pure norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor atomoxetine did not rouse the rats. The D1 receptor appears most important, and the source is the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
  • Adenosine and caffeine: sleep deprivation lowered the dose needed for unconsciousness with propofol, sevoflurane and isoflurane in rats. Caffeine hastened emergence from isoflurane and propofol in rats, and from isoflurane in healthy volunteers in a double-blind crossover study.
  • GABA and flumazenil: flumazenil given to patients who had not received benzodiazepines produced EEG signs of arousal and faster emergence in one study with propofol and remifentanil. In another study it did not speed emergence but improved cognition in recovery.
  • Caveats: narrative review, mostly animal studies. Effects in humans are small or uncertain, and none of the methods is clinically established. No conflicts of interest, NIH-funded.
Kelz, García, Mashour and Solt. Anesth Analg 2019;128:726–736

A brainstem switch for induction and emergence: the PPT and sevoflurane (Li 2024)

Animal study in mice (Br J Anaesth 2024;132:320–333) of glutamatergic neurones in the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPT) of the brainstem. The PPT projects to, among others, the thalamus, hypothalamus, basal forebrain and the ventral tegmental area (VTA), which is important for wakefulness and reward.

  • Activity follows consciousness: neuronal activity fell before the mice lost the righting reflex under sevoflurane, stayed low while they were unconscious, and rose again as they woke.
  • Inhibition gives faster induction and slower emergence: when the neurones were inhibited chemogenetically, the mice lost consciousness faster (76 versus 121 seconds) and woke later (278 versus 145 seconds), and became more sensitive to sevoflurane. The EEG showed more delta.
  • Stimulation wakes during ongoing volatile anaesthesia: light stimulation of the neurones, or of the pathway from the PPT to the VTA, produced awake-like behaviour during steady sevoflurane anaesthesia and activated the cortex. During sevoflurane-induced burst suppression, the suppression ratio fell from about 55 % to about 6 % during stimulation.
  • Shared circuits for both transitions: because both induction and emergence were affected, the authors interpret this as shared circuits for loss and recovery of consciousness. This nuances Kelz 2019, where orexin delayed emergence without changing induction (see the card above and Discrepancies).
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): the finding supports that consciousness under anaesthesia is regulated by brainstem networks and not only by the cortex, and that emergence can be actively influenced. It is not clinically transferable today.
  • Caveats: mice, few animals per group (8–14), sevoflurane only. The authors do not know whether sevoflurane acts directly on the neurones or via their inputs. High-frequency light stimulation may also activate other pathways. No conflicts of interest, funded by Chinese research councils.
  • The editorial (McKinstry-Wu and Kelz 2024, “One node among many”): the finding supports the hypothesis that sleep and anaesthesia share circuits. But the PPT is only one of many neuronal populations in the forebrain, midbrain and brainstem that can promote or oppose anaesthesia, including the parabrachial nucleus, VTA, nucleus accumbens, thalamus, basal forebrain and preoptic area. If induction and emergence were mirror images, and the PPT were a master regulator, activity in the PPT should have recovered before emergence. It did not: it rose only as the mice woke. The authors therefore see the PPT as one node among many, and the next step as understanding how the network works together. They set out three requirements for calling a neuronal population causal: its activity is altered by the anaesthetic, altering its activity changes the anaesthetic state, and it is connected to the rest of the network. Anaesthesia is no longer understood as a “wet blanket” that dampens the whole brain equally. No conflicts of interest; Kelz is also first author of the 2019 review above.
Li, Hu, Tan, Li, Huang and Wang. Br J Anaesth 2024;132:320–333 McKinstry-Wu and Kelz. Br J Anaesth 2024;132:220–223

Nociception is not pain, and EEG shows only part of it

  • The concepts: nociception is the neurophysiological process (receptor, peripheral nerve, dorsal horn, thalamus). Pain is a conscious experience that requires cortical processing. Anaesthesia can remove the latter without removing the former, and that is why an unconscious patient can still develop tachycardia, hypertension, a stress response and postoperative hyperalgesia.
  • What EEG shows: hypnotic level, but noxious stimulation leaves traces. The card below (García 2021) describes the three patterns. An EEG that becomes “deeper” (more delta, less alpha) during surgery may therefore be a nociceptive phenomenon, not overdosing. See also the card on fentanyl and frontal theta (Balanza 2022) in the Agents tab.
  • Several monitors: EEG for hypnosis, nociception monitors (pupillometry, skin conductance, heart rate variability and the like) for autonomic response, haemodynamics for circulation. None of them measures the experience of pain directly. The evidence that nociception-guided opioid dosing improves patient outcomes is still limited, so the figure describes a rationale, not a documented effect.
García 2021, Hight 2020, Balanza 2022

Three EEG reactions to a noxious stimulus: beta arousal, delta arousal and alpha dropout (García 2021)

Narrative review in Br J Anaesth 2021;126:445–457 (García, Kreuzer, Hight, Sleigh). The authors started from key articles and their references, not a systematic search, and grouped the literature into index studies (table 1), raw-EEG studies (table 2) and animal studies.

  • Four dimensions of nociceptive response: somatic (spinal reflexes, movement), autonomic (brainstem and hypothalamus: heart rate, respiration, vasoconstriction, pupil), cognitive arousal and memory (subcortical and midbrain, via forebrain and cortex), and endocrine, coagulation and immune responses. The EEG responses are more transient and do not always occur at the same time as the autonomic ones, but show that the anaesthesia has not completely blocked the brain's response to tissue injury.
  • 1 Beta arousal: increased power at 12–25 Hz, typically at low dose (0.5–1.0 MAC without opioid), often together with movement. The mechanism has been well known since Moruzzi and Magoun 1949: aminergic and cholinergic activation from the brainstem depolarises the thalamus and inhibits the slow thalamocortical oscillations. The indices are designed to capture precisely this and therefore respond with a higher value.
  • 2 Delta arousal (“paradoxical arousal”): increased power at 0.5–4 Hz, at higher doses or balanced anaesthesia with too little opioid, especially with visceral stimulation. Kochs found a 181% increase in delta at incision at 0.5 MAC isoflurane (44% at 1.0 MAC) with alpha halved; Kiyama and Takeda found that epidural blockade prevented the response completely. The mechanism is unclear; the midbrain reticular formation appears to be involved, and the response need not mean that the patient is heading towards consciousness. The clinical problem: the indices interpret more delta as deeper anaesthesia and “wrongly suggest that the hypnotic dose is too high”.
  • 3 Alpha dropout: sudden, episodic loss of frontal alpha power, while delta often persists or increases. Hagihira 2004 showed that alpha fell at incision and returned with fentanyl, and that fentanyl given before incision prevented the fall; Mackay found more alpha loss at low opioid dose. The interpretation is that the thalamus switches from hyperpolarised “burst” mode (idling) to continuous firing, that is, that thalamocortical communication resumes, while the cortex is still GABAergically depressed. That delta can increase at the same time as alpha falls shows that slow oscillations can be cortical and independent of the thalamus.
  • Clinical consequence according to the authors: with delta arousal or alpha dropout, the clinician should not reduce the hypnotic (unless there are other signs of inadequate anaesthesia), but consider more analgesia (opioid or regional block). They argue for titrating opioid to maximal frontal alpha power, with an individual reference (age, cognition, possibly a preoperative baseline or alpha at steady state before surgery). This is an unsolved problem for closed-loop dosing systems. Autonomic responses are linked to cardiovascular complications, but whether pure EEG responses matter for outcome is unknown.
  • What monitors exist (as the article describes it): most commercial “pain monitors” do not use EEG, but heart rate variability, modelled opioid concentrations, the spinal flexor reflex, the plethysmographic pulse wave and heart interval or a multivariable model, which in two studies improved opioid titration and cardiovascular stability. A few are EEG-based. None of them captures all three patterns. The article does not mention skin conductance, which measures the number and amplitude of sympathetically triggered sweat fluctuations in the palm, that is, an autonomic marker on a par with the others.
  • Skin conductance, what has been published (outside the García article): a Swedish prospective observational study (Widarsson Norbeck 2025, BMC Anesthesiol 2025;25:51, 49 patients, monitors blinded to staff) found that NOL and the skin conductance index SCA reacted to jaw thrust, laryngoscopy and intubation more often than heart rate did, and flagged two to three times as many patients above threshold as a 10% rise in heart rate; at skin incision neither of them was better than heart rate, and NOL flagged 57% more than SCA. NOL had an AUC of 0.89 for intubation versus non-painful events; the AUC for SCA is not given in the text. A Norwegian pilot (Scand J Pain 2024, 10 patients undergoing HIPEC) found that SCA rose in 9 of 10 when core temperature rose from 36.2 to 38.4 °C without other signs of pain, and concluded that the method is unreliable during rapid temperature changes. Neither study has outcome measures. The manufacturer's own claims about documentation are not reproduced here.
  • Caveats: narrative, not systematic; few and small studies, many from the 1990s, different agents and stimuli; no randomised trials have tested whether EEG-guided analgesia improves outcome, which the authors themselves emphasise. No conflicts of interest; funded by the James S. McDonnell Foundation.
García, Kreuzer, Hight, Sleigh. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:445–457

Clinical example: alpha disappears during visceral pain (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from one screenshot of a frontal EEG monitor with a skin conductance monitor alongside, and from information given by the person who shared it. The screenshot is not reproduced in the app.

  • What was seen: first a clear alpha band and strong slow-delta in both hemispheres. Around 14:00 the alpha band suddenly became much weaker in both hemispheres, while the power below about 4 Hz remained. Towards the end of the picture alpha partly returned. The spectral edge frequency (SEF) was about 10 Hz, and artefacts 0%.
  • At the same time: according to the person who shared the case, the skin conductance index, heart rate and blood pressure rose at the same time as the change, and the stimulation was visceral.
  • Link to the sources: the picture fits what García 2021 calls alpha dropout: alpha falls suddenly while delta persists. García also describes delta arousal (“paradoxical arousal”), seen particularly with visceral stimulation. Both patterns can make the indices read the EEG as deeper anaesthesia, even though the patient is responding to pain. In such a situation García recommends considering more analgesia rather than reducing the hypnotic.
  • Why it is instructive: it is the simultaneous autonomic signs (heart rate, blood pressure and skin conductance) that point towards nociception. Weakening of alpha alone has several possible causes, for example lower cardiac output (see the card on alpha and cardiac output in the Perfusion tab) or a changed dose.
  • Caveats: one case, described from one screenshot. It is not known which drugs and doses the patient received, whether anything was changed, or what was done afterwards.
Shared clinical example; García 2021

Pain and nociception: the definitions and the pathway

IASP (International Association for the Study of Pain) clearly distinguishes the two terms.

  • Pain: “An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage” (IASP, revised 2020, Raja 2020).
  • Nociception: “The neural process of encoding noxious stimuli.” IASP adds that the consequences may be autonomic (e.g. elevated blood pressure) or behavioural (a withdrawal reflex), and that pain sensation is not necessarily implied.
  • The difference: one of the notes to the definition says that pain and nociception are different phenomena, and that pain cannot be inferred solely from activity in sensory neurons. Another says that inability to communicate does not negate the possibility that pain is experienced.
  • From tissue to spinal cord: nociceptors convert noxious stimuli into nerve signals (transduction). Aδ fibres are myelinated and fast and give pricking pain. C fibres are unmyelinated and slow (Yam 2018). Both end in the dorsal horn, which is the first relay site (D'Mello and Dickenson 2008).
  • From the spinal cord upwards: nociceptive-specific cells lie mainly in laminae I–II, wide-dynamic-range cells deeper, in lamina V. Lamina I projects to the parabrachial nucleus and the PAG (periaqueductal grey) in the brainstem, while lamina V projects mainly to the thalamus via the spinothalamic tract (D'Mello and Dickenson 2008).
  • Descending control: from the PAG, signals run via the RVM (rostral ventromedial medulla) down to the dorsal horn with serotonin and noradrenaline (Yam 2018). This control can both inhibit and facilitate the signals (D'Mello and Dickenson 2008). The brain thus itself regulates how much of the signal gets through.
IASP terminology Raja 2020 D'Mello and Dickenson 2008 Yam 2018

Under general anaesthesia the signal still travels, even though the patient does not experience it

  • Movement is controlled below the cortex: when only the brain of goats received isoflurane, the dose that prevented movement had to be increased from 1.2 to 2.9% (Antognini and Schwartz 1993). The spinal cord is the site where volatile agents suppress movement (Antognini and Carstens 1999). Below 1 MAC, noxious stimuli still activated the midbrain reticular formation, the thalamus and the frontal EEG. At 1.1 MAC or more the activation was blunted.
  • The stress response needs more than unconsciousness: the dose that blocked the adrenergic response to incision in half of patients (MAC-BAR) was 1.45 MAC for halothane and 1.60 MAC for enflurane, with 60% nitrous oxide. Spinal anaesthesia blocked the response completely (Roizen 1981). Volatile agents can block the response, but only at doses well above those needed for unconsciousness and immobility.
  • The traces in the EEG: nociceptive stimulation can give beta arousal, paradoxical delta arousal or alpha dropout (García 2021, see the card above). Hight 2019 found alpha dropout in 31% of 237 patients, more often in abdominal or thoracic surgery and long procedures. The authors suggest it could measure nociception, but it is not validated.
  • In short: a patient who is not conscious does not experience pain, but the nervous system continues to process the signal in the spinal cord, brainstem and partly the thalamus and cortex. This shows up in circulation, hormones and the EEG.
Antognini and Schwartz 1993 Antognini and Carstens 1999 Roizen 1981 García 2021 Hight 2019

The surgical stress response: what it does, how long it lasts and what blunts it

  • What starts it: nerve signals from the injured area, both somatic and autonomic (Burton 2004), and inflammatory mediators from the tissue.
  • Hormones: cortisol rises within 4–6 hours, and ACTH and cortisol stay elevated for a period that depends on the size of the operation. ADH causes water retention that may last 3–5 days. Blood glucose above 12 mmol/L impairs wound healing and increases infection risk (Burton 2004).
  • Inflammation: IL-6 peaks 12–24 hours after surgery (Burton 2004).
  • What blunts it: high-dose opioids can abolish the hormonal response to pelvic and abdominal surgery, but delay recovery and more often require postoperative ventilation. Regional anaesthesia abolishes the hormonal response only when both the somatic and the autonomic nerve supply are blocked, and the inflammatory response is unchanged. Etomidate inhibits cortisol synthesis for up to 8 hours (Burton 2004).
  • Whether it improves outcome: a benefit of regional techniques has not been demonstrated consistently (Burton 2004).
  • Newborns: in 8 + 8 preterm infants undergoing surgery, adding fentanyl gave a smaller hormonal and metabolic stress response, less protein breakdown in the first days and fewer complications (Anand 1987). The study was very small, but it helped change the practice of operating on newborns without analgesia.
  • Does it go away? Yes. The stress response lasts days and is proportional to the size of the operation. Part of it is driven by inflammation, so even good analgesia cannot remove it completely.
Burton, Nicholson and Hall 2004 Desborough 2000 Anand 1987

Neuroplasticity: when pain signals change the nervous system

  • Sensitisation: peripheral sensitisation means that nociceptors in the tissue respond more easily and have a lower threshold. Central sensitisation means that nociceptive neurons in the central nervous system respond more strongly to normal or weak input (IASP).
  • The mechanism: NMDA receptor activation is an essential step both in starting and in maintaining central sensitisation (Latremoliere and Woolf 2009). The phenomenon is prominent after surgical injury.
  • Time course: wind-up, where repeated C-fibre input gives an ever stronger response, disappears within seconds. Central sensitisation lasts from tens of minutes to several hours, and the early phase is transient and reversible (Latremoliere and Woolf 2009). The authors advise against calling it LTP in the spinal cord.
  • Opioids can also cause hyperalgesia: a meta-analysis of 27 RCTs found that high intraoperative opioid doses gave somewhat more pain afterwards and higher morphine consumption at 24 hours, mainly linked to remifentanil. The effect was small (Fletcher and Martinez 2014). More opioid is therefore not automatically better.
  • Ketamine: a Cochrane review (130 studies) found 19% lower opioid consumption and 5 of 100 points lower pain at rest at 24 hours. The effect on the area of hyperalgesia was uncertain (Brinck 2018).
  • The immature brain: extremely preterm-born individuals had altered sensory function at 18–20 years, most after neonatal surgery (Walker 2018). The study is observational and cannot separate pain signals from illness and other factors. About one hour of general anaesthesia in infancy gave no difference in IQ at 5 years compared with regional anaesthesia (GAS, McCann 2019).
Latremoliere and Woolf 2009 Fletcher and Martinez 2014 Brinck 2018 Walker 2018 McCann 2019

Why nociception should be treated properly, and how strong the evidence is

Reflection from the author of the app: the signal is sent even though the patient does not process it, and it gives a stress reaction. It should therefore be stopped. The points below show what the sources support in this.
  • Stable circulation (strong evidence): without enough antinociception, surgical stimulation raises blood pressure and heart rate (Roizen 1981). Nociception-guided remifentanil (NOL) gave fewer episodes of hypotension (5 versus 28%) and 30% less remifentanil (Meijer 2019).
  • The stress response (strong as a biological effect, weak for patient outcomes): opioids and regional blocks blunt the hormonal response (Burton 2004, Anand 1987), but better outcomes in adults have not been shown consistently.
  • Sensitisation (strong in animal studies and as a mechanism, weak in clinical trials): preventive analgesia before incision had an effect for epidural (effect size 0.38), wound infiltration and NSAIDs, but was equivocal for NMDA antagonists and opioids (Ong 2005).
  • Postoperative and chronic pain (moderate for association, weak for cause): persistent pain occurs in 10–50% after common operations, severe in 2–10%. Nerve injury during surgery is probably the main cause (Kehlet 2006). Each 10% more time in severe pain on day 1 gave a 30% higher incidence of chronic pain at one year (Fletcher 2015). This concerns pain after surgery, not nociception during it.
  • Nociception monitors: a meta-analysis of 21 RCTs found less intraoperative opioid, but no difference in postoperative pain or opioid requirement (Ma 2022). One small study found lower pain in recovery with NOL (Meijer 2020).
  • Conclusion (interpretation based on the sources): there is good reason to treat nociception under general anaesthesia to keep the circulation stable and blunt the stress response, and because sensitisation is a known mechanism. That this in itself prevents chronic pain in adults has not been shown. The stress response fades over days. The aim is the right dose, not as much as possible, because high doses of remifentanil can cause hyperalgesia.
Roizen 1981 Meijer 2019, 2020 Ong 2005 Kehlet 2006 Fletcher 2015 Ma 2022

Emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia: before the baby is delivered

In general anaesthesia for caesarean section, opioid has traditionally been withheld until the baby is delivered, to avoid affecting the baby. The mother then has intubation and incision with only a hypnotic and a neuromuscular blocker.

  • The circulatory response: in a meta-analysis of 17 RCTs (987 women), remifentanil, alfentanil and fentanyl at induction lowered peak systolic pressure, mean arterial pressure and heart rate compared with placebo. None of them changed the 1-minute Apgar, but fentanyl gave a lower 5-minute Apgar. Remifentanil and alfentanil did not (White 2019). The authors call for an adequately powered trial.
  • Awareness: NAP5 found about 1 in 670 for caesarean section, versus about 1 in 19,600 overall (Pandit 2014). The OAA and DAS guideline therefore stresses an adequate dose of induction agent (Mushambi 2015).
  • The guidelines on opioid: OAA/DAS 2015 gives no recommendation on opioid at induction (Mushambi 2015). A more recent review describes short-acting or low-dose opioids as safe (Bone and Hoskins 2022). A separate “OAA/AAGBI 2018” guideline for general anaesthesia was not found.
  • Chronic pain after caesarean section: in a study where all had spinal anaesthesia, 11.4% had chronic pain at 3 months, associated with more postoperative pain (Cançado 2012). Cançado cites an earlier study where general anaesthesia was associated with more chronic pain than spinal (Nikolajsen 2004, not read directly). That untreated nociception before delivery gives lasting pain has not been shown.
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): the period from induction until delivery combines strong nociception with a high risk of awareness. That argues for enough hypnotic, and for considering a short-acting opioid at induction. The paediatrician should then be told. The choice must follow local procedures and be made with the anaesthetist.
White 2019 Pandit 2014 (NAP5) Mushambi 2015 Cançado 2012

The brain: perfusion, pressure and positioning

This tab gathers what the sources say about the relationship between the brain's blood supply, pressure and EEG. First the foundations: Miller's chapter 10 on cerebral physiology and the anaesthetic drugs (Patel, Drummond and Lemkuil), Lobo and Lamperti (2025), van Putten and Hofmeijer and Foreman and Claassen on ischaemia and EEG, brought together in one figure of CBF thresholds. Then clinical studies and case reports on EEG as a perfusion marker (Sheorajpanday, Guay, Manquat, Nycz, Ching, Georgii, Xu, Lenstra) and own cases. The last cards cover positioning and perfusion pressure, built on Miller's chapter 30, Kalmar, Nordum and Pisitsak. All numbers are taken from the sources; where they disagree, it is noted in the discrepancy list in the Sources tab.

Perfusion, CPP and autoregulation

  • Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is MAP minus intracranial pressure (ICP). Blood flow (CBF) is CPP divided by cerebrovascular resistance.
  • ICP is affected by volume inside the skull (tumour, oedema, haemorrhage, increased CSF volume), by positioning (for example Trendelenburg), by rotation of the head that compresses the jugular veins, and by high intrathoracic pressure and PEEP that impede venous drainage.
  • With intact autoregulation, MAP between approximately 60 and 160 mmHg does not affect CBF, which is kept at around 50 ml/100 g/min. When autoregulation fails, blood flow follows pressure passively.
  • CBF can fall by 50–60% before compensation fails, because the brain then increases oxygen extraction.
  • Cerebrovascular resistance is affected by vasopressors and vasodilators, by PaCO₂, and can be shifted by chronic hypertension. Treating low blood pressure with a vasopressor alone can reduce cardiac output.
  • Hypercapnia impairs autoregulation, and the anaesthetic agents play a part: propofol preserves it during hypercapnia, whereas sevoflurane at a corresponding PaCO₂ impairs or abolishes it.
  • The brain is about 2% of body weight, but receives 12–15% of cardiac output and uses up to 20% of the oxygen. Approximately 75–80% of oxygen consumption goes to restoring the membrane potential.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 1, 2 and 7

Miller's ch. 10: cerebral physiology and the anaesthetic drugs (Patel, Drummond and Lemkuil)

Normal values, energy use and why EEG and CMR go together

  • Numbers (box 10.1): global CBF 45–55 ml/100 g/min, cortical 75–80, subcortical 8–20. CMRO₂ 3–3.5 ml/100 g/min. The brain is about 2% of body weight and receives 12–15% of cardiac output. rSO₂ 55–80%, SjVO₂ 60–70%, ICP supine 8–12 mmHg.
  • Two energy components: about 60% of energy use supports electrophysiological function (what the EEG shows), the rest cellular “housekeeping”. Anaesthetic drugs (barbiturates, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, propofol, etomidate) lower only the first: CMR falls in step with EEG suppression, and more drug after the EEG is flat gives no further reduction (fig. 10.2). Ketamine and nitrous oxide are exceptions. Hypothermia lowers both components (6–7% per °C; EEG flat at about 18–20 °C; CMRO₂ below 10% of normal at 18 °C), so cooling still works after the EEG is flat.
  • Burst suppression is not one state: at complete EEG suppression CMRO₂ is similar whichever drug is used, but the distribution differs: barbiturates lower CBF and CMR uniformly, isoflurane and sevoflurane most in the neocortex. Cortical SSEPs can be recorded at thiopental doses far beyond those giving a flat EEG, but are hard to elicit with isoflurane in burst suppression (about 1.5 MAC). The burst-suppression pattern just before complete suppression also differs between drugs.
  • What it means for EEG interpretation: a low index or a flat EEG means “maximal metabolic effect” of the drug, not that more dose does anything useful. That is the argument behind the cards on overdose and burst suppression in the Spectrogram and Agents tabs.
Miller's ch. 10, box 10.1 and fig. 10.2

Autoregulation: the Lassen curve is outdated, the lower limit is around 70 mmHg in most people

  • The classical picture (CBF constant at 50 ml/100 g/min from MAP 50 to 150) was built on a heterogeneous sample with single measurements, and the chapter calls it “outmoded”. Newer analyses give a narrower plateau with a gentle upslope, so pressure-passive CBF applies over a wider MAP range than assumed. With rapid pressure changes (dynamic autoregulation) the plateau may be as short as 10 mmHg or absent; with slow changes over about 10 minutes (static) the plateau is at least ±20 mmHg.
  • Lower limit (LLA): across seven studies in awake, healthy subjects the mean LLA ranged from 57 to 91 mmHg, with enormous inter-subject variability. The authors (Drummond) hold that the LLA in the majority is not below 70 mmHg, which with normal ICP (5–10) gives a CPP of 60–65 mmHg, and that 70 mmHg is a prudent threshold without an autoregulation monitor. Upper limit: about 90 mmHg on cardiopulmonary bypass, probably above 140 in hypertensives. Autoregulation is best described as a family of curves (fig. 10.5), not one.
  • Reserve: symptoms of ischaemia appear only when CBF has fallen 35–40% in awake subjects. This cerebrovascular reserve means that brief hypotension below the LLA is usually tolerated; sustained falls are not. Reserve is reduced with CNS injury (autoregulation impaired for about 2 weeks, restored after 1–3 months), raised local tissue pressure (ICP, retractors, cervical stenosis), an incomplete circle of Willis (35–40% of the population) and hypertension.
  • Hypertension: both dynamic and static autoregulation are preserved in hypertensives, and treatment to normal pressure does not reduce CBF. The intraoperative question is hypotension: the authors limit the MAP fall to no more than 20% below baseline measured at head level in the sitting position, in the section on chronic hypertension they give 30–35%, and state that a 25% fall brings both normo- and hypertensive patients to the LLA. See the discrepancy list.
  • Hydrostatic gradient: 2 mmHg per inch (2.5 cm) the head is above the heart; 12 inches give about 24 mmHg. To keep CPP at 60–65 with the head elevated, MAP at heart level must be about 85. The siphon model (closed loop) is rejected: gravity does affect CPP. See the card on perfusion pressure and head height.
  • Practical MAP target: in patients without acute ischaemia and with normal or well-controlled pressure the chapter regards an intraoperative MAP of about 75 mmHg as adequate, and table 10.2 lists subspecialty targets in brain injury (for example SBP above 100–110 in traumatic brain injury depending on age, MAP above 65 after cardiac arrest).
Miller's ch. 10, fig. 10.3–10.5, table 10.2

CO₂, O₂, cardiac output and vasopressors

  • PaCO₂: CBF changes 1–2 ml/100 g/min per mmHg within 25–70 mmHg; the response is attenuated below 25 and above 75–80. Moderate hypotension (MAP fall under 33%) attenuates the CO₂ response markedly, severe hypotension (about 66%) abolishes it. Hypocapnia widens the autoregulatory range, hypercapnia narrows it. The effect of a changed PaCO₂ wanes over 6–8 hours as CSF pH normalises; abrupt normalisation after prolonged hyperventilation gives CSF acidosis and increased CBF/ICP.
  • PaO₂: little effect between 60 and 300 mmHg; below 60 CBF rises rapidly, linearly with falling saturation. Haemodilution gives a smaller CBF rise than hypoxaemia for the same fall in O₂ content. 1 atm oxygen lowers CBF by about 18%.
  • Cardiac output: Meng estimates that a 30% fall in CO gives about a 10% fall in CBF independent of MAP and PaCO₂; a newer study found that a 10% fall in MAP and a 20% fall in CO gave the same fall (about 5%) in MCA velocity. A meta-analysis nevertheless does not confirm an independent relationship, because CO cannot be changed without changing MAP and PaCO₂. The chapter still concludes that low CO probably adds to low MAP in hypotension, that volume should be optimised first, and that bolus phenylephrine may lower CO further. See the Nordum 2024 card (Trendelenburg) and the clinical example with alpha and cardiac output.
  • Vasopressors: α₁-agonists (phenylephrine, noradrenaline) do not change global CBF in humans when autoregulation is intact; they act via MAP. Bolus phenylephrine slightly lowered NIRS-measured SCO₂ in several studies, ephedrine did not, probably because ephedrine maintains CO; extracranial contamination of NIRS exceeds this difference. Koch found that ephedrine, not phenylephrine, increased local CBF, tissue oxygenation and microcirculation in brain-tumour patients. Outcome studies are lacking. Dexmedetomidine lowers CBF 25–30% via CMR; dopamine up to 100 µg/kg/min does not cause cerebral vasoconstriction; dobutamine increased CBF and CMR by 20 and 30%.
Miller's ch. 10, fig. 10.8–10.10, table 10.3

What the anaesthetic drugs do to CBF and CMR

  • Intravenous agents preserve flow–metabolism coupling, autoregulation and CO₂ responsiveness. Propofol lowered regional CBF 53–79% and whole-brain glucose metabolism 48–58% at surgical depth in volunteers; autoregulation and CO₂ response are preserved even at burst suppression. Etomidate 0.2 mg/kg: CBF −34%, CMR −45%. Midazolam 0.15 mg/kg: CBF −30 to −34% (−12% globally with PET). Opioids: small reductions in the unstimulated brain; sedative remifentanil can increase CBF regionally; a bolus with a MAP fall can raise ICP through autoregulatory vasodilation. Flumazenil can give an overshoot in CBF/ICP in patients with poor intracranial compliance.
  • Ketamine is the only one that increases CMR and CBF: subanaesthetic doses (0.2–0.3 mg/kg) increased global CMR by about 25%, most in frontal and anterior cingulate cortex; S-ketamine increases CMR, R-ketamine lowers it. CBF rose 14% (subanaesthetic) and 36% (anaesthetic) without a change in CMRO₂ in one study; CBV +50%. Propofol, benzodiazepines and isoflurane blunt or abolish the ICP rise, and systematic reviews find no ICP rise in head injury. See the ketamine cards in the Agents tab for the EEG pattern.
  • Volatile agents: lower CMR dose-dependently but are also direct vasodilators. Net: at 0.5 MAC CBF falls, at 1 MAC it is unchanged, above 1 MAC it rises (“luxury perfusion”), and autoregulation to rising pressure is impaired. Vasodilating potency: halothane ≫ enflurane > desflurane ≈ isoflurane > sevoflurane. At 1 MAC sevoflurane and desflurane lowered CBF by 38 and 22% and CMR by 39 and 35% (Kety–Schmidt, cortical measurement); PET shows about 50% for both. Maximal CMR reduction is reached at EEG suppression, at 1.5–2 MAC. Sevoflurane lowers regional CBF but not CBV; propofol lowers both. If CMR is already suppressed (for example by propofol), the vasodilation is unmasked: adding a volatile agent then clearly increases CBF.
  • Entropy and sevoflurane: in a dose-escalation study in humans the largest reduction in entropy was at 1 MAC sevoflurane, with smaller reductions at higher concentrations. This fits with CMRO₂ falling sharply with the onset of the anaesthetic EEG pattern and more slowly thereafter.
  • Nitrous oxide increases CBF, CMR and ICP, most alone or with a volatile agent (0.75 MAC isoflurane + 65% N₂O gave 43% higher CBF than 1.5 MAC isoflurane); with intravenous agents the effect is blunted. CBV is little affected.
  • Lidocaine: 5 mg/kg over 30 min + 45 µg/kg/min lowered CBF 24% and CMR 20% in awake volunteers; membrane stabilisation is thought to lower the energy needed for membrane integrity. A 1.5 mg/kg bolus was as effective as thiopental 3 mg/kg against the ICP rise at pin placement, with less MAP fall. After a 2 mg/kg bolus peak concentrations are 6.6–8.5 µg/mL, below the seizure threshold (above 5–10 µg/mL in awake subjects); lidocaine seizures have not been reported in anaesthetised patients. See the card on multimodal anaesthesia in the Agents tab.
  • Neuromuscular blockers have no direct cerebrovascular effect beyond histamine release; succinylcholine can raise ICP by about 5 mmHg as an arousal phenomenon under light anaesthesia, blocked by deep anaesthesia or defasciculation.
Miller's ch. 10, fig. 10.12–10.19

Epileptogenic drugs according to chapter 10

  • Sevoflurane: seizures at induction with high concentrations in children, also without a known predisposition. In two healthy volunteers burst suppression at 2 MAC was accompanied by epileptiform discharges with a clear CBF increase (coupling preserved). In patients with temporal lobe epilepsy 1.5 MAC produced widespread paroxysmal activity that was not confined to the focus and did not help localisation. Tonic–clonic movements at emergence have been reported in healthy patients. No sequelae documented; caution in epilepsy. See the card on epileptiform activity and images 19–20 in the Spectrogram tab.
  • Etomidate often causes myoclonus without epileptiform EEG, but can trigger generalised epileptic activity in epileptics; 0.1 mg/kg is used to activate a quiescent focus intraoperatively. Methohexital activates foci. Ketamine can trigger seizures in predisposed patients, with subcortical activity not always seen in surface EEG, but is also used for refractory status (effective in 56%). Propofol is not confirmed as proconvulsant and shortens ECT seizures; high-amplitude beta is described. Opioids: high-dose fentanyl produced electrical seizure activity in 8 of 9 patients with partial complex seizures during temporal lobe surgery; alfentanil 50 µg/kg augmented spikes in temporal lobe epilepsy. Isoflurane gives spikes and myoclonus but is not regarded as epileptogenic and is used for refractory status. Enflurane is epileptogenic, potentiated by hypocapnia.
  • Why it belongs in an EEG app: seizure activity can raise CMR by up to 400%, and in a paralysed patient the EEG is the only way to detect it.
Miller's ch. 10, section Epileptogenesis

CBF thresholds (fig. 10.20), hypoglycaemia and neuroprotection

  • Thresholds: normal CBF about 50 ml/100 g/min. Symptoms of hypoperfusion in awake subjects only at about 30. EEG evidence of ischaemia from about 20. Isoelectric cortical EEG at about 15. Penumbra 10–20: reversible dysfunction, but cell death if flow is not restored. Signs of irreversible membrane failure (extracellular potassium, lost direct cortical response) only at about 6–10 (the legend says 6–12). The data are from the cortex of barbiturate-anaesthetised baboons and awake monkeys, and the levels vary with drug and species; in humans under halothane and N₂O the threshold for the first EEG change matched the animal data. The thresholds are drawn into the figure above alongside van Putten and Foreman and Claassen.
  • Completeness: with complete global ischaemia (cardiac arrest) energy supply fails within minutes; with incomplete (focal) ischaemia residual flow keeps ATP production going longer, which is why focal ischaemia is apparently better tolerated.
  • Hypoglycaemia in the EEG: with a gradual fall to about 40 mg/dL (about 2.2 mmol/L) the EEG shifts from alpha and beta towards delta and theta; below 20 mg/dL (about 1.1 mmol/L) the EEG becomes flat. Persistence at that level gives seizures and hippocampal injury. Hyperthermia above 42 °C gives an abrupt fall in oxygen consumption (protein denaturation).
  • Neuroprotection: barbiturates, propofol, ketamine, volatile agents and xenon protect in animal models, but only with mild ischaemia and not durably. In humans: in IHAST thiopental, etomidate or propofol to EEG suppression gave no better outcome; in GALA general anaesthesia gave no advantage over local anaesthesia for carotid surgery. Conclusion: inducing burst suppression for brain protection is not supported in anaesthetised patients, and physiological control (CPP, oxygenation, normocapnia, temperature, glucose, seizures) matters more. Etomidate can worsen tissue hypoxia during temporary vessel occlusion. Hypothermia 32–36 °C after cardiac arrest: TTM and TTM2 showed no benefit of lower targets; guidelines keep 32–36 °C and strict avoidance of hyperthermia.
  • Deferring elective surgery after stroke: the risk of death within 30 days was highest in the first 3 months and only stabilised after 9 months; the chapter recommends deferring elective surgery for 9 months, with an exception for early carotid surgery in small infarcts.
Miller's ch. 10, fig. 10.20–10.24

SSEP, ICP and falling blood flow (Lobo and Lamperti ch. 6)

  • The text states that SSEP amplitude changes at a CBF fall to about 15 ml/100 g/min and disappears below 18.
  • Increased ICP changes the SSEP classically: amplitude decreases and latency is prolonged. With herniation, subcortical responses may disappear first.
  • The book does not directly describe how the EEG changes with raised ICP. CBF thresholds for EEG are given in the van Putten and Hofmeijer card and in the figure below.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 6

Figure: where on the CBF scale EEG and the cells fail

Miller's ch. 10 · van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 · Foreman and Claassen via van Putten

What ischaemia does to the EEG (van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016)

  • Energy: the brain accounts for about 20% of the body's energy requirement. In the cortex about 40% of ATP goes to the resting membrane potential and action potentials, and about 35% to synaptic transmission. The rhythms in the EEG arise from summed postsynaptic current in the pyramidal cells, and action potentials contribute little.
  • Normal blood flow is about 750 ml/min, 15–20% of cardiac output, or 50–54 ml/100 g/min.
  • Mild to moderate ischaemia (15–35 ml/100 g/min): it is primarily synaptic transmission that fails. The neurons retain their membrane potential, and CT and MRI are normal. The EEG shows less alpha and beta, then more delta, depending on severity and duration. In severe cases the EEG can become isoelectric, and even an isoelectric EEG can be due to isolated synaptic failure and be reversible.
  • Below 10 ml/100 g/min: the membrane potential shifts towards the Donnan potential (about −15 to −20 mV), and cytotoxic oedema and cell death follow. The EEG rhythms then disappear permanently. Lack of energy for more than 5–8 minutes produces such changes.
  • How fast: a few minutes without blood flow produce synaptic failure with full recovery when perfusion returns. In circulatory arrest the EEG becomes isoelectric within 10–40 seconds. In figure 1 (syncope), slower rhythms appear after a few seconds and clear slowing around 20 seconds after the arrest.
  • Inhibitory neurons are probably more vulnerable than excitatory ones. This may explain increased synchronisation and generalised periodic discharges in severe hypoxic injury.
van Putten and Hofmeijer. J Clin Neurophysiol 2016;33:203–210

EEG in carotid surgery

  • During test clamping of the internal carotid artery, reduced fast activity (often followed by more slow activity) reflects reduced blood flow. In figure 3, loss of fast activity alone corresponds to a CBF in the ipsilateral hemisphere of about 25–35 ml/100 g/min, and loss of fast activity plus more delta to about 15. These figures are taken from Foreman and Claassen and were not measured in the study.
  • Which changes require a shunt is debated. In a study of 57 patients (Blume 1986), moderate changes (8–13 Hz retained, but an amplitude fall of 50% or more and increased delta above 1 Hz) did not lead to postoperative stroke. Major changes (8–13 Hz reduced to minimal or absent, and a doubling of delta) led to stroke in 2 of 22. Most neurophysiologists nevertheless recommend a shunt for any change, and the authors consider that a fall in alpha/beta amplitude of about 10% can probably be accepted.
  • Perioperative stroke rate in a review (AbuRahma 2011): 1.4% with routine shunting, 1.6% with selective shunting guided by EEG and 2% without shunting. With shunting guided by transcranial Doppler it was 4.8% versus 1.6% with EEG. In the authors' own hospitals a shunt was used in about 3–5%.
  • EEG is not sensitive to deep structures, but preserved cortical rhythms are regarded as a reliable indicator of adequate blood flow deep down as well. This is because reduced flow usually produces a corresponding fraction in cortex and deep structures, and because the cortex has the greatest energy requirement.
  • Quantitative: the brain symmetry index (BSI) measures spectral asymmetry between the hemispheres on a scale from 0 to 1, with normal values of 0.05–0.08. A change of 0.05 is regarded as significant and agrees well with visual assessment. Temporal BSI captures global changes over time.
van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 (Blume 1986, AbuRahma 2011)

EEG in acute cerebral infarction

  • The predictive value of EEG for outcome after cerebral infarction is low to moderate. In a study of 110 patients, pdBSI and the (delta + theta)/(alpha + beta) ratio correlated with mRS at 6 months with a Spearman rho of about 0.46–0.47.
  • Continuous quantitative EEG with BSI correlated well with NIHSS in hemispheric infarction and was used to follow the effect of thrombolysis.
  • Spreading depolarisation occurs in acute infarction and may contribute to growth of the injury, but is difficult to measure through an intact skull. So far it has only been demonstrated reliably with electrocorticography.
van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016

EEG after cardiac arrest

  • About half of comatose patients after cardiac arrest have a poor outcome. SSEP and pupillary and corneal reflexes at 72 hours capture only about 20% of those who do not recover.
  • Continuous, normal or diffusely slowed EEG at 12 hours predicted good outcome (CPC 1–2) with specificity 91%, sensitivity 55%, PPV 84% and NPV 70%. Isoelectric, low-voltage (below 20 μV) or burst suppression with identical bursts at 24 hours predicted poor outcome (CPC 3–5) with specificity 100%, sensitivity 42%, PPV 100% and NPV 55%. The figures are based on two prospective cohorts with a total of 377 patients, all treated with mild therapeutic hypothermia and sedated.
  • Evolution towards continuous physiological EEG within 12 hours gives a very good prognosis. The patient's further prognosis then depends on injury to other organs, and the patients with favourable EEG and poor outcome died of failure of other organs, particularly the heart. Deep coma in the first hours does not rule out full recovery.
  • The authors call it a persistent misconception that EEG cannot be used during hypothermia or sedation. Mild hypothermia to 32 °C barely affects the EEG. At usual propofol doses the EEG remains continuous with anteriorisation of alpha, and isoelectricity does not occur.
  • Sedation-induced versus pathological burst suppression: in a relatively healthy brain the bursts are heterogeneous, and they come and go gradually. In postanoxic injury the bursts are identical, the intervals between them are flat, and the transitions between suppression and burst are abrupt. The latter has a poor prognosis.
  • The cerebral recovery index (CRI) combines five quantitative features (mean amplitude, alpha/delta ratio, entropy, coherence and continuity) into one number between 0 and 1. In the patient with good outcome CRI was about 0.7 at 24 hours, and in the patient with poor outcome about 0.3. In the first hours the EEG was almost identical in both.
  • The authors point out that recent guidelines do not include early EEG for prognostication, and expect EEG to be included in future guidelines. Interpretation of reactivity is not simple, and inter-rater agreement is only moderate.
van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016

Consciousness and the dying brain (Mashour 2024)

Narrative review (Anesthesiology 2024;140:1221–1231; Mashour, Lee, Pal and Li) on near-death experiences and EEG around cardiac arrest and death.

  • Incidence: 10–20 % of survivors of in-hospital cardiac arrest report near-death experiences. In AWARE II, 21.4 % of 28 interviewed patients had a «transcendent recalled experience of death».
  • The indices just before death: in seven critically ill patients without brain injury, BIS and SedLine values rose to levels consistent with consciousness just before death, after withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. In a follow-up, 13 of 28 (46 %) had such a surge, while none of seven brain-dead patients did. Other series have not found this.
  • Why the indices cannot be read as consciousness: processed EEG cannot distinguish non-specific activation (for example glutamate release as hypoxic neurones die) from organised activity, cannot distinguish wakefulness from seizures, has only frontal electrodes, and EMG is hard to exclude completely.
  • Animal studies: in rats, a brief surge of gamma and theta with increased coupling between cortical regions occurred within 30 seconds of cardiac arrest. During asphyxia, release of many neurotransmitters increased; serotonin rose more than 20-fold within 2 minutes.
  • Humans: in 2 of 4 dying comatose patients, beta and gamma increased after the ventilator was disconnected. Both had a history of seizures, so seizure activity cannot be excluded. In a study of 8 patients, EEG ceased a median 78 seconds before circulatory arrest. None of the findings is linked to an actual experience.
  • During CPR: in AWARE II, SedLine gave interpretable EEG in 53 of 85 during ongoing CPR, and near-normal activity was seen up to 35–60 minutes into CPR. Detailed analysis has not been published.
  • Isoelectric is not always final: in animal models the isoelectric phase can be reversed by rapid reoxygenation, and the authors do not exclude that experiences may arise while the brain recovers.
  • Relevance and caveats: anaesthesia staff take part in CPR, organ donation and withdrawal of treatment. The authors reject non-neurobiological explanations. Funded by NIH, no competing interests. Note that the findings concern dying patients, not prognosis in survivors.
Mashour, Lee, Pal and Li. Anesthesiology 2024;140:1221–1231

Quantitative EEG, CBF and CPP (Foreman and Claassen 2012)

  • Thresholds: when CBF falls to about 25–35 ml/100 g/min, the EEG first loses fast frequencies. At about 17–18 slow frequencies increase gradually, and the authors call this a critical ischaemic threshold at which neurons begin to lose transmembrane gradients. At 10–12 ml/100 g/min and below the EEG becomes silent, and the cell injury is irreversible.
  • How fast: during carotid clamping the changes occur within about 20 seconds and are reversible. Infarction may only appear after hours at this flow level. Quantitative EEG (qEEG) captures changes in blood flow and metabolism within 28–104 seconds. Diffusion-weighted MRI detects changes at CBF 35–40 after about 30 minutes, whereas EEG detects them within seconds.
  • CPP: the mean frequency in the EEG falls when CPP is below 60 mmHg, also in comatose or sedated patients (Diedler 2009, according to the review). More slow activity (delta and theta) and less fast activity (alpha and beta) follow reduced cerebral oxygen metabolism (CMRO₂).
  • Which measure works: in carotid surgery, spectral edge frequency (SEF) captured ischaemic changes in patients on isoflurane, whereas relative delta percentage (delta/total power) was accurate in patients on propofol. Overall, relative delta percentage gives the most robust correlation with CBF and metabolism in focal ischaemia.
  • Confounding factors: seizures and periodic discharges, changes in intracranial pressure (for example acute hydrocephalus), systemic disease, sedatives, opioids and antipsychotics. Normal slow-wave sleep can resemble ischaemic changes. Raw EEG remains the gold standard, and any qEEG algorithm should be checkable against the raw EEG by someone who knows EEG.
  • The spectrogram (compressed spectral array) gives, according to the authors, the highest ratio of pixels to data and is easy to read, compared with raw EEG.
  • The review does not discuss the operating room beyond carotid surgery. Most of the review concerns intensive care patients. The suggestion of use after high-risk vascular and cardiac surgery, in refractory hypotension and in sepsis is the authors' own, and not documented in studies.
Foreman and Claassen. Crit Care 2012;16:216

EEG in cerebral infarction and subarachnoid haemorrhage

  • Infarction: in the early subacute phase the EEG correlates well with CBF while oxygen extraction increases (“misery perfusion”). Later it correlates more with CMRO₂ (“luxury perfusion”). Loss of reactivity and absent sleep-wake cycling suggest a poor prognosis. Absence of delta or presence of faster frequencies within 24 hours belongs to good outcome. Regional attenuation of fast frequencies without delta (RAWOD) suggests severe early CBF loss (mean 8.6 ml/100 g/min), and in one series mortality was up to 67%.
  • One year after infarction, functional outcome was predicted correctly in 60% of cases with clinical criteria. With EEG this increased to 85%.
  • After thrombolysis, delta power fell 100 minutes before clinical improvement in one study.
  • Delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) after SAH: occurs in 20–40%. Daily transcranial Doppler is about 60–70% sensitive. In the table of studies: in 34 comatose patients, a change of 10% in the alpha/delta ratio over 6 minutes gave sensitivity 100% and specificity 76%, and a change of 50% over one minute gave 89% and 84%. In 12 patients, sensitivity for predicting neurological deterioration increased from 40% with clinical assessment alone to 67% with qEEG (specificity 73%). In one study, relative alpha variability fell in all 19 with vasospasm, on average 2.9 days before vasospasm was confirmed, but also in 7 without vasospasm, mainly because of infarction or increased ICP.
  • All the studies are small, and the authors themselves point out that the findings must be validated prospectively and in randomised trials.
Foreman and Claassen 2012

Asymmetry and reproducibility in ischaemia (Sheorajpanday 2009)

  • Design: exploratory, methodological study in 41 patients: 21 with cerebral infarction (median NIHSS 11, mean DWI volume 79 ml), 10 with TIA and 10 controls aged 55 years or more with subjective memory complaints and normal MRI. One EEG per patient, awake with eyes closed for at least 10 minutes, 19 electrodes with impedance below 5 kΩ. 128 seconds free of artefacts were analysed after visual artefact removal. The study was not done under anaesthesia.
  • pdBSI: a variant of the brain symmetry index that compares the power spectrum between homologous channel pairs (8 pairs, 1–25 Hz), instead of the average for the whole hemisphere.
  • Reproducibility: minimum Cronbach's alpha was 0.95–0.99 for standard spectral measures and 0.96–0.99 for pdBSI, both within the same recording and between and within raters. The authors say that visual artefact removal by a skilled person is a critical first step that cannot be replaced by automatic artefact removal. Automation can confuse ischaemic delta with slow activity from eye movements and drowsiness.
  • Clinical correlation: pdBSI correlated with NIHSS (rho 0.64–0.70) and with DWI volume (rho 0.79–0.84). Standard measures such as relative alpha and the delta/alpha ratio correlated moderately with NIHSS, but not significantly with DWI volume after adjustment for multiple testing.
  • Group difference: pdBSI distinguished infarction from TIA and controls. The standard measures did not after adjustment. Neither pdBSI nor the standard measures could distinguish TIA from controls.
  • Broad frequency bands: pdBSI over 1–25 Hz was better than narrower bands, and 1–3 Hz alone was not significant. The authors interpret this as the whole frequency range being affected in acute ischaemia.
  • Relative measures: the authors used relative power, because absolute power is affected by skull thickness. The skull is on average about 80 times less conductive than brain and scalp, and a 10% thinner skull can produce a change of 800% in amplitude.
  • Caveats: small study, one recording per patient, and no ambition of diagnostic value for individual patients. Asymmetry measures are not specific for ischaemia, and pdBSI will not detect equal injury on both sides of a channel pair.
Sheorajpanday et al. Clin Neurophysiol 2009;120:845–855

EEG and raised intracranial pressure: sparse evidence

  • Mechanism: increased ICP lowers CPP and thereby CBF, which limits the supply of oxygen and energy to the cortex. The EEG changes are thus assumed to arise via CPP, CBF and metabolism (and possibly herniation), not from ICP itself. Lenstra 2026 describes that neurogenic mechanisms may then dominate over vasomotor, chemical and metabolic ones in the regulation of CBF.
  • Systematic review (Lenstra 2026): adults with moderate to severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) and ICP measurement. Of 873 hits, only 4 studies met the criteria (all with ICP measured via ventricular drain or parenchymal probe). Three concerned post-traumatic seizures and ICP, and one the direction between EEG and ICP. The authors conclude that there is very little evidence and that larger studies are needed. They do not write that a validated pattern is lacking, but say that personalised EEG-ICP thresholds must be developed in future studies. Studies without original data, case reports and series, paediatric patients and invasive EEG were excluded.
  • Direction (Sanz-García 2018, cited in the review): 21 patients (15 TBI, 6 SAH), a total of 1055 hours. On average, 38% of the time showed significant Granger causality from EEG to ICP, with a delay of 25–50 seconds, most often in relative alpha (12 patients). In one patient the direction was reversed. The authors interpret this as possible neurovascular coupling. The study did not examine the EEG during the intracranial hypertension episodes themselves, and sedation boluses did not change the finding.
  • Conflicting findings (McNamara 2003, cited in the review): in 17 intensive care patients with acute ICP rise, quantitative EEG showed no changes during the ICP peaks. There were only 30 minutes of EEG per patient, so late changes may have been missed.
  • Case reports and series (outside the review's criteria): Sheikh 2022 (retrospective series, J Clin Neurophysiol) describes that cyclic patterns and varying degrees of slowing and attenuated fast activity often preceded clinical deterioration in intracranial hypertension. It is described that generalised rhythmic delta activity and loss of fast activity about 30 minutes before clinical change are mentioned in presumed plateau waves. The review describes the series as seven non-traumatic neurocritical patients. Alsallom 2022 describes two patients with herniation in whom increased low-frequency power and asymmetry in the spectrogram appeared roughly an hour before clinical deterioration.
  • Animal study (Pose, pilot): the median cross-correlation between total EEG power and ICP was 0.7, and 0.55 for CPP. A model with only three variables had accuracy 0.70, sensitivity 0.53 and specificity 0.79. The direction of the correlation is not stated.
  • What the sources do not test: how processed indices and the spectrogram change with raised ICP under general anaesthesia. Foreman and Claassen mention that ICP changes, sedatives and sleep can confound EEG interpretation. Guay 2025 lists intracranial hypertension as one of the causes of reduced cerebral oxygen delivery and writes that such changes can resemble deeper sedation on frontal EEG, but shows no data from patients with raised ICP. That processed indices may confuse them with deeper anaesthesia is therefore a reasonable assumption, not a demonstrated finding for ICP.
Lenstra 2026, Sheikh 2022, McNamara 2003 and Pose

EEG in pathology, age and the vulnerable brain

  • Septic encephalopathy: EEG slowing is the earliest finding and can be seen even with a normal neurological examination. The chapter also mentions increased theta, dominant delta, triphasic waves, periodic epileptiform discharges and suppression.
  • Burst suppression: the risk increases with age and with impaired neurological status. In older patients the bursts and suppression phases are less distinct, and the pattern is difficult to detect.
  • High-dose ketamine does not itself produce burst suppression, but can lower the threshold. Pain and nociceptive input can also lower the threshold.
  • Processed BSR algorithms do not pick up suppression until it is around 40%. The chapter therefore recommends assessing the raw EEG.
  • Two theories explain burst suppression: cortical hyperexcitability, and a metabolic theory in which falling ATP opens ATP-gated potassium channels. The metabolic theory fits with findings that low perfusion can produce burst suppression, but it is not proven.
  • ENGAGES did not change the incidence of delirium, but found lower 30-day mortality in the EEG group. The book calls this an observation that should be investigated further.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 1, 5 and 11

Schematic example: fall in cardiac output and loss of alpha

The image was made for teaching and is simulated. It is not patient data and not a printout from any equipment. It shows haemodynamics (arterial pressure, MAP and CI) above an EEG spectrogram for the left and right hemispheres, with a fall in CI and loss of alpha starting at the same time.

  • What is simulated: CI goes from about 3.1 to about 1.7 l/min/m², stroke volume falls, and MAP and pulse pressure fall. Alpha (about 8–12 Hz) disappears in both hemispheres while delta (below 4 Hz) persists. The numbers were chosen to illustrate the pattern.
  • Simultaneity is a choice: Foreman and Claassen state that quantitative EEG captures changes in blood flow and metabolism within 28–104 seconds. The delay between a fall in cardiac output and EEG change will vary, and the image does not show it.
  • Loss of alpha has several possible causes: Miller's chapter 36 describes that both an increase and a reduction in alpha have been reported with noxious stimulation, and Foreman and Claassen mention sedatives and sleep as confounding factors. The image therefore shows no cause, and it cannot be used to distinguish perfusion from other causes. Guay 2025 describes both noxious stimulation and low cardiac output as possible causes of such changes on frontal EEG.
Foreman and Claassen 2012, Miller's ch. 36

Frontal EEG as a perfusion marker in clinical practice (Guay 2025)

Review article from MGH and MIT (Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618) on physiological EEG signatures in the critically ill, with three case reports.

  • Main point: signs of reduced cerebral oxygen delivery (CDO₂) during sedation or general anaesthesia resemble deeper anaesthesia on frontal EEG: a shift of power towards lower frequencies, broadband power loss, burst suppression and sustained suppression. The same applies to hypothermia and increased GABAergic effect. They must therefore be distinguished from one another before the anaesthetic is adjusted. CDO₂ is proportional to CBF, haemoglobin and SpO₂, and the authors emphasise the balance between CDO₂ and oxygen consumption (CMRO₂) more than the exact numbers.
  • Differential diagnosis for reduced neuronal activity: with normal CDO₂: anaesthetic effect, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hypercapnia, postictal suppression and noxious stimulation. With reduced CDO₂: shock, intracranial hypertension, venous congestion, hypoxaemia, hypocapnia, anaemia and stroke. Primary brain injury can produce both.
  • Carotid surgery: the criteria for shunting (more than 50% power reduction in 8–15 Hz, more than 50% increase in slow-delta, more than 50% broadband reduction, or suppression) typically arise when global CBF falls to below 35–40% of normal (about 18–20 versus 50–55 ml/100 g/min).
  • CPP and autoregulation: CPP is MAP minus the greater of ICP and CVP. The lower MAP limit for autoregulation varies from 40 to 90 mmHg in adults, and autoregulation is impaired in many critically ill patients. Reduced CBF can go unnoticed with high haemoglobin and high saturation, whereas anaemic and hypoxaemic patients tolerate less.
  • Burst suppression: suppression is amplitude below 10 µV (typically below 5 µV), and electrocerebral inactivity is 2 µV or lower. In dogs with haemorrhagic shock (fentanyl and nitrous oxide), burst suppression appeared at MAP 31 ± 7 mmHg together with loss of diastolic transcranial Doppler flow (Werner 1995). A randomised trial (Georgii 2022) abolished burst suppression in more than 50% by raising MAP to the baseline value. The authors say it is unclear whether this is due to physiology, pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics. Shock can increase the propofol concentration and make the brain more sensitive.
  • Unintended burst suppression and “triple low”: sedation-induced burst suppression has been linked to lower mortality after traumatic brain injury, whereas unintended burst suppression is linked to higher mortality in intensive care. The authors interpret this as the patient's underlying disease, not burst suppression in itself, driving the risk.
  • Age and alpha: frontal alpha is weaker in old age, poor cognitive function, frailty and severe illness. In older patients without visible alpha, a broadband fall in power may be the first warning.
  • Loss of alpha can also occur with noxious stimulation under inadequate analgesia (Hight 2019), and unexpected beta and gamma during neuromuscular blockade should lead to more anaesthesia and analgesia.
  • Case reports (one patient each): (1) 39-year-old on propofol: burst suppression disappeared with lower propofol. Two days later, loss of alpha and burst suppression appeared when MAP fell below 70 mmHg with right heart failure and rising CVP, and the EEG normalised after adrenaline. The authors also mention that reduced cardiac output may have increased the propofol concentration. (2) 89-year-old after mitral valve surgery: broadband fall in power (slow-delta from 30–40 to 10–20 µV) and then burst suppression at a cardiac index of 1.3. The EEG normalised when CI increased to 2.7 after PVAD. (3) 65-year-old in LVAD surgery: burst suppression during weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass, while the radial artery showed MAP 80–90. Direct aortic pressure was 35 mmHg, probably due to vasoplegia and a fault in the radial line.
  • Limitations: a frontal montage can miss focal temporal seizures and occipital strokes, and acute strokes rarely produce burst suppression frontally. The case reports illustrate, but do not validate, and the article shows no EEG data from patients with raised ICP. They give no thresholds for which MAP or CI produces EEG change in an individual patient.
  • Caveat: Brown reports royalties from Masimo, and Guay reports travel support from Masimo.
Guay et al. Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618

Alpha peak frequency as a marker of lost autoregulation under propofol (Manquat 2022)

Prospective pilot study from Lariboisière (Paris), BJA Open 2022;1:100004. The hypothesis was that frontal EEG can show whether cerebral autoregulation is preserved during propofol anaesthesia.

  • Patients and set-up: 56 included, 36 analysed (median age 57.5 years), elective interventional neuroradiology. Propofol TCI (Schnider, starting at 5 µg/ml) and remifentanil; noradrenaline for MAP above 65 mmHg. SedLine with four frontal channels (Fp1, Fp2, F7, F8; spectrum from Fp2), NIRS, transcranial Doppler in the middle cerebral artery during induction and 30 minutes after, and continuous MAP from a finger cuff (Clearsight).
  • Autoregulation: Mxa = correlation between 10-second averages of MAP and Doppler velocity over 30 epochs.
