Mxa ≥ 0.3 was regarded as lost autoregulation (CA−); the cut-off is taken from traumatic brain injury. The EEG was analysed only in stable windows (PSI 25–35, no burst suppression, SEF 8–15 Hz, MAP above 65, stable for at least 5 minutes).
  • Main finding: 18 CA+ and 18 CA−. The groups were similar in age (53 versus 57 years), MAP (71 mmHg), Doppler velocity, PSI and SEF. Alpha peak frequency was lower with lost autoregulation: 9.4 [9.0–9.9] versus 10.5 [10.1–10.9] Hz (p < 0.001), with a correlation of r = −0.556 against Mxa. Alpha, delta and total power did not differ. Univariate AUC 0.88; in a multivariate model OR 0.038 [0.004–0.409] per Hz (p = 0.007). Lower alpha peak frequency is also associated with postoperative delirium in the meta-analysis by Xu 2025 (Spectrogram tab) and in Gutiérrez 2019. Adding alpha peak frequency to age, ASA and noradrenaline dose increased the AUC from 0.76 to 0.93.
  • What did not discriminate: NIRS (rSO₂ minimum 50 versus 57%, p = 0.08). The CA− group had a higher ASA class and more noradrenaline (0.06 versus 0.03 µg/kg/min). The authors consider NIRS to be insensitive here (extracranial contamination, vasoconstrictor), and that the indices hide the frequency information.
  • Interpretation: alpha frequency, not alpha power, tracks loss of autoregulation, and does so independently of age. Power loss and slow waves (Guay 2025, the carotid criteria) probably only appear with more severe ischaemia. A slower alpha may thus be an earlier and more subtle sign than the patterns described in the cards above. This is a hypothesis from a single pilot study.
  • Limitations: small, single centre, short Mxa window, static analysis (one time point), no clinical outcome measure, and the Mxa cut-off is not validated under anaesthesia. Alpha frequency also falls with age (Purdon 2015 BJA) and with deeper propofol effect, so a low value in an individual patient cannot simply be interpreted as loss of autoregulation. The authors call for a dynamic study. No conflicts of interest declared; funded by the AP-HP foundation.
  • Practical: The alpha peak frequency can be read approximately from the spectrogram, also where the monitor does not display it as a number. An alpha band sitting around 9 Hz in a middle-aged patient with stable PSI and MAP is worth noticing, not acting on alone.
Manquat et al. BJA Open 2022;1:100004

Clinical example: alpha weakens when cardiac output falls (own case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared by the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed, and is included because it illustrates what Guay 2025 and Manquat 2022 describe.

  • What was seen: an adult during maintenance with an unchanged hypnotic dose, PSI 30, SR 0, EMG 0, SEF 10–11 Hz. On the same screen, a pulse contour monitor showed MAP and cardiac index falling for a few minutes (CI down towards about 1 l/min/m²). Over the same period the alpha band became weaker and drifted downwards in both hemispheres, and the spectrogram became “thinner” without suppression. When MAP was 83 mmHg and CI 3.5 again, the alpha band was back as before.
  • Why it is instructive: without the haemodynamic trend alongside, the picture would easily have been interpreted as nociceptive loss of alpha (García 2021) or as a dose that “drifts”. The coincidence in time with cardiac output, the absence of a dose change and the complete return point to transient cerebral hypoperfusion. Guay 2025 describes the same in an 89-year-old in whom the EEG normalised when CI rose from 1.3 to 2.7.
  • Caveat: one case, no measurement of CBF, NIRS or Doppler, and alpha weakening has several possible causes. The point is not that EEG “proves” hypoperfusion, but that EEG and haemodynamics should be read together. See image 17 in the image quiz.
Own clinical example; Guay 2025, Manquat 2022, Nycz 2022

The cards on burst suppression are collected in the tab.

Hemispheric asymmetry on frontal EEG and blood pressure (Nycz 2022, case report)

  • Patient: one 65-year-old man with dialysis-dependent renal failure, complete left-sided ICA occlusion and severe (70–99%) right-sided ICA stenosis, for first rib resection and balloon dilatation of the subclavian vein. Preoperative MAP was 81 mmHg. Induction with fentanyl, lidocaine, propofol, suxamethonium, rocuronium and ketamine, then sevoflurane at 0.7 age-adjusted MAC guided by EEG. The EEG monitor was applied after induction, and the text mentions no EEG baseline before induction.
  • The event: after induction, hypotension occurred (MAP 50–60 mmHg, non-invasive 50–80), treated with noradrenaline boluses and later an infusion. The EEG showed asymmetry: spectral edge frequency (SEF) 10 Hz on the right and 25 Hz on the left, with a hot band at 20–30 Hz probably due to ketamine. When MAP was above 95 mmHg the spectrogram became almost symmetrical.
  • Reduced support: the authors set the lower MAP limit to above 70 mmHg (85% of baseline) and reduced the noradrenaline infusion. Within minutes, fast activity above 12 Hz disappeared in both hemispheres, most on the right (nadir 65 mmHg according to the figure legend). Symmetry returned at MAP above 95 mmHg. The pattern returned after a new fall to 75 mmHg (at 10:32) and did not recur after MAP was kept above 95. The patient was extubated on low-dose noradrenaline, had no new neurological deficits, and at 6 months the stenoses were unchanged.
  • The authors' interpretation: the pattern is “concerning for focal ischaemia”. They also mention possible intracerebral “steal” with exhausted vascular reactivity and increased venous pressure during manipulation of the superior vena cava, and that ketamine disturbs the EEG. They claim this is the first reported case of cerebral hypoperfusion captured by frontal EEG in a non-carotid procedure.
  • The authors' suggestion: MAP alone cannot always be relied on in patients with impaired autoregulation, and the lower MAP limit can be set from EEG symmetry on beat-to-beat arterial pressure. This is a suggestion from one case and has not been tested.
  • Limitations: case report. No CBF, NIRS, Doppler or imaging was measured to confirm ischaemia, the patient had no new deficits, and ketamine and sevoflurane affect the EEG. The edge frequency and asymmetry may have other explanations, and the authors point out that EEG interpretation is not a core skill in anaesthesia training.
  • Connection within the app: the pattern agrees with ischaemia first producing loss of fast activity (Foreman and Claassen) and with asymmetry as a sign of hemispheric involvement (BSI, Sheorajpanday). Guay 2025 describes other case reports in which pressure and cardiac output affect frontal EEG. All are single cases or reviews, not proof.
Nycz et al. Neurol Int 2022;14:1018–1023

Blood pressure targets and delirium (Xu 2020)

  • Design: randomised trial at a single hospital. 150 patients aged 65–80 years underwent hip arthroplasty and were divided into three groups by MAP target: 10–20% below baseline (D), 0–10% below (M) and 0–10% above (H). The anaesthetist could not be blinded.
  • Delirium day 1: 22% (D), 16% (M) and 4% (H), p = 0.031. On days 2 and 3 there was no difference.
  • Group H had higher rSO₂ from five minutes after incision, less emergence agitation (24%, 22% and 6%), a shorter stay in the recovery room (63 versus 92 minutes) and a shorter hospital stay (12 versus 15 days). BIS was similar between the groups.
  • The authors consider that higher rSO₂ may explain the effect. The study shows an association and does not test the mechanism.
  • Caveats: small sample, only one method for delirium, no blood markers, and discrepancies between text and tables (see Sources).
Xu et al. J Clin Anesth 2020;62:109730

Individual blood pressure targets from autoregulation monitoring: Johns Hopkins protocol (Brown and Hogue)

Protocol (version 2, 8 July 2014) for a randomised substudy nested in Hogue’s trial (NCT00981474), with Charles Brown as substudy lead. The file contains only the protocol, not the results.

  • Background: blood pressure targets are currently set empirically. In the elderly, hypertension, diabetes and vascular disease may shift the lower limit of autoregulation, and autoregulation is dynamic, influenced among other things by rewarming from hypothermia, inhaled agents (dose-dependently) and anaemia.
  • Patients: 55 years or older, surgery on cardiopulmonary bypass (coronary bypass, valve or ascending aorta), high risk of neurological complications, and with a TCD window.
  • Measurement: TCD over both middle cerebral arteries and NIRS on the forehead. MAP, flow velocity and rScO₂ are averaged in 10-second blocks. A moving correlation between MAP and flow velocity over 300 seconds (30 points) gives the mean velocity index (Mx), and the same with NIRS gives the cerebral oximetry index (COx). Values are sorted into 5 mmHg MAP bins. When autoregulation is intact, the correlation is near zero or negative; when lost, it approaches 1.
  • Intervention: MAP on bypass is kept above the patient’s own lower limit based on Mx. If MAP falls below the limit, phenylephrine 100 µg is given and isoflurane reduced (to a minimum of 0.5%), with vasopressin if needed. The control group is managed with standard MAP targets.
  • Endpoint: postoperative delirium, from 2014 defined by a consensus committee.
  • Caveats: this is a protocol, not results. Funded by the NIH.
Protocol, NCT00981474 (substudy), Johns Hopkins 2014

What is the blood pressure limit? The evidence is divergent

  • Chapter 11 in Lobo mentions that expert consensus recommends MAP above 60–70 mmHg. Long cumulative time with low pressure, a relative fall of 40% from baseline and MAP below 55 mmHg are linked to cardiac and brain injury, including delirium, and to cognitive impairment and dementia within one year.
  • A meta-analysis found no association between permitted MAP below 60 and mortality, and several studies found no association between hypotension and postoperative neurocognitive impairment.
  • Georgii defines baseline as the lowest measured MAP before anaesthesia. Xu uses an average of measurements before surgery. The definitions are not the same, so the studies cannot be compared directly.
  • “Triple low” (low pressure, low EEG index and low MAC) may be a marker of vulnerable patients rather than a cause. A randomised trial with alerts for such events did not affect 90-day mortality, but few alerts were acted on.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 11

Monitoring perfusion

  • rSO₂: the normal range is wide (55–80%). A fall of 15–20% from baseline, or values below 50%, is regarded as significant. Sensitivity 60–100% and specificity 94–98% for cerebral ischaemia.
  • Carotid surgery: a fall of 20% after clamping is linked to impaired consciousness with a high negative predictive value (about 2.6% develop neurological deterioration with smaller falls). The positive predictive value is low, and many use rSO₂ more to guide haemodynamics than to decide on shunting.
  • Preoperative rSO₂ of 60% or lower is linked to delirium in older patients after cardiac surgery, and below 50% to higher 30-day mortality.
  • Autoregulation: invasively, the pressure reactivity index (PRx) and optimal CPP (CPPopt) are used. With NIRS, the indices TOx and COx can be used as surrogates, with moderate to good correlation but lower precision. TCD requires an awake baseline.
  • The book refers to a randomised trial of 255 patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy in which multimodal guidance (EEG spectrogram, NIRS, TCD and haemodynamics) gave less delirium.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 1, 7 and 9

Positioning (Miller's chapter 30)

Perfusion pressure and head height

  • When the head lies at a different height from the heart, you must account for the hydrostatic pressure in the arteries and veins of the brain when estimating cerebral perfusion pressure. The chapter recommends documenting any pressure gradient.
  • Head above the heart lowers cerebral perfusion pressure and can produce systemic hypotension. With invasive blood pressure measurement the transducer should be zeroed at the level of the circle of Willis.
  • Trendelenburg increases intracranial and intraocular pressure, and the position is contraindicated in raised intracranial pressure.
  • General anaesthesia blunts the normal compensatory mechanisms (baroreceptor reflex, sympathetic vasoconstriction). Haemodynamic changes with positioning are therefore more pronounced.
Miller's ch. 30

Steep Trendelenburg and pneumoperitoneum (Kalmar 2010)

  • Design: observational study of 31 patients (age 62, range 49–76) undergoing robot-assisted prostatectomy in 40° Trendelenburg with CO₂ pneumoperitoneum at 10 mmHg. Mean time in the position was 159 minutes. Anaesthesia with propofol, sufentanil and sevoflurane (1 MAC).
  • Measurement of CPP: the pressure transducers were zeroed at the external auditory meatus, so CPP could be determined independently of position. CPP was calculated as MAP minus CVP, on the assumption that CVP is at least as high as ICP in this position. ICP was not measured.
  • Results: MAP rose from 79 to 95 mmHg and CVP from 8 to 26 mmHg, and CPP was unchanged (71 versus 70 mmHg in table 1). CPP stayed well above the lower limit of autoregulation. After return to the supine position MAP and CVP fell by the same amount, and CPP was briefly down at 61 mmHg before normalising within 3 minutes.
  • Cerebral oxygenation: SctO₂ (NIRS, second generation) rose from 70 to 73% (p < 0.001) and remained above 55% throughout, which the authors use as the limit below which ischaemia is very unlikely. The authors assume that higher CPP and higher PE′CO₂ increased blood flow and lowered oxygen extraction.
  • CO₂: PE′CO₂ rose from 4.12 to 4.79 kPa, and the gradient between arterial and end-tidal CO₂ increased from 1.06 to as much as 1.46 kPa. The authors recommend using PE′CO₂ with caution in this situation, because it underestimates PaCO₂ most at high values.
  • Lungs: plateau pressure rose from 14 to 26 cmH₂O, and compliance fell from 50 to 23 ml/cmH₂O. Compliance was still lower than baseline after return to the supine position.
  • The authors refer to earlier work describing intracranial hypertension with this combination, and lower SctO₂ in older patients and in patients with raised ICP. These groups were not the focus here. Raised CO₂ also increases intraocular pressure and may carry a risk of visual loss.
  • Limitations: small observational study, no control group, no ICP or EEG measurement, and only patients who tolerated the procedure. The findings cannot be transferred to patients with raised ICP.
Kalmar et al. Br J Anaesth 2010;104:433–9

What determines cerebral blood flow in Trendelenburg? Cardiac output, not MAP (Nordum 2024)

Prospective observational study from Ahus (Front Anesthesiol 2024;3:1395973): 44 men (mean 67 years) for robot-assisted prostatectomy in 30° Trendelenburg, propofol/remifentanil with BIS 40–60, deep neuromuscular blockade, PEEP 8 and tidal volume 6 ml/kg. 37 had intraoperative measurements at six time points: blood flow in the internal carotid artery (ICA) by ultrasound, cardiac output, CVP via the external jugular vein, optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) as a surrogate for ICP, and PaCO₂. Cognitive testing (CANTAB) before, and 10 and 180 days after.

  • Induction is the largest fall: ICA flow fell about 30% after induction (483 to 344 ml/min) and CPP from 98 to 73 mmHg. Tilt and pneumoperitoneum produced no further fall in ICA flow, even though CPP fell further to 61–62 mmHg after one hour and ONSD increased from 5.8 to 6.4 mm. After return to the supine position ICA flow rose to 407 ml/min.
  • Predictors: cardiac output was the strongest predictor of ICA flow (1 l/min/m² more gave 92 ml/min more), PaCO₂ had a small positive effect (1 kPa gave 49 ml/min), while MAP had a small negative effect (10 mmHg more gave 29 ml/min less) within the classical autoregulatory range. The authors consider monitoring of cardiac output more important than the traditional focus on MAP in this position.
  • Wide spread: during tilt CVP varied from 10 to 28 mmHg and CPP from 49 to 99 mmHg between patients. Vasopressor was used in 78% during tilt.
  • Cognition: no sign of postoperative cognitive dysfunction at 10 or 180 days; small improvements on several tests are consistent with a learning effect. None of the intraoperative measures predicted cognitive outcomes.
  • Versus Kalmar 2010: Kalmar found unchanged CPP at 40° with the zero point at the auditory meatus; Nordum found falling CPP at 30°, but preserved ICA flow, which argues for at least partly functioning autoregulation. Both found an increased CO₂ gradient and a fall in compliance.
  • Caveats: observational study without control group or power calculation, unilateral ICA measurement (the ICA supplies about 80% of cerebral blood flow), non-blinded ultrasound analysis, vasopressor at discretion, non-Scandinavian speakers excluded, and considerable dropout at 180 days (25 of 37). Publicly funded, no conflicts of interest.
Nordum et al. Front Anesthesiol 2024;3:1395973

How reliable is end-tidal CO₂ in Trendelenburg? (Pisitsak 2019)

20 healthy women (mean 42 years) for laparoscopic gynaecological surgery in 30° Trendelenburg with pneumoperitoneum 13 mmHg, thiopental/sevoflurane/nitrous oxide, PEEP 5 (J Med Assoc Thai 2019;102:122–128).

  • The gradient increases, but only a little: PaCO₂–PETCO₂ rose from 2.3 to 3.9 mmHg after 45 minutes of pneumoperitoneum (p = 0.02) and returned to 2.85 after desufflation. The correlation between ETCO₂ and PaCO₂ was maintained (r about 0.5). Static compliance fell from 32 to 22 ml/cmH₂O. Minute ventilation had to be increased about 14% to keep ETCO₂ at 28–35 mmHg.
  • Predictor: plateau pressure during pneumoperitoneum predicted the gradient (R² 0.40). Oxygenation (PaO₂/FiO₂) fell from 516 to 415 and was still reduced (398) at the end, probably atelectasis.
  • Conclusion: ETCO₂ remains usable with pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg in healthy patients, but the gradient is larger in older patients, obese patients and with low cardiac output. The authors recommend higher PEEP and recruitment. Small sample, only healthy women.
Pisitsak et al. J Med Assoc Thai 2019;102:122–128

Sitting and “beach chair”

  • Hypotension is common. Mean arterial pressure, systolic pressure and cardiac index fall in the sitting position, and the chapter recommends gradual positioning with fluid and vasopressor ready.
  • Possible mechanisms of cerebral ischaemia: reduced cardiac output, deliberate or permitted hypotension, lost compensation under general anaesthesia, failure to account for head height in blood pressure management, dynamic narrowing or occlusion of the vertebral artery on rotation, and air embolism.
  • Cerebral oximetry: in an observational study of 124 patients undergoing shoulder arthroscopy, 80% in the “beach chair” position had cerebral desaturation, versus none in the lateral position. The chapter says there is no gold standard for threshold values, and that trends should be interpreted with stable ventilation and position. Murphy 2010: prospective cohort study with 61 patients in the “beach chair” position and 63 in the right or left lateral position, where the surgeon chose the position (not randomised). All received standardised anaesthesia with sevoflurane, BIS 40–60 and blood pressure within 20% of baseline. Cerebral desaturation (CDE) was defined as a fall of at least 20% from baseline or SctO₂ below 55% for 15 seconds, measured with FORE-SIGHT and treated according to a fixed protocol (increased blood pressure, increased EtCO₂ or increased FiO₂). 80.3% (49 of 61) in the “beach chair” position had CDE versus 0% in the lateral position, with a median of 4 episodes per patient (0–38). SctO₂ fell from about 80% to about 70% within 9 minutes and stayed between 66 and 70%, even though brachial blood pressure did not differ between the groups. Eight patients had 12 episodes below 55%, all in the “beach chair” position. After the first treatment SctO₂ rose in 61%. The authors calculate that a brachial mean pressure of 80 mmHg with a 38 cm height difference to the forehead corresponds to about 52 mmHg at the brain, which may have been too low for some. No obvious neurological deficits were seen, but no cognitive testing was done. Among patients without an interscalene block, nausea was 50.0% versus 6.7% and vomiting 27.3% versus 3.3% in those with CDE, but the CDE group consisted only of “beach chair” patients (none in the lateral position), so position and CDE cannot be separated. The probes were supplied at cost by CAS Medical Systems, and the first author has received honoraria from CASMED.
  • Recommendation in the chapter: measure blood pressure with the level of the brain in mind, avoid and treat hypotension and bradycardia promptly, and avoid extreme head positions.
  • The neck: hyperextension, hyperflexion and forceful rotation are implicated in cervical cord injury. The chapter mentions quadriplegia and spinal infarction. It is recommended to examine range of motion preoperatively and to keep a gap between chin and chest (classically two finger breadths).
Miller's ch. 30 (Murphy 2010, Hindman 2011)

Venous air embolism (VAE)

  • The surgical field lies above the heart, and the dural veins lack valves and are held open by the skull. VAE can cause arrhythmias, desaturation, pulmonary hypertension, circulatory collapse and cardiac arrest.
  • With a patent foramen ovale there is a risk of paradoxical arterial embolism with stroke or myocardial infarction. A more recent review in the chapter found no paradoxical emboli in patients with known patent foramen ovale, even though VAE was detected in 40%. The decision is made together with the patient, surgeon and anaesthetist. Klein 2018: systematic review of four observational studies published after 2007 (Ammirati 2013, Ganslandt 2013, Hervías 2014 and Feigl 2014). Among 82 patients with known patent foramen ovale (PFO), 33 (40.2%) had air embolism, and none had paradoxical embolism. The figure of 82 counts only the 4 of 10 PFO patients in Ammirati who were operated on sitting (6 were operated on prone because the shunt was judged to be significant). Most come from Feigl (52 patients, 29 with air embolism detected by transoesophageal echocardiography, without clinical deterioration) and Ganslandt (24 patients, 4 with air embolism). An earlier review (Fathi 2009) reported nine clinically relevant paradoxical emboli in 2866 operations (0.3%), and an estimated 2.5% in presumed PFO patients among those not examined. The authors consider that surgery in the semi-sitting position is justifiable at experienced centres even with PFO, but that closure before surgery can be considered for a large PFO (over 4 mm) or a permanent right-to-left shunt in patients who have had paradoxical embolism. Limitations: only four observational studies, no controlled studies, and patients with a large shunt may have been operated on in another position (selection bias). Zero events among 82 patients does not rule out a risk of up to about 4% (own calculation with exact 95% confidence interval, not given in the article).
  • Transoesophageal echocardiography is the most sensitive (down to about 0.02 ml/kg of air), transcranial Doppler almost as sensitive, and transthoracic Doppler is the most sensitive non-invasive method (about 0.05 ml/kg). End-tidal CO₂ and pulse oximetry are much less sensitive.
  • Treatment: stop further air entry (flood the field with saline, bone wax), 100% oxygen, fluid and vasoactive agents, and consider left lateral position and Trendelenburg if possible.
  • Pneumocephalus is almost always found on imaging after surgery in the sitting position. Tension pneumocephalus is very rare.
Miller's ch. 30 (Mirski 2007, Klein 2018)

Perioperative visual loss (POVL)

  • Causes: central or branch retinal artery occlusion, anterior and posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, cortical blindness, acute glaucoma and gas expansion after retinal surgery.
  • Ischaemic optic neuropathy occurs in about 1 in 60,000–125,000 anaesthetics, but more often in spinal surgery and cardiac surgery. After spinal fusion a case-control study found increased risk with male sex, obesity, Wilson frame, long anaesthesia time, large blood loss and a low colloid fraction in replacement fluid.
  • Central retinal artery occlusion is most often caused by external pressure on the eye. The chapter recommends a foam head rest with the eyes in a cut-out and checking the head and eyes about every 20 minutes.
  • The American advisory (2012, confirmed in the 2019 edition) says there is no evidence that facial oedema or ocular compression causes ischaemic optic neuropathy. Direct pressure on the eye should nevertheless be avoided to prevent central retinal artery occlusion.
  • High-risk patients should have the head level with or above the heart when feasible. Vision should be assessed when the patient is awake, and if there is suspicion, prompt ophthalmological assessment is required.
  • Nitrous oxide must not be used in patients who have recently received a gas bubble (for example perfluorocarbon) after vitrectomy, because the bubble expands and can cause visual loss.
Miller's ch. 30 (ASA 2012 and 2019, Shen 2009, Rubin 2016)

ASA Practice Advisory for perioperative visual loss in spinal surgery (2019)

  • What it is: updated advisory from the ASA, the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society and the Society for Neuroscience in Anesthesiology and Critical Care (Anesthesiology 2019;130:12–30). It applies to adults and children over 12 years undergoing spinal surgery in the prone position under general anaesthesia and covers posterior and anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, retinal artery occlusion, cortical blindness and PRES. “High-risk patients” are defined as prone position with procedures over 4 hours, blood loss over 800 ml, or both.
  • Evidence: no randomised studies. The recommendations are based on observational studies, case reports (82 articles in total) and surveys among experts and members of the professional societies. They are not standards and cannot guarantee any outcome.
  • Before surgery: review risk factors (anaemia, hypertension, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, coronary disease, previous stroke, carotid stenosis, smoking and obesity) and inform high-risk patients of the increased risk. The literature is insufficient for glaucoma and for the optic disc “cup-to-disc” ratio.
  • Blood pressure and blood loss: assess baseline blood pressure, monitor blood pressure continually in high-risk patients (the advisory distinguishes “continual”, meaning repeated regularly and frequently, from “continuous”, without interruption) and treat prolonged significant falls. Hypotension as a cause is uncertain in the literature. Controlled hypotension should be considered case by case and used only if anaesthetist and surgeon agree that it is necessary, with higher pressures in hypertensive patients. Hb or Hct should be measured regularly with large blood loss, but there is no documented lower Hb limit linked to visual loss, and a transfusion threshold that removes the risk cannot be stated. Crystalloid or colloid may be used, and vasopressors may be used when needed.
  • Positioning: the head should be level with or above the rest of the body when possible, in a neutral position, without pressure on the eyes, and the eyes should be checked regularly. The literature is insufficient to recommend any particular head rest equipment or a particular frequency for checking the eyes. Staged surgery can be considered case by case, but the effect has not been studied.
  • After surgery: assess vision when the patient is awake and request immediate ophthalmological assessment if there is suspicion. CT or MRI can be used to rule out intracranial causes. Optimise Hb, haemodynamics and oxygenation. There is no evidence for steroids, antiplatelet agents or pressure-lowering agents in ischaemic optic neuropathy (14 case reports without improvement and two with improvement).
  • Note: the Task Force writes that there is no mechanism by which facial oedema causes ischaemic optic neuropathy, and that there is no evidence that ocular compression causes isolated neuropathy of this kind. The recommendation to check the eyes “about every 20 minutes” appears in the chapter in Miller's, not in this advisory.
  • Conflicts of interest: three of the authors have served as expert witnesses in cases concerning perioperative visual loss.
ASA Task Force et al. Anesthesiology 2019;130:12–30
Miller's chapter 30 does not describe EEG. The EEG section above is based on Lobo and Lamperti and the studies. The evidence for EEG in raised ICP is sparse (see the card on ICP). Foreman and Claassen mention that the mean frequency falls when CPP is below 60 mmHg. Kalmar measured neither ICP nor EEG.

Burst suppression

All the cards on burst suppression are collected here: what the pattern is, when it is wanted, when it is not needed, and what it means for outcomes.

When is burst suppression wanted, and when is it not needed?

A synthesis of the cards in this tab. Sources are given with each point.

  • As a deliberate treatment: burst suppression is induced in refractory status epilepticus, raised intracranial pressure and aneurysm surgery with temporary clipping to lower metabolism and ICP. Gruenbaum 2026 writes that it should be individualised and time-limited, with concurrent attention to perfusion, oxygenation and temperature. In status epilepticus it is part of third-line treatment (Intensive care tab).
  • Is it neuroprotective? The rationale rests on oxygen consumption and blood flow falling together. Gruenbaum 2026 points out that this coupling weakens with age, vascular disease and anaesthesia. In aneurysm surgery the evidence is mixed, and animal studies suggest that protection does not require burst suppression (Jegarl 2026). After cardiac arrest, Jegarl 2026 and Forgacs 2020 describe the hypothesis of a protective down-regulated state.
  • Not needed for general anaesthesia: propofol produces burst suppression at about 4.9 µg/ml, whereas movement to incision is prevented only at about 15 µg/ml (Pilge 2014). Unconsciousness occurs at much lower concentrations (Components tab). The Pilge authors write that a «silent second» is too deep for clinical anaesthesia, and Gruenbaum 2026 that excessive cortical silencing gives no additional protection against awareness but may carry a cognitive cost.
  • Not needed during ICU sedation: in Watson 2008 nobody had burst suppression as a goal, and burst suppression was associated with higher mortality (HR 2.04). In Andresen 2014 more time in burst suppression gave higher odds of delirium (OR 4.16). Hogan 2020 found that burst suppression is mostly a marker of how ill the patient is, but that titrating to the lowest necessary dose may have a modest effect.
  • When it appears unintentionally: look for the cause before increasing or accepting the dose: blood pressure, oxygenation, haemoglobin, glucose and temperature (Gruenbaum 2026). In Georgii 2022 burst suppression disappeared in 55 % of cases simply by raising MAP to the patient's baseline.
  • If it is the goal, it must be verified: a flat EEG is not the same as the intended burst suppression (the herniation case below). Unilateral suppression may mean focal ischaemia or a technical fault (Gruenbaum 2026, the ECMO case in the Intensive care tab).
  • Interpretation based on the sources: the sources support that burst suppression can have a place as a deliberate, time-limited treatment, but that it is not needed for unconsciousness, amnesia or immobility during anaesthesia or sedation. Unintended burst suppression is a signal to look for the cause, not a sign of adequate anaesthetic depth.

What it is and why it occurs

Burst suppression: mechanisms, age and delirium (Lobo and Lamperti, ch. 5)

  • What it is: alternating periods of almost absent activity and high-amplitude bursts. Never seen in natural sleep. The bursts are thought to reflect brief periods of thalamic disinhibition.
  • Two proposed mechanisms: cortical hyperexcitability (extracellular calcium and a refractory period after the burst) and a metabolic theory in which falling ATP opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels.
  • Who gets it most easily: the risk increases with age and with impaired neurological status. In older patients the pattern is less distinct: weaker bursts and shallower, shorter suppression, which makes it harder to detect in the most vulnerable (fig. 5.2).
  • Thresholds: high-dose ketamine does not usually produce burst suppression, but affects the threshold; opioids do not produce it directly, but pain and nociception can lower the threshold.
  • Delirium: several groups have found an association, but ENGAGES was inconclusive and has been criticised for the lack of standardised analgesia and for not taking age and cognitive frailty into account. See ENGAGES in the Components tab.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 5

Why burst suppression? A neurophysiological-metabolic model (Ching 2012)

Computational model from MGH, MIT and Boston University (PNAS 2012;109:3095–3100; Ching, Purdon, Vijayan, Kopell and Brown). It attempts to explain why anaesthesia, hypothermia, hypoxic-ischaemic coma and early infantile encephalopathy (Ohtahara) produce the same EEG pattern.

  • The idea: the common denominator is reduced cerebral metabolism. In the model (10 pyramidal neurons and 4 interneurons, Hodgkin-Huxley type), neuronal firing is coupled to ATP production via ATP-gated potassium channels (KATP). When ATP production is reduced, ATP is depleted during a burst, the KATP channels open, the cells hyperpolarise and fall silent; ATP slowly builds up again, and the next burst can start. 50% of normal ATP production gave a suppression ratio of about 0.5, 30% gave about 0.75; bursts and pauses lasted 4–10 seconds.
  • A continuum: burst suppression is not a separate state, but a gradually increasing suppression ratio with deeper inactivation, ending in a completely isoelectric EEG. The authors show an example of rewarming after cooling to 18 °C in which the suppression ratio gradually falls until the EEG is continuous again.
  • The bursts carry the old pattern: during propofol-induced burst suppression the alpha rhythm lives on inside each burst; the spectrogram looks “as if it has been multiplied by a sequence of zeros and ones”. The model predicts that the spectral content of a burst should be the same as just before burst suppression started, regardless of agent. It also predicts a slow frequency drift within each burst (about 11 to 8 Hz) and that fast activity is limited by metabolism, not by GABA inhibition; these two have not been confirmed experimentally.
  • Why it is relevant to perfusion: anaesthetic agents reduce firing and thereby CMRO₂ secondarily, whereas hypothermia and ischaemia reduce metabolism directly without changing the synapses. Both end in the same KATP mechanism. This is the basis for suppression being able to mean either too much agent or too little energy (Guay 2025, Georgii 2022). Ketamine, which increases CMRO₂, does not produce classic burst suppression at clinical doses.
  • The authors' interpretation: each burst is “an attempt to restore basal cortical dynamics”, and suppression is an energy-saving protection. In severe ischaemia even complete isoelectricity cannot preserve ATP, and injury follows. They suggest that the character of the bursts could be used to detect ischaemia during surgery and to distinguish burst suppression from seizures, and that the difference between a low suppression ratio and full isoelectricity should be clarified before “burst suppression” is used as a target in neuroprotection.
  • Limitations: a model with 14–20 cells, without spatial extent, and the KATP channel is a hypothesis; other channels and extracellular calcium (Kroeger and Amzica 2007) may act together. The model explains, but does not prove. No conflicts of interest declared.
Ching et al. PNAS 2012;109:3095–3100

Burst suppression during anaesthesia: a four-step clinical approach (Gruenbaum 2026)

Narrative review (Br J Anaesth 2026;136:1843–1854; Gruenbaum, Safavynia and Bilotta). The authors describe burst suppression as a context-dependent marker of cortical energy balance, neither a therapeutic target nor a pure dose phenomenon.

  • Two processes: down-regulation by anaesthetics (excessive dose, hypothermia) and metabolic failure from insufficient substrate or oxygen (hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, ischaemia). When ATP falls, ATP-gated potassium channels open and neurones hyperpolarise. Astrocytes supply lactate to neurones, and this works less well with age and vascular disease. Low ATP can also weaken the blood–brain barrier and admit inflammatory mediators; the injury markers S100B and GFAP are linked to delirium. With severe hypoperfusion or anoxic injury the EEG can become isoelectric.
  • Who tolerates it: burst suppression may be tolerated in young, healthy people without measurable consequences, whereas recurrent or persistent burst suppression in vulnerable patients more often reflects exhausted reserve. The authors argue that its meaning depends more on the brain's metabolic reserve than on its duration.
  • Raw EEG over the index: The indices are affected by suppression only when it dominates the analysis window, so acceptable index values can coexist with clear discontinuity. Automated detection underestimated duration compared with visual scoring and missed burst suppression in about 14 % of cases. On the spectrogram, burst suppression produces a «checkerboard» pattern with dark horizontal stripes. Electrocautery and poor electrode contact can mimic burst suppression: true bursts have organised spectral content, whereas artefacts give broadband spikes.
  • Numbers: in a retrospective study of more than 38,000 adults nearly half had burst suppression, and both likelihood and duration increased with age. Sevoflurane produces burst suppression at about 2.9 % (above 1 MAC), propofol at about 4.9 µg/ml, whereas more than 15 µg/ml is needed to prevent movement. Meta-analyses show about 1.5 times higher risk of postoperative delirium.
  • Four steps: (1) confirm on the raw EEG: electrode contact and impedance, artefacts, and the lowest scale that shows the trace without clipping. (2) Assess symmetry: unilateral suppression may mean focal ischaemia or a technical fault; keep the dose unchanged and assess perfusion. (3) With symmetric suppression and a high dose: reduce by 0.1–0.2 MAC or propofol by 10–20 %. (4) If it persists at a low dose: look for hypotension, hypoxaemia, anaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and hypocapnia.
  • Pain and opioids: nociception can produce beta or delta arousal that is misread as too-light hypnosis, and more hypnotic then increases the risk of burst suppression. Opioids can unmask or accentuate burst suppression together with propofol or volatile agents.
  • Caveats: narrative review without a systematic search, focused on surgery rather than cardiac arrest or intensive care. No conflicts of interest. The authors state that a language model from OpenAI was used for editing. Safavynia is a co-author both here and of Jegarl 2026.
Gruenbaum, Safavynia and Bilotta. Br J Anaesth 2026;136:1843–1854

Measurement: the suppression ratio is an estimate

How deep should therapeutic burst suppression be? SR below 5 % versus 10-second pauses

The author of the app questions why Rasulo 2023 recommends SR below 5 % when burst suppression is used therapeutically, since other sources describe pauses of about 10 seconds and as little epileptiform activity in the bursts as possible. The sources diverge, and the evidence is weak either way.

  • Rasulo 2023: if burst suppression is used, SR should be kept below 5 % (strong consensus in a Delphi panel). The article does not justify the figure. The background text also notes that the degree of suppression varies widely, and that burst suppression is still part of many treatment algorithms for refractory status epilepticus.
  • Pauses of about 10 seconds: a 2022 review of therapeutic burst suppression in refractory status epilepticus states that experts consider an interburst interval of about 10 seconds for 24 hours reasonable, but that the evidence is weak. In retrospective data burst suppression was achieved in only about 40–60 % of patients, and one quantitative study of 17 patients found no association between suppression ratio and outcome.
  • Target and reality (An 2018): 35 patients with refractory status epilepticus at Massachusetts General Hospital, with a target burst suppression probability of 0.8 ± 0.15. Patients were within the target for a median of only 8 % of treatment time and below it 84 % of the time. The same weight-adjusted dose gave different suppression in different patients, and some drifted without any change in infusion.
  • The content of the bursts matters more than the pauses (Johnson 2016): in 19 patients (37 weaning attempts) the amount of epileptiform activity in the bursts was the only feature that separated successful from failed weaning (p = 0.008). A maximum burst amplitude below 125 µV had a sensitivity of 84.6 % and specificity of 61.1 % for successful weaning. Interburst interval, suppression ratio and burst length did not.
  • Rasulo's wording: the statement reads “If burst suppression is used, the suppression ratio should be kept at < 5%”. The author of the app has read it as SR below 5 % being the ideal when burst suppression is not wanted. That would fit the panel's first statement about avoiding burst suppression, but the text does not say so.
  • The definition: ACNS 2021 defines burst suppression as suppression in 50–99 % of the record, and a scoping review divides it into incomplete (20–49 %) and complete (50–99 %) burst suppression (Fisch 2026). SR below 5 % is far below both thresholds.
  • SR 40–60 % as a treatment target: the author of the app has heard this but does not remember the source. It has not been found in peer-reviewed literature. The 2026 scoping review gives no SR treatment target.
  • Does burst suppression improve outcome? (Fisch 2023 and 2026): all patients with refractory status epilepticus received continuous intravenous anaesthesia, and the question was how deep they should be taken. In a nine-year cohort of 102 patients without anoxic brain injury, reaching burst suppression was not associated with lasting seizure termination, in-hospital survival or return to previous function in adjusted analyses. The scoping review concludes that current evidence does not support burst suppression over seizure cessation as the target for most patients with refractory status epilepticus.
  • Norwegian practice (Heuser 2024): according to the author of the app, many Norwegian hospitals have protocols with burst suppression for 24 hours as the treatment target. The review of the treatment of status epilepticus in adults in the Journal of the Norwegian Medical Association states that general anaesthesia should be started as soon as possible, with propofol as the most common agent, that full burst suppression is “hardly strictly necessary”, but that “burst suppression for 12 to 24 hours can be a practical goal”. The right depth of anaesthesia based on the EEG is “not fully clarified”, and the EEG is the most important monitoring tool. The need for continued propofol should be reassessed after two to three days because of the risk of propofol infusion syndrome.
  • The arithmetic (interpretation based on the sources): SR is the proportion of time spent in suppression. Pauses of 10 seconds with bursts of 1–3 seconds give an SR of about 75–90 %. An SR of 40–60 % means bursts and pauses last about equally long. An SR below 5 % means an almost continuous EEG, which is hardly burst suppression at all. The figures from the different sources therefore describe very different depths.
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): there is no single documented target. The raw EEG and the content of the bursts (epileptiform activity) should be followed, not just SR, and SR from a frontal monitor is an estimate that can be wrong in both directions (see the card below). The target should be agreed with a neurologist or neurointensivist for each patient.
Rasulo 2023, An 2018, Johnson 2016, Fisch 2023 and 2026, Heuser 2024, review 2022 (doi 10.1007/s10309-022-00539-z)

Suppression ratio and «suppression time»: an algorithm that can be wrong in both directions

Many studies and much teaching emphasise minutes in suppression. The number comes from the monitor's algorithm, not from someone reading the raw EEG.

  • How the number is made: the monitor calculates what proportion of a time window (BIS: the last 63 seconds) lies below an amplitude threshold and calls it suppression (Andresen 2014). The monitors do not recognise bursts, only low amplitude (Kratzer 2020). Studies then multiply this proportion by time to obtain «minutes in suppression».
  • Falsely low SR: noise above the threshold prevents the algorithm from seeing suppression. EMG is the most common source. In image 2 of the image quiz (shared case) SR was 0 and BIS 64 while the EEG was almost flat. After a neuromuscular blocker, with no change in dose, SR rose to 82 and BIS fell to 8. In older patients low bursts can fall below the threshold, and Muhlhofer 2017 found that the suppression ratio underestimates suppression compared with visual reading (Kratzer 2020). Gruenbaum 2026 reports that automated detection missed burst suppression in about 14 % of cases.
  • Falsely high SR: poor electrode contact or high impedance can produce a low-amplitude signal that resembles suppression, and electrocautery, suction and movement can produce large transients followed by signal dropout that resemble bursts and pauses (Gruenbaum 2026). On visual reading, low-amplitude but continuous EEG in older patients can be misread as suppression if the scale is not adjusted (Gruenbaum 2026).
  • Small changes, large swings: Gruenbaum 2026 writes that SR is highly sensitive to the amplitude threshold and to noise, and that small changes in amplitude or artefacts can cause large fluctuations in low-amplitude EEG.
  • What it means for research: Jegarl 2026 cites a study (41 patients) in which visually determined suppression duration was associated with delirium (p = 0.039), whereas duration calculated from the monitor's SR was not (p = 0.275). Gruenbaum 2026 argues that such measurement limitations probably explain why strong associations in observational studies have not translated into benefit in randomised EEG-guided trials. In Fritz 2016, values for 141 patients were read from screenshots every 5 minutes and interpolated, and in Watson 2008 BIS was recorded for only 10–20 minutes per day.
  • Documenting suppression time: many ask for a separate suppression time (ST) number for documentation. Some monitors give a separate suppression time, others only SR as a percentage of time, and the time window and calculation are not always described by the manufacturer. Interpretation based on the sources: an ST number rests on the same amplitude threshold as SR and inherits the same sources of error, so it does not make documentation more precise than the raw-EEG assessment behind it.
  • In practice: read SR together with the raw EEG at the right scale, the EMG bar, signal quality and the spectrogram. Gruenbaum's first step is to confirm the pattern on the raw EEG before anything else.
  • Interpretation based on the sources: «suppression time» in studies and on the monitor is an algorithmic estimate that can be too low (noise, EMG, low bursts) or too high (poor contact, artefacts, low-amplitude continuous EEG). The number should be used as a warning to be checked, not as ground truth.

Dose and age

Burst suppression MAC and CP50 (Pilge 2014)

  • What it is: a study proposing the “silent second” (EEG suppression for at least 1 second) as a measure of the anaesthetic agent's effect on the brain, instead of movement at incision (MAC, which mostly reflects the spinal cord).
  • Design: 55 unpremedicated ASA I–II patients for elective surgery were randomised to sevoflurane (16), isoflurane (21) or propofol (18). The concentration was held constant for 15 minutes and EEG analysed in the 16th minute, and the next patient received a 10% lower concentration if suppression occurred and 10% higher if not (Dixon's “up-and-down” method, six independent crossover pairs per group). The values were calculated with logistic regression.
  • Result: sevoflurane 2.93 vol% (95% CI 2.80–3.15), isoflurane 1.51 vol% (1.45–1.60) and propofol 4.85 (CI 4.25–5.40; the article states “mg/ml”, probably micrograms/ml). That is over 1.4 times MAC for sevoflurane (2.05 vol%), over 1.3 times MAC for isoflurane (1.15 vol%) and under a third of the propofol concentration that prevents movement at incision (15.2 µg/ml, from Smith 1994).
  • Reservations: the starting concentrations were above the population value, and the authors write that the confidence intervals may therefore be too wide, particularly for propofol. The sample is small. Burst suppression does not occur with ketamine, so the measure cannot be used for ketamine. The pattern also differs between agents, and the authors write that a “silent second” is too deep for clinical anaesthesia.
  • What the article does not say: it does not state that fentanyl reduces the propofol concentration by about 80%. That figure comes from Smith 1994 via Miller's.
  • Conflicts of interest: none declared. Funded by departmental funds.
Pilge et al. Br J Anaesth 2014;112:1067–1074

The bursts become weaker and more irregular with age (Kratzer 2020)

Retrospective analysis from TU Munich and Columbia (Front Syst Neurosci 2020;14:599962) of the first burst after burst suppression appeared during propofol induction. The data are from Hesse 2019 (Atlanta), recorded with SedLine (Legacy) and analysed by an independent university group.

  • Method: 102 of 408 patients had a distinct first burst after a “silent second” (at least 1 s below 10 µV). Only the first 1.5 seconds of the burst were analysed, so that differing duration and dose would not affect the result. Median age 56 years; 16 patients under 45 years (YOUNG) and a group over 65 years (OLD). Fentanyl equivalents did not differ with age.
  • Findings: older patients had lower absolute power in 1–15 Hz and relatively more power above 15 Hz within the burst. Absolute alpha power fell linearly with age (AUC 0.86 for young versus old), while normalised alpha did not change: it is the amplitude, not the architecture, that disappears. Maximum amplitude was 20.3 µV in the young versus 13.1 µV in the older patients (AUC 0.84), steepest slope 1.22 versus 0.86 µV/ms, and permutation entropy was higher in the older patients (more irregular signal). Subanalysis of the 83 who received midazolam premedication gave the same result.
  • Why it matters for the monitor: The indices detect burst suppression by looking for suppression, that is EEG below an amplitude threshold for a certain time, not by recognising the bursts. When the bursts in older patients are lower and flatter, they can themselves fall below the threshold, and Muhlhofer 2017 showed that the suppression ratio underestimates suppression compared with visual reading. The authors argue that burst information should be used as a plausibility check, but then age-adjusted. This is the mechanism behind Image 6 and 13 in the image quiz: in older patients both normal EEG and bursts can look “weak”.
  • Connection in the app: the same age-related change that Purdon 2015 (BJA) and Kreuzer 2020 described for maintenance without burst suppression, and which Ching 2012 predicts: the spectral content of the burst mirrors the EEG just before the suppression started. Obert 2024 (the card above) shows that slow induction can avoid burst suppression in older patients in the first place.
  • Limitations: frontal EEG, only propofol-induced bursts (Fleischmann 2018 showed that the agent affects the shape of the burst), no adjustment for comorbidity, and the midazolam subgroup among the older patients was small. Funded by the James S. McDonnell Foundation (García); no conflicts of interest declared.
Kratzer et al. Front Syst Neurosci 2020;14:599962

After burst suppression the brain is not the same: non-linear pharmacodynamics (Sepúlveda 2026)

Prospective, non-randomised dose–response study from Osorno (Anesth Analg 2026;143:261–270, NCT06417645): 23 healthy patients under 60 years received slow induction (10 mg/kg/h) to loss of response, then Eleveld TCI, remifentanil 4.5 ng/ml and rocuronium. After intubation, propofol was increased to 15 mg/kg/h until BIS showed a 1% suppression ratio (“perturbation”), and the effect-site concentration was then set back to the level at loss of response. Observed BIS was compared with BIS predicted by the Eleveld model (TIVA Trainer), and the EEG spectrum and delta–alpha phase-amplitude coupling were analysed.

  • Before the perturbation: observed and predicted BIS were the same (no significant difference).
  • After the perturbation: with the same calculated effect-site concentration as before, observed BIS lay consistently below predicted BIS (largest bias −17.5 in the phase after the perturbation), and the difference persisted for the rest of the operation. Alpha power (absolute and relative) was lower than before, and the delta–alpha modulation (Kmod) was stronger (0.21 versus 0.16, p = 0.01), which the authors interpret as deeper thalamocortical synchronisation. Same concentration, deeper effect.
  • Slow induction gives a lower Ce at loss of response: on average 2.0 µg/ml, versus an EC50 of about 3 µg/ml in the Eleveld model for the same age. The authors believe the models were built on bolus and rapid-infusion data without plasma–effect equilibrium (“front-end” kinetics), and that ke0 is a mathematical device to collapse the hysteresis loop.
  • Interpretation: the brain under anaesthesia behaves as a non-linear system (the same dose does not give the same effect, no return to the starting point). Linear PK/PD models therefore cannot predict the effect after a disturbance, whether experimental (brief burst suppression) or clinical (haemorrhage shrinking V1, altered infusion rate). The conclusion is continuous EEG monitoring, especially in vulnerable patients. The authors discuss nociception as an alternative explanation for the lower alpha (surgery was under way after the perturbation), but consider that the stronger delta–alpha coupling argues against it.
  • Caveats: no control group without perturbation, so time alone cannot be excluded; circularity because “the same concentration” is defined by the model being tested; no plasma measurements; only healthy subjects under 60; the BIS prediction from Eleveld is itself debated (Coetzee 2024). The numbers in the abstract and the results section do not agree (see discrepancies). No conflicts of interest, public funding (ANID).
Sepúlveda, Barra, Baloian, Gutiérrez. Anesth Analg 2026;143:261–270

Burst suppression and outcomes

EEG suppression during surgery and subsequent delirium (Fritz 2016)

Observational study from Washington University (Anesth Analg 2016;122:234–242), a sub-study of the SATISFY-SOS registry. This is the study most often cited for the association between burst suppression during anaesthesia and delirium.

  • Patients: 727 adults (mean 62 years, 63% men) for general anaesthesia with planned intensive care stay, 86% cardiac surgery. Induction with propofol, maintenance with a volatile agent. Suppression ratio from one BIS channel (Fp1–F7), recorded once a minute, summed to minutes with suppression. In 141 patients the values were read from screenshots every 5 minutes and interpolated. Delirium was assessed with CAM-ICU twice daily on days 1–5 in 619 patients.
  • Findings: median suppression 4.5 minutes (IQR 0.7–17.4). 162 (26%) developed delirium, 73% of them hypoactive. More minutes in suppression gave a higher incidence of delirium across quartiles (p < 0.0001), and the association held after adjustment for age, ASA, comorbidity, type of surgery, opioid, ketamine, transfusion and end-tidal concentration: OR 1.22 per log unit of minutes of suppression (99% CI 1.06–1.40). Suppression time predicted delirium better than time with BIS below 20 (c-statistic 0.62 versus 0.57), but both are weak predictors on their own.
  • What produced suppression: higher end-tidal concentration (OR 1.5 per 0.5 MAC) and lower opioid dose (OR 0.5 per 1 morphine equivalent/kg). The authors cannot say whether less opioid led to more suppression, or whether deeply anaesthetised patients without signs of nociception simply received less opioid.
  • Interpretation, the authors' two possibilities: either too deep anaesthesia as the cause, or that suppression arises more readily in patients with subclinical brain pathology, so that anaesthesia acts as a “neural stress test”. The study cannot separate the two; see Hogan 2020 and Jegarl 2026 below.
  • Limitations: observational study without causal inference, delirium measured as part of routine care (low sensitivity), no preoperative Barthel measurement, only planned intensive care patients, and mostly cardiac surgery. Almost all (548 of 619) had some suppression, so the comparison group without suppression was small (71). No conflicts of interest reported. The follow-up ENGAGES (Wildes 2019) from the same group found that EEG-guided anaesthesia reduced suppression time without reducing delirium.
Fritz et al. Anesth Analg 2016;122:234–242

Burst suppression during sedation and mortality (Watson 2008)

Post hoc analysis of a prospective cohort (Crit Care Med 2008;36:3171–3177) from the medical ICU at Vanderbilt: 125 adult ventilated patients without known neurological disease, APACHE II 27, 98% received sedation (lorazepam, midazolam, diazepam, propofol, fentanyl, morphine), titrated to the Ramsay scale. BIS (A1050, 2-channel frontal) was recorded for 10–20 minutes daily together with RASS and CAM-ICU. Burst suppression was defined as BSR above 0.

  • How common: burst suppression in 49 of 125 (39%), and in almost half of the comatose patients (46 of 93). 54% of the episodes occurred in the first 72 hours. None had burst suppression as a goal in the chart.
  • Mortality: 59% (29 of 49) died within 6 months versus 33% (25 of 76) without burst suppression. Adjusted for age, comorbidity, dementia, APACHE II, SOFA, coma and delirium: HR 2.04 (95% CI 1.12–3.70, p = 0.02). ICU mortality 37% versus 18% and hospital mortality 49% versus 24% were not significant individually. Length of stay on the ward after the ICU was longer (HR 1.84).
  • Drugs: the lorazepam dose in the preceding 24 hours was higher before burst suppression (27.8 versus 7.5 mg/day, p = 0.004). Propofol, morphine and fentanyl did not differ, and none of the agents differed when the dose was adjusted for weight. The groups were similar at inclusion.
  • The authors' main point: once the patient is unresponsive, no sedation scale can capture that the sedation is becoming deeper. Burst suppression is an EEG sign of deep sedation that can be read without EEG expertise, and which is probably less affected by encephalopathy than the index value itself. They propose that pEEG should be evaluated alongside sedation and delirium scales.
  • Sources of error they describe: EMG can give a falsely high index in intensive care patients, while hepatic and renal encephalopathy give slower, higher-amplitude EEG that resembles sedation and can give a falsely low index.
  • Caveats: post hoc, hypothesis-generating, 125 patients, only 10–20 minutes of EEG daily (burst suppression probably underestimated), yes/no classification without duration, and the sensor was applied just before recording, which may have stimulated the patient. Aspect provided monitors and partial salary for a research nurse; Ely and Watson report honoraria or support from Aspect, Hospira, Pfizer and Lilly. The authors themselves warn against firm conclusions.
Watson et al. Crit Care Med 2008;36:3171–3177

Time in burst suppression during coma and subsequent delirium (Andresen 2014)

Prospective observational cohort nested in BRAIN-ICU (Crit Care Med 2014;42:2244–2251), Vanderbilt, medical, surgical and cardiovascular intensive care. 124 ventilated patients had continuous BIS for up to 7 days; 69 were comatose (RASS −3 or deeper) and later awoke, and were included in the analysis. RASS twice daily, CAM-ICU twice daily when not comatose. Staff were blinded to burst suppression with a cover over the monitor. None received neuromuscular blocking agents.

  • Main finding: 42 of 69 (61%) developed delirium after coma. Most had burst suppression, but briefly: median 6.4 minutes (IQR 1–58). Adjusted for time with BIS below 40 and a component of APACHE II and cumulative doses of benzodiazepine, opioid and propofol during coma, more time in burst suppression gave higher odds of delirium (OR 4.16, 95% CI 1.27–13.62, p = 0.02) and later resolution of delirium (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.53–0.98, p = 0.04).
  • In practice: about 1 hour of burst suppression (75th percentile) versus 1 minute (25th percentile) gave four times higher odds of delirium and a 22% lower probability of it resolving during follow-up.
  • How time was calculated: BIS recorded the suppression ratio every minute (proportion of the last 63 seconds that was isoelectric); the mean was multiplied by time in coma. Minutes with low signal quality were excluded.
  • The authors' interpretation: sedation scales “lose their usefulness” when the patient is comatose, and pEEG can reveal the deepest sedation. The findings support lighter sedation strategies, but the authors themselves say that no firm conclusions can be drawn until larger studies have been done.
  • Caveats: small sample (69), monitoring did not always start at the onset of coma, maximum 7 days, eight patients would have dropped out with RASS −4 as the coma threshold, and no adjustment for hypoxia, hypotension, sleep or diagnosis. Watson reports research support from Aspect; several authors fees from Hospira and Orion.
Andresen et al. Crit Care Med 2014;42:2244–2251

Is burst suppression cause or marker? Causal analysis (Hogan 2020)

Retrospective observational study from Massachusetts General Hospital (Neurocrit Care 2020;33:565–574): 471 ventilated patients from seven intensive care units (2014–2017) with continuous EEG for at least 18 hours, after excluding anoxic encephalopathy after cardiac arrest and intentional burst suppression (raised ICP, status epilepticus, neuromuscular blockers). Median age 61 years, 27% died in hospital, half had unintentional burst suppression, and 63% had structural brain injury. The authors applied prediction models and causal inference (counterfactual “randomised” comparison, mediation, E-values) to the observational data.

  • Severity of illness drives both: going from mild to severe illness (10th versus 90th percentile) gave 39% (95% CI 8–66) more burst suppression burden and 35% (29–41) higher mortality.
  • Burst suppression contributes, but little: 100% versus 0% burst suppression burden gave 12% (7–17) higher mortality, and burst suppression mediated 10% (2–21) of the effect of critical illness on death.
  • Propofol matters less than assumed: high cumulative dose (1316 mg/kg) versus low (284 mg/kg) gave only 6% (0.8–12) more burst suppression, and propofol had no direct effect on mortality; the whole effect went via burst suppression.
  • The authors' interpretation: unintentional burst suppression is “primarily an effect of critical illness, not iatrogenic propofol use”, either because the illness itself produces the pattern (as in sepsis) or because it alters the brain's sensitivity so that ordinary doses produce burst suppression. Burst suppression thus becomes a marker of vulnerability. Avoiding overdosing will probably have little effect on mortality, but individual titration to the lowest necessary dose may still have a modest effect.
  • Versus Watson 2008: the authors consider that the difference in effect size may be due to differing methods and differing populations, and that intensive care versus operating theatre may be an effect modifier.
  • Caveats: selection (continuous EEG is obtained when brain dysfunction is suspected, hence 63% brain injury), coarse burden calculation in 8–12-hour windows, arbitrary distinction between mild and severe illness, in-hospital mortality only, cumulative dose without time course, binary clinical variables, no adjustment for unit, and seizure burden as an explicitly stated possible confounder. No conflicts of interest reported. Code is openly available.
Hogan et al. Neurocrit Care 2020;33:565–574

Burst suppression: good, bad or indifferent? Context decides (Jegarl 2026)

Narrative review from Weill Cornell (Anesth Analg 2026;142:1169–1179) that attempts to explain why observational studies find an association between burst suppression and postoperative delirium, while the large randomised trials do not.

  • The definitions diverge: ACNS 2021 distinguishes attenuation (≥ 10 µV, but below 50% of background) from suppression (below 10 µV), requires that “burst-suppression” makes up 50–99% of the recording, and that a burst lasts ≥ 0.5 s with ≥ 4 phases. The anaesthesia literature uses the term more loosely, calls suppression “isoelectric”, and measures with 1–4 frontal channels and a proprietary suppression ratio that underestimates burst suppression compared with visual interpretation. In one study (41 patients), visually determined suppression duration was associated with delirium (p = 0.039), but SR-based duration was not (p = 0.275).
  • The Ching model: a neurophysiological-metabolic model in which falling ATP opens ATP-gated potassium channels, hyperpolarises the neurons and produces burst suppression at about a 50% fall in ATP production, with suppression duration proportional to the ATP deficit. The model unifies deep anaesthesia, hypoxia/ischaemia, hypoglycaemia (below 50 mg/dl), the postictal state and hypothermia (CMRO2 falls about 6% per °C, isoelectric at 18–20 °C). Ketamine, dexmedetomidine and xenon do not produce burst suppression.
  • The trials: ENGAGES (n = 1232) and ENGAGES-Canada (n = 1140) gave lower MAC (0.69 versus 0.8 and 0.66 versus 0.8) and less burst suppression (7 versus 13 and 4 versus 12 minutes) in the EEG group, but no difference in delirium (26.0 versus 23.0% and 18.2 versus 18.1%). Balanced (n = 655, BIS 50 versus 35) gave 17 versus 29% delirium and longer suppression in the delirious (7 versus 2 minutes), but with greater dose separation and differing anaesthetic sensitivity between centres. 27 healthy volunteers with 3 hours of isoflurane at 1.3 MAC: 93% developed burst suppression, none developed delirium.
  • When burst suppression is used deliberately: in aneurysm surgery with temporary clipping the evidence for barbiturate-induced burst suppression is mixed, and animal studies suggest that protection does not require burst suppression. In hypothermic circulatory arrest, temperature below 12.5 °C and cooling for more than 50 minutes were the only reliable predictors of isoelectric EEG (only 60% were isoelectric at 18 °C), and each degree above the temperature at which the EEG became continuous again gave RR 1.56 for neurological injury.
  • Protective down-regulated state: the painted turtle survives months of anoxia with burst suppression-like EEG and 80 times higher GABA. The authors (via Schiff and Brown) propose a corresponding “protective down-regulated state” in humans after cardiac arrest and severe covid-19, where prolonged unconsciousness without structural injury may be protective. In 795 intubated covid patients, time to recovery of consciousness increased from 9 to 22 days with the degree of hypoxaemia.
  • Conclusion: the suppression phase looks the same regardless of cause, so incidence and duration alone cannot distinguish oversedation from ischaemia, hypothermia or hypoglycaemia. The burst content (intraburst spectrum, preburst activity, spatial distribution) may be more informative. In any case, burst suppression can be limited not only by the dose, but by raising the blood pressure, avoiding hypothermia and ensuring oxygenation.
  • Caveats: narrative review without a systematic search. Goldstein is a co-inventor on patents for alkylphenols against neuropathic pain.
Jegarl et al. Anesth Analg 2026;142:1169–1179

Burst suppression and blood pressure (Georgii 2022)

  • Design: randomised trial at a single clinic. Patients ≥60 years, at least 60 minutes of surgery under general anaesthesia, without neuropsychiatric disease. 104 were analysed, and 68 had a burst suppression ratio (BSR) above 0 (control 32, intervention 36).
  • Intervention: when BSR was above 0, MAP was first raised to the patient's baseline (lowest measured MAP before anaesthesia, mainly with catecholamines). If BSR was still positive, the anaesthetic concentration was reduced. The control group received standard anaesthesia with the EEG concealed.
  • Result: cumulative BSR was 433 versus 1385 (p = 0.002), duration 5.9 versus 10.1 minutes (p = 0.002) and maximum BSR 35 versus 50 (p = 0.027). The effect occurred at induction. During maintenance the difference was not significant.
  • MAP at the start of the BSR episodes was significantly lower than baseline in both groups. When MAP was raised to baseline (44 cases), BSR was reduced, and in 55% (24 of 44) it went to 0 without other measures. During maintenance this happened in 7 of 11.
  • Delirium: no one developed postoperative delirium on days 1–3. 28% developed delirium in the recovery room, with no difference between the groups.
  • The authors' caveats: the study does not prove a causal relationship between hypotension, hypoperfusion and burst suppression. Processed BSR may underestimate suppression, and 57% had a maximum state entropy of 80 or more. The sample is small.
Georgii et al. Front Syst Neurosci 2022;16:786816

After cardiac arrest

Burst suppression with theta in the bursts after cardiac arrest: a recovery marker? (Forgacs 2020)

Ann Neurol 2020;87:618–632 (Forgacs, Devinsky and Schiff). Three patients who awoke from coma after cardiac arrest after 17–37 days and became functionally independent, plus a prospective cohort of 53 cardiac arrest patients of whom 17 had burst suppression on the acute EEG.

  • The three: short time to ROSC (10–20 minutes), therapeutic hypothermia to 33 °C, minimal cortical injury on CT or MRI, preserved SSEP in two. Eye opening came 23–26 days and command following 37–67 days after all sedation had been stopped, far beyond the half-lives of the drugs. All had prominent burst suppression with a theta peak (about 4–7 Hz) in the bursts.
  • The cohort: of the 17 with burst suppression, 3 had a good outcome (CPC 2) and 14 a poor one (13 died). All three with a good outcome had a persistent theta peak in the bursts with increasing peak frequency over time. In the 14 with a poor outcome, the spectra were either flat or without lasting features (7), had only transient theta or falling frequency (5), or a shallow peak around 4 Hz (2).
  • The hypothesis: prolonged burst suppression may reflect impaired metabolism in post-hypoxic neurons that are still alive. The authors propose maintaining nutrition and fluids during the observation period and considering a time-limited trial of amantadine, and point out that withdrawal of treatment after cardiac arrest usually occurs within 5–7 days, so that the literature is marked by self-fulfilling prophecy.
  • Caveats: three case reports and a small cohort, analysis of burst content requires full EEG and spectral analysis, and no causal test. No conflicts of interest, NIH-funded.
Forgacs, Devinsky and Schiff. Ann Neurol 2020;87:618–632

Clinical example: young patient with prolonged burst suppression after cardiac arrest who woke up with good brain function (shared case)

Shared with the author of this app. Young patient with a short anoxic time after cardiac arrest. The EEG showed prolonged burst suppression without other criteria for a poor prognosis. The patient survived with good brain function.

  • What the sources say about morphology: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 (Perfusion tab) regard burst suppression with identical bursts after 24 hours as a sign of poor prognosis, but distinguish it from burst suppression where the bursts vary and come and go gradually. The term «burst suppression» is therefore not enough on its own; what the bursts look like matters.
  • Forgacs 2020 (above): the three who woke late and became independent had a short time to ROSC (10–20 minutes), little cortical injury on imaging and prominent burst suppression with theta in the bursts. Jegarl 2026 describes the hypothesis of a «protective down-regulated state».
  • Gruenbaum 2026: burst suppression may be tolerated in young, healthy people, and its meaning depends on the brain's metabolic reserve.
  • Interpretation based on the sources: the case fits the profile in Forgacs 2020: young patient, short anoxic time and no other signs of severe injury. Whether the bursts contained theta is not known. The case illustrates that burst suppression alone should not be read as a poor prognosis, and that prognostication should rest on several criteria over time.
  • Caveats: a single case. Sedation, timing of the EEG and burst morphology are not described here.
Shared case

Clinical examples

Clinical example: burst suppression during bleeding that resolves after transfusion (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from two screenshots of a frontal EEG monitor taken about 20 minutes apart. The screenshots are not reproduced in the app.

  • During the bleeding: PSI was first around 35–40 and then fell to 10. The suppression ratio (SR) was 44%, EMG 0% and artefacts 0%, and the spectral edge frequency (SEF) was not calculated. In the spectrogram, power lay mostly below about 10–12 Hz without a clear alpha band, followed by increasingly frequent suppression periods in both hemispheres. The raw EEG was almost flat and low-amplitude. Electrode impedances were acceptable.
  • After transfusion: the suppression periods became shorter and disappeared, and the EEG became continuous again. PSI was 44, SR 0% and SEF 15.8 Hz on the left and 16.4 Hz on the right. The raw EEG showed high-amplitude slow waves with faster activity superimposed, and the spectrogram showed power from slow-delta up to about 15 Hz.
  • Why it is instructive: the picture during the bleeding resembles deep anaesthesia: power shifting to lower frequencies, power loss and then burst suppression. Guay 2025 describes that reduced cerebral oxygen delivery (CDO₂) produces exactly this pattern, and that anaemic patients tolerate falls in blood flow less well. CDO₂ depends on blood flow, haemoglobin and saturation. Bleeding can lower both blood pressure and haemoglobin, and transfusion can improve both. Georgii 2022 found that burst suppression often resolved when MAP was raised to the patient’s baseline.
  • What we cannot tell from the screenshots: blood pressure, haemoglobin, temperature, the patient’s age and whether anaesthetic doses were changed. It therefore cannot be determined whether blood pressure, haemoglobin or both mattered most, or whether other factors contributed. Miller’s chapter 10 and Guay 2025 mention hypothermia, hypoglycaemia and hypnotic overdose as other causes of the same pattern.
  • Caveats: a single case without measurement of CBF, NIRS or Doppler. The point is not that the EEG «proves» hypoperfusion, but that unexpected suppression should prompt a search for the cause, including bleeding and anaemia, before the dose is simply reduced.
Own clinical example; Guay 2025, Georgii 2022, Miller’s ch. 10

Clinical example: burst suppression was the goal, but the EEG was flat because of herniation (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed, and it is described from verbal information.

  • The course: a neurosurgical patient was transferred from another hospital, with no complications expected. The goal was burst suppression. When the EEG was connected, it was completely flat, and this turned out to be due to herniation.
  • Why it is instructive: when the EEG is connected only after the patient is deeply sedated, there is no baseline to compare with. A flat EEG may then be due to the drugs, but also to a brain that has stopped functioning. Guay 2025 writes that patterns persisting without sedation should be investigated as primary neurological disease. Electrocerebral inactivity is defined as 2 µV or lower, whereas the suppression in burst suppression is below 10 µV. Alsallom 2022 describes two patients with herniation in whom increased low-frequency power and asymmetry in the spectrogram appeared roughly an hour before clinical deterioration.
  • What the sources say about starting: Rasulo 2023 recommends starting processed EEG as early as possible and monitoring continuously in patients who need deep sedation, and burst suppression should only be used to control raised intracranial pressure. Whether earlier EEG would have changed the course for this patient, one case cannot say.
  • What it may mean in practice (interpretation based on the sources): EEG from arrival, preferably before deep sedation, gives a baseline and makes it possible to see when the pattern changes. If burst suppression is the goal, you should know that the brain can produce bursts before titrating towards it. An unexpectedly flat EEG should not be read as the goal having been reached.
  • Caveats: one case without screenshots. The diagnosis, drugs and time course are not known. Frontal EEG sees only part of the cortex.
Shared clinical example Guay 2025, Rasulo 2023, Alsallom 2022

Quiz

Pick a topic, or take all of them. The order is fixed, so you can carry on where you left off.

Image quiz: spectrogram and raw EEG

Fifteen drawn images based on clinical examples and source descriptions (Purdon 2015, Akeju 2014, García 2021, Hight 2020, Cornelissen 2015/2018). Spectrogram: time along x (about 15 minutes), frequency 0–40 Hz along y, red = high power. None of the images are patient recordings.

What the studies show

  • BAG-RECALL (Avidan 2011, NEJM, three centres): 6041 high-risk patients under volatile-based general anaesthesia were randomised (5713 interviewed and analysed). A BIS protocol (audible alarm outside 40–60) was not better than a protocol based on end-tidal gas concentration (alarm outside 0.7–1.3 age-adjusted MAC). Definite awareness: 7 of 2861 (0.24%) in the BIS group versus 2 of 2852 (0.07%) in the gas group (difference 0.17 percentage points, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.38). Definite or possible: 19 (0.66%) versus 8 (0.28%). Median BIS was 41 and median end-tidal gas 0.9 MAC in both groups, and 30-day mortality was 1.96% versus 2.21%. Five of nine with definite awareness had neither BIS above 60 nor end-tidal gas below 0.7 MAC. The study compared two structured protocols and had no group without monitoring.
