  • Sandin 2000 (Lancet, two Swedish hospitals, observational study): 11,785 patients were interviewed three times (before leaving the recovery unit, after 1–3 days and after 7–14 days) with a modified Brice questionnaire. 18 had awareness with recall (0.15%) and one had awake paralysis before unconsciousness. The incidence was 0.18% when neuromuscular blocking agents were used (14 cases) and 0.10% without (4 cases). None of 325 with propofol TIVA had awareness. End-tidal gas was measured in 15 of the 18, and the authors considered that measurement of gas concentration would not have prevented the cases. Benzodiazepine premedication made no difference, but the study was not randomised. Of 14 with neuromuscular blockers, 11 had pain, anxiety or later neurotic symptoms, while none of the four without neuromuscular blockers had anxiety or later symptoms, and all symptoms resolved within three weeks. Only 11, and probably 9, of 18 would have been detected if the interview had been done only in recovery, and some patients forgot and then remembered again. The authors calculated that at least 861 patients must be monitored to avoid one case of suffering from awareness under neuromuscular blockade, assuming a monitor with 100% sensitivity.
  • Michigan Awareness Control Study (Mashour 2012, Anesthesiology): 18,836 unselected surgical patients at three hospitals were interviewed 28–30 days after surgery (one telephone call). Operating theatres were randomised every three months (even versus odd) to alerts if median BIS above 60 or age-adjusted MAC below 0.5. The study was stopped for futility. Definite awareness was 11 of 9376 (0.12%) in the MAC group and 8 of 9460 (0.08%) in the BIS group (p = 0.48). Because the BIS module failed in 36% of the BIS group (a software error), these were used as a post hoc “no intervention” group: definite or possible awareness was 0.08% with BIS, 0.20% with MAC alert and 0.38% without (4.7 times more without than with BIS, p = 0.001). This is a non-randomised, post hoc comparison, and the group without intervention had more women and more patients with lung disease. The authors found no reduction in anaesthetic dose, time to discharge from recovery or nausea. They mention as a possible cause that BIS produced more alerts (2.2 versus 1 per operation), but write that there were many false alarms.
  • RECITE-US (Saager 2019, J Clin Anesth): prospective, blinded cohort study at ten American hospitals (8 university, 2 community hospitals) in 255 adults ASA 1–3 for elective abdominal surgery with non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agents. Research staff measured train-of-four (TOF) with acceleromyography (TOF-Watch SX), while the clinicians were blinded and used routine practice. At extubation 64.7% (165 of 255) had a TOF ratio below 0.9, and 31.0% (79) below 0.6, despite neostigmine (the only reversal agent) and qualitative nerve stimulation. Independent risk factors were male sex (OR 2.60), higher BMI (OR 1.04 per unit), community hospital (OR 3.15, only 2 hospitals) and shorter time between intubation and extubation (OR 0.67 per hour). Patients with residual blockade more often had unplanned interventions (8.5% versus 1.1%), but the study was not powered for clinical outcomes. The study was funded by Merck (which makes sugammadex), which also participated in design, analysis and writing, and several authors have ties to the company. The study was done before sugammadex became available in the USA.
  • ENGAGES (1232 patients ≥60 years): EEG-guided dosing gave about 14% lower anaesthetic dose and shorter EEG suppression (13 to 7 minutes), but no change in postoperative delirium. ENGAGES-Canada (cardiac surgery, 1140 patients) gave the same result. An independent discussion in BJA (Ackland and Pryor 2019) states that 26.0% (157 of 604) in the EEG group and 23.0% (140 of 609) in usual care had delirium (difference 3.0 percentage points, 95% CI −2.0 to 8.0, p = 0.22). Median cumulative time with EEG suppression was 7 versus 13 minutes, but both groups were above the threshold of about 4.5 minutes that the study's own authors had earlier linked to clearly higher delirium incidence (about 45% versus 25%). The discussion therefore considers that the probability of showing an effect was small, and that the result does not rule out that a protocol giving a larger reduction might help. The difference in volatile agent was small: median 0.69 versus 0.80 MAC, a difference of 0.11 MAC (95 % CI 0.10–0.13), and opioid doses were similar (Wildes 2019). Reflection from the author of the app: ENGAGES shows that an EEG protocol that changes practice little does not change outcome. It does not show that guiding anaesthesia by EEG is ineffective. Balanced, with a larger difference in depth (BIS 50 versus 35), found less delirium (see the Burst suppression tab). The screening has also been criticised: delirium was assessed once daily after 1 pm from postoperative day 1, with the CAM and chart review (Wildes 2019). Koch, Radtke and Spies 2019 write that delirium can occur soon after emergence and fluctuates through the day, and recommend screening already in the recovery room and once per shift. They point out that the CAM has low sensitivity for hypoactive delirium (0.43), and that chart review detects only about 7 % of cases. Delirium on the day of surgery was reported as an exploratory outcome (19.2 versus 21.9 %), but the method is not described in the main article. Quiet delirium: after surgery, hypoactive delirium is the most common form. A review gives 71 % hypoactive, 29 % mixed and rarely hyperactive, citing Marcantonio 2002 (Robinson and Eiseman 2008). Could ENGAGES capture these? The main article does not report motor subtype, and RASS was used only to exclude deeply sedated patients from assessment, not to distinguish subtypes. With one afternoon CAM assessment, which has low sensitivity for hypoactive delirium, and chart review as a supplement, quiet cases may have been missed (interpretation based on the sources). If this happens equally in both groups, it makes a difference harder to detect. This is disputed. The authors' reply (Wildes and Avidan 2019): the trial's own authors write that the CAM has excellent psychometric properties for both hypoactive and hyperactive delirium, that delirium was assessed on the day of surgery (19.2 versus 21.9 %, p = 0.26), and that 42 % of delirium episodes were detected by chart review, not 7 %. If screening were insensitive, incidence should have been lower than in similar trials, but it was higher than in CODA, SuDoCo and PODCAST. Three sensitivity analyses removing the patients with the most suppression, the longest time with BIS below 40 or the highest volatile concentrations did not change the result. They interpret suppression under volatile anaesthesia as a sign of pre-existing brain vulnerability rather than a cause of delirium, comparing it with ST depression on an exercise ECG. Clinicians in ENGAGES were trained to read the raw EEG and not to rely on BIS. The reply is written by the trial's authors, and they themselves point out that SuDoCo, led by Radtke and Spies, was partly funded by the BIS manufacturer. See Discrepancies. 30-day mortality was 4 of 614 (0.7%) versus 19 of 618 (3.1%), a post hoc observation described as difficult to explain. Unwanted movement during the procedure was 22.3% versus 15.4%. The study was single-centre and the anaesthetists could not be blinded, and the researchers gave real-time feedback on the EEG, which may have influenced treatment. The article is an assessment by two BJA editors and not a new study.
  • CODA: BIS-guided anaesthesia was associated with a lower incidence of delirium. The results across the studies are therefore not unambiguous, and a commentary in JAMA interprets this as meaning that EEG guidance with suppression time as the only target is unlikely to prevent delirium.
  • BALANCED (6644 patients ≥60 years at increased risk): 1-year mortality was 6.5% with a BIS target of 50 and 7.2% with a BIS target of 35, without significant difference (HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.73–1.07). In the delirium substudy the incidence was 19% with BIS 50 and 28% with BIS 35 (OR 0.58), and cognitive impairment after one year was 9% versus 20%. Chapter 27 discusses only the mortality result.
  • Georgii 2022: raising MAP to baseline eliminated burst suppression in 55% of cases, and EEG-guided treatment reduced cumulative BSR. Delirium was not affected, and during maintenance the difference was not significant.
  • Xu 2020: MAP from baseline to 10% above gave less delirium on day 1 (4% versus 22%) and higher rSO₂ in 150 older patients undergoing hip arthroplasty. No difference on days 2 and 3.
  • Monk 2005 (observational): cumulative time with BIS below 45 was an independent predictor of mortality in chapter 27 (RR 1.244 per hour). The chapter says it is not established whether this is a causal relationship. BALANCED randomised to deep and light anaesthesia and found no difference in mortality. From Miller's ch. 27

Further findings from the chapters

  • Chapter 36 cites a Cochrane review (Lewis 2019, 52 studies, 41,331 participants). According to the chapter, brain monitoring more than halved the incidence of awareness with recall compared with clinical monitoring (OR 0.36), but there was no significant difference versus end-tidal gas monitoring. The certainty of the evidence was low. The Cochrane review (Lewis et al. 2019, search to March 2019). Versus clinical monitoring: Peto OR 0.36 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.60; 27 studies, 9765 participants), corresponding to 9 versus 3 per 1000, but only 5 of the 27 studies had events, and two large studies dominated (Myles 2004: 2 events with BIS versus 11 with clinical monitoring, Zhang 2011: 4 versus 15). The certainty was graded as low because the anaesthetists could not be blinded and because the result is imprecise. Sensitivity analyses weaken the finding: with a random-effects model the RR was 0.32 (CI 0.10 to 1.01), and when only studies with low risk of selection bias were included the OR was 0.60 (CI 0.29 to 1.23). Versus end-tidal gas (5 studies, 26,572 participants): OR 1.13 (CI 0.56 to 2.26), with 17 versus 15 events (about 1 per 1000 in both groups). In the subgroup analysis the effect was clear for propofol (OR 0.24, CI 0.10 to 0.60; 10 studies), while isoflurane showed no difference (OR 0.58, CI 0.26 to 1.28) and no studies with desflurane or sevoflurane had events. Time to eye opening was 1.78 minutes shorter (22 studies, I² 83%), to orientation 3.18 minutes (6 studies) and to discharge from recovery 6.86 minutes (13 studies, I² 79%). When only studies with low risk of bias were counted, the difference in recovery time was 1.62 minutes (CI −5.96 to 2.72), and the funnel plot may suggest publication bias. All BIS targets were between 40 and 60. Five studies had support from, or authors with honoraria from, BIS manufacturers (Ahmad 2003, Bruhn 2005, Gan 1997, Myles 2004, Wong 2002). The authors of the review declare no conflicts of interest. From Miller's
  • Chapter 21 cites the Cochrane review by Messina (2016) on agents and awareness. See the Agents tab. From Miller's

Original references in Miller's

The originals each claim is based on, according to the chapters' reference lists.

Discrepancies and disagreements between sources

  • Reference that does not fit (ch. 8): The chapter describes a randomised study said to have shown more PTSD after propofol than sevoflurane in trauma patients, citing reference 292. That reference in the list concerns heart rate variability and anxiety in healthy adults (Mujica-Parodi 2009). It does not appear to support the claim.
  • Memory without consciousness? Chapter 8 (Mashour and Pryor), the section on amnesia: “the “amnesia” of general anesthesia is not a primary failure of memory, but rather a failure of consciousness. It simply reflects that a conscious experience cannot be reconstructed by memory processes when it never existed in the first place. [...] Awareness is necessary for the establishment of memory under anesthesia, but it is not sufficient.” Figure legend 36.1 in chapter 36 (Sleigh, Gaskell and Hight): “Occasionally AWR may present absent of conscious experience at the time.” Neither of the two sentences has a reference in the chapters. Chapter 8 at the same time defines dreaming as disconnected consciousness (ref. 8, Sanders 2012), and Leslie 2009 (ref. 32 in ch. 36) shows that dreams reported after anaesthesia probably occur during emergence. Ref. 1 in ch. 36 (Mashour 2013, editorial on frontal-to-parietal feedback) is not about awareness. Mashour and Avidan 2015 (ref. 7 in ch. 8) write that the Brice questions can “elicit false reports or memories” and that true and false reports cannot be reliably distinguished. The most plausible reading is therefore that chapter 36 refers to reports (false memories, dreams, emergence experiences, reconstruction), not to genuine episodic memory without experience. Read this way it is a difference in definition, not a contradiction. Neither chapter says so explicitly.
  • Order of magnitude: Chapter 36 estimates that IFT response is about two orders of magnitude more frequent than AWR, citing Sanders 2017 and Lennertz 2023. Sanders 2017 (260 patients, six centres) found a response in 4.6% (12 of 260) after intubation, 5 of the 12 reported pain, and none of 253 asked had explicit recall; the authors call it “up to 10 times lower than expected”. Lennertz 2023 found 11%. Against AWR of 0.1–0.2% this gives about 25–45 times (Sanders) and 55–110 times (Lennertz), that is one to two orders of magnitude. Linassi 2018 gives 34.8% versus 6.2%, from different populations and with low methodological quality. The figures are not directly comparable.
  • Age and alpha: Purdon 2015 (BJA) reports that alpha power falls more than slow power in older patients. Chapter 36 says the findings on relative alpha power and age are inconsistent. Both are reproduced in the app.
  • Purdon 2015, alpha in older patients: the abstract and results say that the EEG form looked similar regardless of age, with distinct alpha and slow activity. The legends to figures 3 and 4 say that the group spectrogram and coherogram for older patients show a “visible absence” of alpha power and alpha coherence. Guay 2025 writes that alpha may be impossible to see in some older patients, and case report 2 (89 years) had no visible alpha. That agrees with the figure legends and not entirely with the abstract. The difference may be because the group median for 8–12 patients shows less alpha than individual patients.
  • Purdon 2015, internal figures: the difference between young and old in alpha power (8.68 dB) minus the difference in slow power (4.91 dB) gives 3.77 dB for propofol, but the alpha-to-slow ratio is given as 2.81 dB lower. For sevoflurane 8.56 − 5.45 = 3.11 dB, while the ratio is given as 2.07 dB. The difference may be because peak and mean within the bands are measured differently, but this is not explained. The article also states that this corresponds to a reduction in relative alpha power of about 90% (propofol) and 61% (sevoflurane). Calculated, 2.81 dB gives a reduction in power of about 48% and 2.07 dB about 38%. The text also gives a decrease in propofol rate of about 0.39 mg/kg/min with age without a clear unit, so it has not been used.
  • Propofol and EEG (ch. 21): Chapter 21 describes an initial increase in alpha followed by a shift to gamma and theta. Purdon 2015 and chapter 36 describe alpha-delta during maintenance. The app follows alpha-delta.
  • Burst suppression concentration: Chapter 21 gives over 8 µg/ml (blood, rapid infusion), while chapter 36 gives a median of about 5 µg/ml. The measurement methods may differ.
  • Neural inertia: Chapter 21 says that the wake-up concentration equals the concentration for loss of response when equilibration is allowed. Chapter 36 describes neural inertia as a difference between induction and emergence, and refers to debate about pharmacokinetics.
  • CMRO₂ at isoelectric EEG: about 50% of baseline in chapter 21 (thiopental), about 60% in chapter 10 (burst suppression). Different measures and agents.
  • Flumazenil (ch. 21): The chapter first says that flumazenil reliably reverses amnesia, and later that it reverses hypnotic and respiratory effects more than amnestic ones.
  • Propofol dose in older patients: chapter 21 gives about half the dose in 80-year-olds, chapter 16 a reduction of 65%. Purdon 2015 writes that doses in older patients may be up to half of doses in younger patients (citing Martin 2003), and that the propofol rate in their cohort decreased slightly with age.
  • Depth and outcome: chapter 27 refers to an observational study (Monk 2005) in which long time with low BIS was associated with mortality. BALANCED found no difference in mortality, but fewer cases of delirium with light anaesthesia in the substudy. Different outcomes and designs give different answers.
  • Lower limit of autoregulation (Guay 2025 vs ch. 10): Guay 2025 writes that the lower MAP limit of autoregulation ranges from 40 to 90 mmHg in adults, citing Vu et al. 2024, without stating which population the range applies to. Chapter 10 states that mean LLA ranged from 57 to 91 mmHg in seven studies of awake, healthy people, and considers that the limit in most is not below 70 mmHg. Both stress large variation between individuals.
  • Xu 2020, discrepancies in the article: the abstract gives p = 0.031 for the difference between groups on day 1, while the text gives p = 0.007 for D versus H. The sample size calculation says 60 per group, while 50 per group were analysed. These discrepancies do not change the main finding, but should be mentioned when used.
  • Kalmar 2010, internal discrepancies: the abstract states that CPP fell from 77 to 71 mmHg (p = 0.07), while table 1 shows 71 before and 70 during Trendelenburg. The abstract states that the gradient between arterial and end-tidal CO₂ rose to 1.41 kPa, while the text gives 1.46 kPa. The discussion recommends PE′CO₂ of 4.0–4.66 kPa for PaCO₂ 4.66–6.00, while the conclusion gives 3.40–4.66 kPa.
  • CPP formula: Lobo and Miller's use CPP = MAP − ICP. Kalmar uses MAP minus CVP in Trendelenburg, because CVP is then assumed to be at least as high as ICP. The zero point is the external auditory meatus in Kalmar and the circle of Willis in Miller's ch. 30.
  • Gaskell 2017, strength of the conclusion: the abstract and conclusion say that alpha-delta “is not sufficient” for unconsciousness. The discussion says the findings show that the pattern “is not causally linked” to unconsciousness. These are two different claims. The latter is stronger than three alpha-delta responders and six responders in total can support, and the editorial (Mashour and Avidan 2017) points out that the finding must be replicated and that the timing (after laryngoscopy) may matter.
  • Lennertz 2023, figures: the abstract gives p = 0.041 for continuous anaesthesia, while the results section gives p = 0.043. The text gives 4.6% for older adults (Sanders 2017), while the introduction says “at least 5%”. “100 times higher than explicit recall” holds for 11% versus 0.1–0.2% (55–110 times), but in the study's own assessment possible recall was 1.5% and definite 0.3%, that is about 7 and 37 times lower than 11%. The introduction also reports a subgroup analysis (13% under 40 years versus 1.1% over 40 years) as “unpublished”.
  • Mashour and Avidan 2017, BIS and awareness: the editorial considers that processed indices probably still reduce awareness with recall, while BAG-RECALL found no better effect of BIS than of end-tidal gas. The comparisons concern different questions: BAG-RECALL tested two structured protocols against each other and had no group without monitoring. According to the BAG-RECALL article, B-Aware found a reduction of 0.74 percentage points versus standard practice, while B-Unaware found 0 percentage points (CI −0.56 to 0.57) for BIS versus end-tidal gas. The editorial is an assessment, not a data study.
  • Hight 2017, figures: the text states that 53 of 149 patients with a laryngeal mask (36%) and 82 of 114 with an endotracheal tube (28%) reported high pain. Table 2 shows only 53 patients in the high-pain group in total (25 men and 28 women), and 82 of 114 is not 28%. In addition, 149 and 114 are not the same figures as 154 and 119 for the airway devices (eight patients could not report pain). The text also says that the odds of high-MAC activation increase equally per decibel of alpha, but alpha was removed from the final model.
  • Klein 2018, figures: the abstract gives 977 patients in the four studies, but the figures in the text (48 + 600 + 136 + 200) add up to 984. Further, 16.6% and 55.7% are given for air embolism in Ganslandt and Feigl, while 4/24 and 29/52 give 16.7% and 55.8%. Ammirati had 10 PFO patients, but only 4 of them (those operated on sitting) are included in the 82, which makes “all PFO patients” in the abstract not entirely precise.
  • Murphy 2010, association: nausea and vomiting were analysed by CDE, but all patients with CDE were in the “beach chair” position. Logistic regression retained only CDE as predictor, but position and CDE overlap so much that they cannot be separated.
  • Pilge 2014, unit: the abstract and text give propofol CP50BS in “mg/ml” (4.85), but the comparison with Smith 1994 (15.2) implies micrograms/ml. In Miller's it is given as µg/ml. In addition, the figure of about 80% reduction with fentanyl comes from Smith 1994, not Pilge.
  • Lewis 2019 (Cochrane), wording: the plain-language summary says that BIS gave “three per 1000 fewer” cases of awareness versus nine per 1000 with clinical monitoring. The figures in the table are 3 per 1000 in the BIS group versus 9 in the control group, that is six fewer per 1000. The text gives 29 studies that measured awareness, 27 in the analysis and only 5 with events. Recovery time after end-tidal gas is given as “3 minutes lower” (95 and 98 minutes in the text), but the table shows a confidence interval of 2 to 2 minutes, which makes no sense.
  • Ackland and Pryor 2019, wording: the commentary says that the EEG group in ENGAGES had an exposure to suppression that exceeded the threshold previously found “associated with reduced incidence of delirium”. This must mean increased incidence, since the authors otherwise describe that suppression over about 4.5 minutes gave higher delirium incidence.
  • Akeju 2015, figures: the abstract states that EEG power increased until about 6 years and then fell to a plateau at about 21 years, while the results give a peak at 5–8 years and a plateau at 18–21 years.
  • Proekt and Kelz 2021, figure legend: the legend to figure 4 says the data are “identical to those in figure 4”, but it must mean figure 3. There is also a difference between “MBK” in the author list and “MPK” in the author contributions.
  • Warnaby 2017, figures: the text says that the mean concentration for saturation for sevoflurane is about 0.7 MAC, while table 1 gives 0.6 ± 0.3 MAC. The discussion says that about one third of patients have abrupt emergence, but table 3 shows 20–26% of all datasets (about 30–37% of those with successful fitting). The results text gives the frequency of confusion and CAM-ICU positivity in an order that is easily confused (14/110 versus 17/65).
  • Practice advisory 2019, frequency of eye checks: the advisory says that the literature is insufficient to specify a frequency. Miller's chapter 30 gives about every 20 minutes, which does not come from the advisory.
  • Johnson 2010, wording: the results say that the mean “probability of response” at emergence was 53% with the effect-site model and 9% with the end-tidal model. This must refer to the probability of unresponsiveness (OAA/S = 1), since the text otherwise says that the end-tidal model predicted emergence too early.
  • Saager 2019, incomplete sentence and table: the results section says that residual blockade occurred “most often” in an unnamed hospital and was present in 83% of patients (the sentence is missing a word). 83% holds if community hospitals and community teaching hospitals are combined (44 of 53). The discussion says that shorter time from neuromuscular blocker to extubation was associated with residual blockade in multivariate analysis, while table 3 and the results show that it was not significant (p = 0.088). The Apfel row in table 1 has figures that appear to be in the wrong column.
  • Sandin 2000, numbers: the abstract says that “no more than 11” of 18 would have been detected if the interview had been done only in recovery, while the discussion says “no more than 11 and probably only nine”. The first is an upper limit, the second an estimate.
  • Mashour 2012, typographical error: the results section says that 50% of those with awareness in the BIS group “had no 5-minute period with BIS below 60” and that 50% had at least one with median BIS above 60. The first part is probably a typographical error for “above 60”, since the two statements otherwise make no sense together. Agreement between the assessments of the cases was only “fair” (kappa 0.25).
  • Fu 2021, figures: the abstract gives CI −0.57 to −0.015 for music and opioid requirement and p = 0.039, while the text gives −0.57 to −0.02 and p = 0.04 (rounding). The percentage for implicit memory is 41% (7 of 17 studies with priming), 33% (2 of 6 with behavioural change) and 39% (9 of 23 in total), and the unit is studies, not patients or cohorts. It is therefore not directly comparable with Linassi's 36% (cohorts).
  • Linassi 2021, figures: the abstract gives CI 0.13–0.93 for benzodiazepine premedication under general anaesthesia, while the text gives 0.13–0.92. Table 1 (all regimens) shows OR 0.47 (0.18–1.20, p = 0.16) for premedication. The figure of 0.35 applies only to general anaesthesia.
  • Pryor 2010, number of participants: the abstract says that 61 volunteers were randomised, while the methods section says that 67 were randomised and 61 analysed (six excluded).
  • Bulach 2005, p-values and retrograde time: the text says there was no difference in retrograde recognition (P over 0.99 up to the dose), while table 2 shows p = 0.10 for the poster at the time of the dose itself and p = 0.55 for the poster one minute before. The event “mask preoxygenation” is counted as present time by the authors, but could be interpreted as possible immediate retrograde amnesia.
  • MAC per decade, Morgan and Mikhail 2022 internally and versus Miller's: Morgan ch. 8 states that MAC falls 6% per decade regardless of agent, while ch. 43 in the same book gives 4% per decade over 40 years. Miller's ch. 61 gives 6% per decade after 30 years citing Mapleson 1996. The Mapleson meta-analysis is the original source for 6%; 4% has no reference in Morgan ch. 43.
  • Burst suppression in older patients: recommendation versus evidence: Miller's ch. 61 suggests pEEG and lower doses to avoid burst suppression, based on Fritz 2016 and 2018 (observational studies), while the chapter itself calls the RCT evidence for pEEG-guided anaesthesia an “equipoise”. Hogan 2020 and Jegarl 2026 consider burst suppression primarily a marker of vulnerability. Obert 2024 shows that slow induction can eliminate burst suppression in older patients, but did not measure delirium. The recommendation in ch. 61 is therefore a suggestion with a low level of evidence, not a documented effect on outcome.
  • The Marsh model's ke0 in Sepúlveda 2021: table 3 gives “Marsh (ke0 1.6)”, while the methods section in the same article and Sepúlveda 2020 give ke0 1.21 min⁻¹ for modified Marsh; 1.6 minutes is the time to peak effect, not ke0. Probably a mix-up in the table. The figures (2.7 versus 4.6 µg/ml) are the same as for modified Marsh in Sepúlveda 2020.
  • “Regardless of model” versus Eleveld: Sepúlveda 2010 concludes that Ce at loss of consciousness after a bolus cannot be used as a maintenance target “regardless of TCI model” (tested: Schnider and two Marsh variants). Sepúlveda 2021 finds that the Eleveld model gives the same Ce with fast and slow induction (3.1 versus 3.2 µg/ml), so the conclusion from 2010 does not automatically apply to Eleveld. Sepúlveda 2026 in turn finds that Eleveld fails after a burst suppression perturbation, so the criticism has shifted from induction speed to non-linearity.
  • Sepúlveda 2020 versus Obert 2020, number of patients: the Anaesthesia article gives 16 included (8 + 8) in the period August–December 2016, while the Sci Rep article from the same study (NCT03140982) gives 18 randomised (9 + 9), of whom three in the fast group were excluded for burst suppression. Which patients are included in which analysis is not explained in either article. The times to loss of response (10.5 versus 1.4 minutes; 834 versus 90 seconds) and the effect-site concentrations (2.6 versus 4.6 µg/ml) are the same in both.
  • Sepúlveda 2026, figures in abstract versus results section: the abstract gives observed versus predicted BIS 64.5 versus 61.3 before and 38.2 versus 55.5 after the perturbation, while the results section gives 28.9 versus 38.8 from the post-PERT phase and sets up 51.8 versus 38.1 as both “predicted” and “observed” pre- versus post-PERT, which is obviously an error in the text. The direction (observed below predicted after the perturbation) is the same throughout, but the size of the difference is uncertain from the article.
  • Two GABAergic hypnotics: additive or synergistic? Miller's ch. 16 (reproduced in the Agents tab) summarises that combinations of two GABAergic hypnotics are largely additive. Hendrickx 2008 found that propofol + sevoflurane and propofol + thiopental are additive (one study synergistic), while propofol + midazolam is synergistic in all studies, probably because they bind different sites on the GABAA receptor. Miller's summary thus holds for hypnotic + volatile agent, but not for benzodiazepine + propofol. Both are reproduced in the app.
  • Dexmedetomidine and the α2A receptor (ch. 21 vs ch. 8): chapter 21 writes that α2A receptors are mainly peripheral, and α2B and α2C are in the brain and spinal cord. The same chapter links dorsal horn analgesia to α2C and α2A. Chapter 8 cites that selective removal of α2A receptors from the locus coeruleus in rodents prevents the hypnotic effect of dexmedetomidine, i.e. that α2A matters centrally. Mizobe 1996 found that α2A in the locus coeruleus mediates the hypnotic effect in rats, and writes that α2A and α2C predominate in the central nervous system, while α2B is sparsely represented. Giovannitti 2015 writes the same: α2A and α2C are mainly central and α2B is in the vessel wall. The description in chapter 21 of α2A as mainly peripheral is thus not supported by the other sources here. The app reports all of them.
  • Clonidine and anaesthetic requirements (Giovannitti 2015 vs Hendrickx 2008): Giovannitti writes that clonidine reduces anaesthetic requirements by 40–60%, citing a paediatric anaesthesia textbook. The studies reviewed by Hendrickx 2008 found that clonidine reduced isoflurane MAC by about 30% and sevoflurane MAC by 17–34%, with a ceiling.
  • Selectivity for α2 vs α1 (Giovannitti 2015 internally and vs ch. 21): Giovannitti gives 200:1 for clonidine in the clonidine section and 220:1 in the dexmedetomidine section, and 1620:1 for dexmedetomidine. Chapter 21 gives 220:1 and 1600:1.
  • Blood pressure rise with a rapid dexmedetomidine bolus (Giovannitti 2015 and Mizobe 1996): Giovannitti gives two explanations in the same section: loss of selectivity with activation of peripheral α1 receptors, and transient activation of peripheral α2B receptors. Mizobe 1996 points to α2B.
  • MAC after spinal transection (Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 vs Jinks 2010): Morgan and Mikhail write that MAC is unchanged after spinal cord transection in rats, without citing a source. Jinks 2010 cites Rampil 1994 finding no change after hypothermic transection, but chronic transection without spinal shock reducing MAC by about 50% (Jinks 2005). Both support immobility occurring mainly in the spinal cord, but the brainstem influences how high MAC is.
  • Jinks 2010, obex transection: the results report that MAC fell to 40% of the intact value (a 60% fall, as in the abstract), while the discussion writes that MAC fell to 50% of control.
  • Frequency band boundaries: Gruenbaum and García (Lobo and Lamperti ch. 5) give alpha 8–12 Hz (extended alpha 7–17 Hz), beta 15–30 Hz and gamma above 30 Hz, in the text 30–80 Hz. The simulator in the app uses alpha 8–13 Hz and beta 13–25 Hz, and García 2021 uses 12–25 Hz for beta arousal. The sources thus use different boundaries, and a pattern can fall into different bands depending on the definition used.
  • Propofol concentration preventing movement at incision (Aitkenhead ch. 3 vs Miller's ch. 21 and 36): Aitkenhead states that the TCI target concentration that prevented movement at incision in half of female patients was 6 µg/ml with oxygen and 4.5 µg/ml with 67% nitrous oxide. Miller's gives 15–16 µg/ml for propofol alone (Smith 1994). The difference may reflect different patient groups and the fact that the TCI target is a predicted, not measured, concentration (Aitkenhead himself writes that the actual concentration may differ by more than 50%), but Aitkenhead gives no source for the figure. Aitkenhead is also an older textbook (5th ed. 2007), whereas Miller's 10th ed. is much newer, so where the two disagree, Miller's and newer studies should carry more weight.
  • MAC of sevoflurane: Aitkenhead (ch. 2) gives 1.7–2% in adults and 1.48% in the elderly, Morgan and Mikhail about 2.0% for 30–55-year-olds, and Pilge 2014 uses 2.05%.
  • Delirium and EEG slowing (Guay 2025 vs Eskioglou 2021): Guay 2025 links hypoactive delirium to slow-delta and writes that power shifts towards higher frequencies as the delirium resolves. In Eskioglou 2021 (91 ventilated patients), the dominant frequency did not distinguish delirious from non-delirious patients, because theta was common in about 70% of both groups. Burst suppression, rhythmic or periodic patterns and seizures did distinguish them. The difference may reflect different populations, different sedation and the fact that Eskioglou measured when delirium was already present.
  • Sleep monitoring in the ICU (PADIS 2018 vs Guay 2025 and Rasulo 2023): PADIS 2018 advises against routine physiological sleep monitoring, including with BIS and EEG, but the recommendation is conditional and based on very low quality of evidence. Guay 2025 writes that natural sleep is readily recognisable on the frontal EEG, and Rasulo 2023 that the spectrogram and raw EEG can distinguish sleep stages. PADIS predates the other two, and they answer different questions: routine monitoring for everyone vs interpreting an EEG that is already connected.
  • EEG during propofol movements (Reddy 1993 and Walder 2002 versus Jeon 2007): Reddy found no seizure activity with propofol, and most EEGs after the episodes in Walder's review were normal. Jeon described polyspike-and-wave complexes coinciding with the jerks. Voss 2015 points out that a normal scalp EEG does not exclude epileptic activity deeper in the brain.
  • Neuromuscular blockade to see the EEG behind myoclonus (Newey 2017 versus ERC-ESICM 2025): Newey found that cisatracurium improved the EEG in 9 of 12 and revealed seizures. The guideline advises against routine use in comatose post-arrest patients, because it interferes with the clinical examination. Newey was retrospective, and all patients died after withdrawal of treatment.
  • Does the stress response go away? (reflection from the author of the app versus Burton 2004): the reflection in the app was that nociception gives a stress reaction that does not go away. The sources show that the stress response lasts days, is proportional to the size of the operation and then subsides. Part of it is driven by inflammation that analgesia does not stop.
  • LTP in the spinal cord (Latremoliere and Woolf 2009 versus other literature): some authors describe central sensitisation as LTP in the dorsal horn. Latremoliere and Woolf advise against using the term LTP for the spinal cord, because the mechanisms are not the same as in the hippocampus.
  • Anxiety and propofol requirement (Maranets and Kain 1999 and Kil 2012 versus Morley 2008 and Kim and Choi 2013): the first two found that anxiety increased the propofol requirement, the last two found no relationship with dose. Kim and Choi did, however, find higher entropy at loss of consciousness in anxious patients. The studies used different measures of anxiety and different endpoints.
  • Music and opioid requirement (Fu 2020): overall, music gave somewhat fewer opioids, but the three fully blinded studies showed no effect. The effect may therefore partly be due to lack of blinding.
  • Phenobarbital in alcohol withdrawal (Umar 2023, abstract versus results): the abstract calls the reduction in intubation significant, but the results give RR 0.52 with 95% CI 0.25–1.08. The interval includes 1, so the difference is not significant. The app uses the figures from the results.
  • Pallor after dexmedetomidine in children (clinical experience versus the literature): pallor has been observed in clinical practice, but was not found described as a side effect in peer-reviewed sources. Potts 2010 shows that dexmedetomidine can constrict peripheral vessels at higher concentrations, but whether this gives visible pallor has not been studied.
  • Are induction and emergence different processes? (Kelz 2019 versus Li 2024): Kelz 2019 points out that orexin and noradrenaline affect emergence more than induction, and uses this as an argument that emergence is not induction in reverse. Li 2024 found that the same glutamatergic PPT neurones affected both induction and emergence under sevoflurane, and interprets this as shared circuits. The editorial accompanying Li 2024 (McKinstry-Wu and Kelz) points out that PPT activity did not recover before emergence, and that the PPT therefore does not control the process alone. Both may be true: some circuits may be shared, others specific to emergence (interpretation based on the sources).
  • Did ENGAGES capture quiet delirium? (Koch, Radtke and Spies 2019 versus Wildes and Avidan 2019): Koch and co-authors write that the CAM has low sensitivity for hypoactive delirium (0.43), that chart review detects only about 7 % of cases, and that screening started too late. The trial's authors reply that the CAM has excellent properties for both subtypes, that 42 % of episodes in ENGAGES were detected by chart review, and that delirium was also assessed on the day of surgery. Both sides have their own trials to defend.
  • Depth of therapeutic burst suppression: SR below 5 % (Rasulo 2023) versus pauses of about 10 seconds (2022 review) and suppression probability 0.8 (An 2018): the Rasulo panel recommends SR below 5 % without justification, whereas the 2022 review describes expert practice with pauses of about 10 seconds, which corresponds to an SR of about 75–90 % (calculated from the figures in the sources). Johnson 2016 found that the content of the bursts, not the pauses or SR, separated successful from failed weaning. See the card in the Burst suppression tab.
  • The limit for an electrographic seizure: 2.5 Hz or more, or more than 25 per 10 seconds? (Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4 vs Guay 2025): Lobo and Lamperti count epileptiform discharges at 2.5 Hz or more for at least 10 seconds as an electrographic seizure. Guay 2025 writes «greater than 2.5 Hz, i.e., more than 25 discharges in a 10-s window» and places 11–25 per 10 seconds in the ictal–interictal continuum. Exactly 25 per 10 seconds therefore falls into different categories. The ACNS 2021 terminology, which is the formal definition, uses the same limit as Guay: averaging more than 2.5 Hz for at least 10 seconds (more than 25 discharges in 10 seconds). The simulator in the Intensive care tab follows ACNS and Guay.
  • How well does ketamine work in refractory status? (Espinosa 2023 vs Gaspard 2013): Espinosa 2023 found complete seizure control in 63 % of 19 case reports, whereas Gaspard 2013 could attribute only a likely response in 12 % and a possible response in 20 % of 60 episodes to ketamine. Interpretation based on the sources: case reports are more often published when treatment works, and in Gaspard all patients received other drugs at the same time, so the numbers do not measure the same thing.
  • Frontal alpha–delta and unconsciousness (Purdon 2015 vs Montupil 2023): the app describes alpha–delta as typical of unconsciousness during maintenance with propofol or sevoflurane, as Purdon 2015 does. Montupil 2023 writes that patients with the pattern may still respond to command, and that patients without it can be unresponsive. The pattern is thus a signature of the drug and depth, not proof that the patient is unconscious.
  • Burst suppression as a warning sign or protection (Gruenbaum 2026 vs Jegarl 2026 and Forgacs 2020): Gruenbaum 2026 argues that burst suppression during routine anaesthesia should be seen as a red flag of reduced reserve, not a target. Jegarl 2026 and Forgacs 2020 describe the hypothesis of a protective down-regulated state after cardiac arrest. Safavynia is a co-author of both reviews. Interpretation based on the sources: the difference probably reflects different contexts (surgery vs hypoxic brain injury) more than conflicting findings.
  • Propofol + midazolam: synergistic or additive? (Hendrickx 2008 and ch. 21 vs ch. 16): Hendrickx 2008 reports three studies that found synergy for hypnosis (Short and Chui 1991, McClune 1992, Short 1992), and chapter 21 states that midazolam often acts synergistically with other hypnotics. Chapter 16 calls the interaction «primarily additive», citing Fidler 2006 and Vinik 1994. The difference may reflect model and endpoint, but the sources do not explain it.
  • Midazolam and beta (Brandt 2020 vs Purdon 2015): Brandt 2020 writes that midazolam at sedative doses is associated with beta oscillations, citing among others Purdon 2015 Part I. Purdon 2015 mentions benzodiazepines only in passing and describes no beta signature for midazolam. The other source Brandt cites (Brown 2011) has not been checked.
  • Dexmedetomidine, spindles and depth (Purdon 2015 vs Huupponen 2008): Purdon 2015 describes the spindles disappearing and slow-delta increasing when the infusion is increased (0.65 vs 0.85 µg/kg/h, two single patients), a picture resembling NREM 3. Huupponen 2008 described the EEG during deep sedation (measured 5.1 ng/ml) as NREM 2 with many spindles, in eleven volunteers who could be roused. The doses are given in different ways (infusion rate vs plasma concentration) and cannot be compared directly. Huupponen used one frontal channel and a different monitor.
  • Dexmedetomidine and arousability (Ebert 2000 in ch. 21 vs Huupponen 2008): chapter 21 states that unrousable deep sedation is thought to occur above about 1.9 ng/ml. Huupponen 2008 writes that participants in an earlier study by the same group could be roused with verbal commands and possibly light shaking at a measured 5.1 ng/ml. The difference may reflect different definitions of arousability and different stimuli, but the sources do not discuss it.
  • Dexmedetomidine, blood flow and metabolism (ch. 21 vs Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014): chapter 21 writes that the fall in CBF is not accompanied by lower CMRO₂, but also cites a study of six volunteers in which both fell. Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014 found that blood flow and glucose metabolism fell together in the same areas.
  • Which coupling breaks first? (Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014 vs Schroeder 2016): Akeju writes that unconsciousness with disrupted cortical coupling but preserved thalamocortical coupling does not appear to occur in sleep and anaesthesia. Schroeder 2016 found in monkeys under ketamine that transfer from the thalamus to the primary somatosensory cortex was preserved, while transfer between cortical areas failed. The studies use different drugs, species and methods (fMRI vs microelectrodes).
  • Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014, figure legend: the text describes dexmedetomidine acting on locus coeruleus projections to the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus, while the legend of figure 1 says «hypothalamus».
  • Ketamine and analgesia, where in the spinal cord: Purdon 2015 writes that analgesia most likely results from NMDA receptors «at the dorsal root ganglia, the first synapse of the pain pathway in the spinal cord». Chapter 21 links the spinal analgesia to inhibition of wide dynamic range neurons in the dorsal horn. The dorsal root ganglion contains the cell bodies of the sensory neurons, while the first synapse lies in the dorsal horn, so the wordings point to different places.
  • Propofol, LTP and amnesia (ch. 8): chapter 8 describes that propofol inhibits LTP via GABAA, but also cites one study in which LTP was inhibited only at anaesthetic, not amnestic, concentrations. Amnesia at low doses therefore cannot simply be explained by LTP inhibition.
  • Flumazenil and amnesia (ch. 21 internally): chapter 21 writes both that flumazenil «reliably reverses» sedation, respiratory depression and amnesia, and that flumazenil reverses hypnotic and respiratory effects more than amnestic ones. The chapter explains the difference with receptor occupancy: a small dose of flumazenil reduces effects that need high occupancy, but not drowsiness and amnesia, while large doses reverse everything.
  • Opioids and EEG at low doses (ch. 22, ch. 36 and Balanza 2022): chapter 22 writes that small doses of fentanyl (2–5 µg/kg) give minimal EEG changes, and chapter 36 that opioids change the EEG little. Balanza 2022 found that frontal theta rose with fentanyl concentration at repeated doses of 2 µg/kg. The difference may be due to method (spectral analysis versus reading the raw EEG), but the sources do not explain it.
  • Opioids and consciousness (ch. 22 vs Hendrickx 2008): chapter 22 cites loss of consciousness in volunteers given fentanyl infused to 15 µg/kg, and high-amplitude delta waves at 30–70 µg/kg «consistent with anaesthesia». The same chapter writes that opioids are not complete anaesthetics and that high doses can abolish breathing without unconsciousness. Hendrickx 2008 writes that fentanyl alone does not give full hypnosis.
  • Biased agonism (ch. 22 internally): the chapter cites that mice lacking β-arrestin-2 had less respiratory depression from morphine (2005), and a newer study that found no difference (2021). The chapter itself concludes that the question is unresolved.
  • Ketamine, cortex and thalamus (ch. 21, ch. 8 and Schroeder 2016): chapter 21 writes that ketamine depresses parts of the cortex and thalamus. Schroeder 2016 writes that ketamine does not depress the cortex or thalamic metabolism, and chapter 8 that ketamine is the exception to metabolic depression of the thalamus.
  • Propofol and ketamine: synergy or not? (Tian 2023 vs Hendrickx 2008): Tian writes that propofol and ketamine appear to work synergistically to maintain unconsciousness, citing Brown 2018. Hendrickx 2008 found additivity and on reanalysis infra-additivity for propofol + ketamine.
  • Tian 2023, dB values: the article reports changes in mean power of more than 100 dB (for example a 159 dB gamma increase in the cingulate and a 214.9 dB beta increase after propofol). 100 dB corresponds to a ten billion-fold increase in power, which is physiologically implausible, while 3–4 Hz changes of 1–3 dB are described as «dramatic». The article does not explain the scale. The direction of the changes can be used, but the magnitudes should not be interpreted.
  • Tian 2023, HCN1: the abstract and introduction call HCN1 a «potassium channel», while the discussion describes the current as «cationic» (Ih). Purdon 2015 lists HCN channels as a separate group alongside potassium channels.
  • Liu 2023, citations: (1) an experiment with transcranial magnetic stimulation and transfer entropy is attributed to Alkire, Hudetz and Tononi 2008, which is a review in Science. (2) Section 3.1 writes that BIS and MAC gave similar awareness (Avidan 2008), while section 5.3 writes that awareness increases when BIS is used, citing Sebel 2004, which is a study of the incidence of awareness. (3) The claim that ketamine disrupts information transfer cites Schroeder 2016 in one place and a propofol study (Lee 2017) in another.
  • Miyasaka 2025, how certain is the main finding? The abstract and “Key Points” say that PAED was significantly reduced by 14%. The discussion itself says the effect was marginal, that the difference is not significant with a PAED cut-off of 12, and that the interim analysis makes the p-value uncertain (0.03–0.05 depending on method). The dose reduction and faster emergence, on the other hand, are robust. The title in Key Points calls it a 14% fall, while the absolute difference of 35 versus 21% corresponds to a 40% relative reduction.
  • Aperiodic exponent, different figures: Widmann 2025 gives α 1.61 awake and 2.60 during maintenance; Leroy 2023 gives 1.6–1.8 before and 1.9–2.2 after loss of consciousness; Connor 2026 mentions β 2.45 for propofol and 2.71 for sevoflurane from Dragovic 2025. The differences are due to different frequency ranges, FOOOF settings (with or without “knee”) and timing (induction versus maintenance), so the values are not interchangeable.
  • Hysteresis in humans: Huang 2021 summarises that Kuizenga 2018 and Warnaby 2017 did not find hysteresis for propofol (Kuizenga found it for sevoflurane), while Ferreira 2020, Nir 2019, Sepúlveda 2019 and Huang themselves found it. Huang points out that by adjusting PK/PD parameters one can get both yes and no out of the same behavioural data, because the concentration is calculated, not measured.
  • Suppression ratio and delirium, two meta-analyses: an earlier meta-analysis of burst suppression found that higher BSR was associated with delirium; Xu 2025 did not (BSR non-significant in all analyses), but found occurrence (OR 2.5) and duration. Xu explains the difference by their use of mean difference in percent, exclusion of index-derived measures and the requirement of delirium after the recovery unit. Fritz 2016 and Fritz 2018 (same cohort) moreover reported different significance for OR per minute of suppression, probably because of different analysis.
  • Delta and delirium: Xu 2025 found lower delta in those with delirium in the main analysis, but not without index guidance; Gutiérrez 2019 found an equal delta increase in both groups. The authors consider the delta finding an artefact of index-guided dosing.
  • Epileptiform activity with sevoflurane, incidence: Schultz 2012 found 20% in children at about 73 seconds with 8%, Kreuzer 2014 found 52–76% at 5 minutes with 6% or 3 minutes with 8%. Both are from the same centre, the same monitor (Narcotrend) and visual assessment, so the difference is most likely due to exposure time, but neither study has a control group without sevoflurane, and the definitions of the patterns are the centre's own. The direction of BIS during such activity is inconsistent across studies (Gimson 2021), and whether the findings apply to other indices has not been studied.
  • Magnesium and BIS: Walia 2018 found lower BIS and less propofol requirement with Mg before induction, Memiş 2003 found unchanged BIS with Mg during sufentanil sedation in intensive care. Dosing, patient group and which agent was titrated differ, and neither study separates EEG effect from EMG and haemodynamic effects. The app therefore describes Mg as opioid- and hypnotic-sparing without its own EEG signature, and marks the explanation as a hypothesis.
  • Miller's ch. 10, internal discrepancies: the key points state that CMR is reduced by about 60% at burst suppression, while the barbiturate section gives about 50% at complete EEG suppression with thiopental (the same discrepancy as against ch. 21). The permitted MAP fall is given as no more than 20% below baseline in the section on reduced reserve and as 30–35% in the section on chronic hypertension, which also states that a 25% fall brings the patient to the LLA. Membrane failure is given at about 6–10 ml/100 g/min in the text and 6–12 in the legend to fig. 10.20. CBF reduction at 1 MAC sevoflurane is given as 38% (Kety–Schmidt) and about 50% (PET); midazolam 0.15 mg/kg as 30–34% and 12% (PET). The chapter itself explains the last two by measurement method.
  • CBF thresholds across sources: Miller's ch. 10 puts EEG change at about 20 and isoelectric EEG at about 15; Foreman and Claassen put loss of fast activity at 25–35, increased slow activity at 17–18 and silence at 10–12; van Putten and Hofmeijer put synaptic failure at 15–35 and membrane change below 10. The figures overlap, but the definitions (“EEG signs”, “fast activity lost”, “isoelectric”) differ, and Miller's data are from primates under different anaesthetics. The figure in the Perfusion tab shows all three rows.
  • The Michael Jackson case, who testified: Emery Brown is widely linked to the trial of Conrad Murray, but in the trial reports (CNN, Medscape 2011) the anaesthesia experts were Steven Shafer and Paul White, and the sleep specialist Nader Kamangar. Brown has discussed the case in interviews, not in court. The app therefore does not list Brown as a witness.
  • Dexmedetomidine and sleep, how similar: Brown 2010 writes that the EEG under dexmedetomidine “closely resembles” NREM sleep; Akeju and Brown 2017 specify that spindles and slow waves resemble N2, that K-complexes have not been described, and that dexmedetomidine does not produce physiological sleep either. Telias and Wilcox 2019 report better sleep efficiency in small pilot studies and reduced delirium with low-dose nocturnal use, without better self-reported sleep. The app follows the strictest wording.
  • Between the standards: the Norwegian standard 2024 says depth monitoring “must be individually considered”, while the Association of Anaesthetists 2021 says pEEG “should be used” with TIVA and a neuromuscular blocker. Both are consensus documents; the British one builds explicitly on NAP5. The app presents both without choosing.
  • Walsh 2018, p-value: the abstract gives p < 0.01 for the difference in burst suppression (23.0 vs 12.2%), the results section p < 0.05 and a posterior probability of 0.973. The app uses the numbers, not the p-value.
  • Dexmedetomidine and sleep stages: Pinheiro 2026 writes that the pattern resembles stage II or III of NREM sleep; Akeju and Brown 2017 say N2-like spindles and slow waves without K-complexes, not physiological sleep. The app follows Akeju.
  • Nitrous oxide and the index: Pinheiro 2026 writes that nitrous oxide mostly does not change the index in patients under GABAergic anaesthesia; Purdon 2015 (Part I) writes that nitrous oxide, like ketamine, produces faster oscillations that tend to raise the index at clinically accepted doses, and that the switch to a high concentration gives a transient slow-delta pattern. The difference is probably dose and context (adjunct on top of GABAergic anaesthesia versus high concentration at emergence). Neither explains why the NMDA antagonist nitrous oxide leaves a weaker EEG footprint than ketamine at clinical doses.
  • Is sedation “sleep-inducing”? Miller's ch. 9 versus Brown 2010 and Akeju 2017: the legend of fig. 9.11 in ch. 9 says that sedation shows EEG traces “comparable to slow-wave sleep, indicating the sleep-inducing effect of anesthetics”, and the chapter describes sedatives as producing states “similar, if not identical, to” NREM sleep. Akeju and Brown 2017, which the chapter itself cites for this, argue the opposite: propofol's slow waves are asynchronous with long pauses, GABAergic alpha is not a feature of sleep, and neither anaesthetics nor sleep medications produce physiological sleep. The chapter's main text agrees that sleep and anaesthesia differ (sharp versus gradual transition, arousability, stages), so the disagreement is mainly about the wording used for sedation.
  • Propofol and REM: Miller's ch. 9 writes that propofol sedation in long-term ventilated patients abolishes REM (Kondili 2012) but that REM is possible at low dose; Telias and Wilcox 2019 describe propofol primarily as a potent suppressor of slow-wave sleep. Both may be correct for different doses and populations, but the sources emphasise different sleep stages.
  • Age and index, opposite directions: Purdon 2015 (BJA), Besch 2011 and Ni 2019 (and Obert 2021, cited by Aasheim) find that the elderly get higher index values at the same or age-adjusted dose (less EEG effect, so the index “overestimates” wakefulness). Aasheim 2026 finds the opposite in the OUS cohort: BIS falls 0.05 per year of age and more with high ASA. The authors discuss this themselves: in daily practice with standard Schnider TCI, the old and sick are dosed relatively deeper than the experimental equal-dose studies would suggest, so the findings describe practice, not pharmacodynamics. The two sets of findings are therefore not in conflict but answer different questions.
  • Sex and anaesthetic sensitivity: Wasilczuk 2023 (mice and healthy volunteers) and Braithwaite 2023 (systematic review) find that women are more resistant to anaesthetics, emerge faster and have more awareness. Aasheim 2026 nevertheless finds lower BIS in women in practice. The authors suggest that women are dosed higher because sex is perceived as a risk factor, or that the Schnider model's fixed V1 produces relatively deeper anaesthesia in women. Unresolved.
  • Aasheim 2026, internal: the results section says the ASA difference was significant for ASA 2 and 3 versus ASA 1, whereas table 3 also shows ASA 4 (−0.86, p < 0.0001). The text refers to figure 6 for the proportion with BIS above 65, but it is figure 5 that shows this; figure 6 shows minutes below 30. The OUS guideline defines light anaesthesia as BIS above 60, whereas the analysis uses 65 as the cut-off.
  • Dreams at emergence, how many: Leslie 2009 found dreams in 27–28% with propofol or desflurane titrated to BIS 40–55 and interview at orientation; Sikka 2026 found 69%, and 93% with full adherence to a bundle of priming, propofol, EEG-guided preemergence state, 10 minutes hands-off and interview immediately after extubation. The difference is expected: the Sikka study is designed to increase recall and has no control group, and the group's scoping review shows that experimental studies typically yield 40–80% versus 3–8% in large clinical studies. The figures therefore cannot be compared as incidence.
  • Sikka 2026, 93% in the bundle study versus the review: in the bundle study 93% applies only to the 57 of 452 interviewed (12.6%) in whom all five elements were delivered; overall 69% dreamed. The scoping review from the same group writes that the bundle “achieved 93% dream recall” without mentioning that the figure comes from this subgroup. The review’s total of 87,866 participants also counts some volunteers more than once, since the 16 experimental studies (620) rest on only 10 unique samples (n = 356).
  • Newman 2026, direction of the inflection point: the text and figure legend say that those below the threshold (about 0.13–0.14) show paradoxical excitation and those above show suppression. That is the opposite of the regression (higher baseline SC gives the largest fall in SC, that is paradoxical excitation) and of table 1 (baseline median 0.143 for responsive, 0.128 for drowsy). The app follows the regression and the table. The threshold is given as “~0.13” in the text and “~0.1378” in figure 4.
  • Newman 2026, abstract, text and table: the abstract gives r = −0.88 for baseline SC against change in SC, but in the results it is r = −0.70 (all of Chennu) and −0.89 (responsive); −0.88 is the correlation with hit rate in the drowsy (n = 7). The U and p values in the text differ from table 1 (for example LZC in responsive U = 41.0, p = 0.027 versus U = 38.5, p = 0.019; SC in responsive p = 0.018 versus 0.046; deep sedation SC p = 0.050 versus 0.038). ReCCognition is n = 8 in the abstract and methods, but the correlations in figure 2b and table 2 use n = 7, while only one excluded individual is justified (for time to loss of consciousness). Estimated concentration is given as 0.6 and 1.2 µg/ml in the methods, whereas figure 2 has axes of 400–1,800 labelled µg/ml.
  • Cornelissen 2015, propofol: the methods say propofol was used for intubation in 19 of 36 (15.8 ± 6.3 mg/kg), while table 1 gives 11 of the 30 analysed (36.7%). That cannot be right if only six were excluded. Nitrous oxide (29 of 36 versus 23 of 30) can be reconciled.
  • Kratzer 2020, number of older patients: the OLD group is given as 20 patients in the methods section, “16” in the sentence about midazolam (“6 of 16 did not receive midazolam”) and “6/25 received midazolam” in the results section. The two midazolam sentences contradict each other. The card in the app therefore does not give the number in the OLD group.
  • Short and Chui 1991, synergy coefficient: the results section gives the coefficient 0.78, the discussion and abstract 0.87 and “44% lower ED50”. Which figure is correct is not apparent; the direction (synergy, p < 0.01) is the same.
  • Opioid and suppression, opposite direction: Fritz 2016 found that lower opioid dose gave more EEG suppression during volatile anaesthesia, while an earlier study of volatile anaesthesia that Fritz refers to found high opioid dose as a risk factor (Besch 2011 found age, coronary disease and male sex with propofol-remifentanil). Fritz suggests that deeply anaesthetised patients without signs of nociception simply received less opioid, and that the sequence cannot be determined.
  • Manquat 2022, internal typographical errors: the table gives “Female 47 (38.9%)” in the CA− column where 7 must be correct, SEF95 appears as “13.79 (41.26)” in the text versus 1.26 in the table, and the table headings have “AC+/AC−” for CA+/CA−. None of the errors changes the main finding, but the figures are taken from the table where the text and table disagree.
  • Older patients and alpha: Obert 2024 versus Purdon 2015 (BJA) and the simulator: Purdon found that alpha falls more than other bands with age during maintenance, and that burst suppression approaches certainty in the oldest patients under propofol. Obert found no burst suppression in 25 older patients and the same relative spectral composition as in younger patients with slow induction. The studies measure different phases (induction versus maintenance) with different dosing (titrated infusion versus bolus in clinical practice), so both may be correct. The simulator's “older” option (weak or no alpha) is based on Purdon and on clinical experience, not on Obert.
  • Continuous versus intermittent EEG: Taccone 2026 concedes that outcome studies (Rossetti 2020, CERTA) have not shown that continuous EEG is better than routine EEG, but nevertheless argues that the two are not interchangeable because the value depends on the question. Miller's ch. 80 says that EEG “should be used continuously” in unconscious neurointensive care patients without this caveat.
  • PbtO2 normal range: Miller's ch. 80 gives normal PbtO2 as 20–45 mmHg, Lobo and Lamperti ch. 12 as 20–35 mmHg. Both set the ischaemic threshold at around 15–20 mmHg (ch. 80 cites van den Brink 2000), so the disagreement concerns only the upper normal limit.
  • Popular EEG notes versus the textbook: handwritten overview sheets circulating online (without peer review) say that bipolar montage is “an older method used less often”. Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4 recommend both bipolar and referential montage, and ACNS/IFCN specify a minimum set of both. The same notes give fixed amplitude ranges per band (for example delta 20–200 µV); such figures are not reproduced here because they are not documented in the sources the app is based on.
  • Alpha coma and burst suppression as “malignant” patterns: Miller's ch. 80 calls burst suppression, alpha coma and low-voltage delta malignant after anoxia. Sutter and Kaplan 2012 show that all three also occur in intoxication and sedation with favourable outcome, and that it is the cause and the reactivity, not the pattern, that carries the prognosis. The sentence in chapter 80 therefore applies only to the anoxic cause, and it does not say so explicitly.
  • Burst suppression after anoxia: Miller's ch. 80 calls burst suppression a malignant pattern after anoxic brain injury, without a reference and without distinguishing between spontaneous and drug-induced burst suppression. Forgacs 2020 (17 analysed patients) and Jegarl 2026 describe patients with burst suppression after cardiac arrest who regained good consciousness, and Sandroni 2020 (which ch. 80 cites for N20) requires that EEG patterns be assessed after 24 hours and without sedation. The chapter's wording is thus cruder than the more recent literature.
  • Hypothermia: Miller's ch. 80 says that therapeutic hypothermia is not recommended after TBI (Andrews 2015, Eurotherm) and that it did not improve outcome in head injury, while the Forgacs 2020 card describes hypothermia to 33 °C as part of the treatment in the patients after cardiac arrest. This is not a contradiction (different diagnoses), but easy to confuse.
  • Nordum 2024, table 3: cardiac index at T4 (one hour of tilt) is given as −0.07 (SE 0.10) with p < 0.001, which does not add up; table 2 shows 1.80 versus 2.40 l/min/m², so the coefficient is probably around −0.6. The abstract gives 44 included, while 37 had intraoperative measurements and 25 completed all cognitive tests.
  • Pisitsak 2019, figures: minute ventilation at T1 is given as 7.0 l/min in the text and 7.2 in table 2; the p-value for the gradient is 0.025 in the abstract and 0.02 in the text. The table 1 reference for temperature in the text refers to table 2.
  • Jegarl 2026 on Forgacs 2020: the review says that Forgacs “analysed intraburst spectra in 53 patients”, but in Forgacs 2020, 53 was the size of the whole cohort; only 17 had burst suppression and were analysed.
  • Fischer 2026, figures: theta is given as 3.5–7 Hz in the text and 3.5–8 Hz in the legend to figure 3; beta is given as 13–30 Hz in the discussion and 12–33 Hz in the legend to figure 5. The figure references in the case description do not match the figure legends (improved skin perfusion is referred to figure 3, which describes the shock phase).
  • Rasulo 2023, contradictory consensus: under “when should monitoring start” it says that patients with only light sedation (RASS 0 to −2) do not benefit from monitoring, with strong consensus, while the same statement under the question on procedural sedation and in table 2 (statement 6) is listed without consensus. The percentages in the results section (3.3%, 4.9%, 8.2%) match 61 statements, not the 59 given.
  • Eskioglou 2021, figures: the abstract gives rhythmic/periodic patterns in 43 versus 22%, the text 43 versus 22.5%. Table 1 gives sepsis as the primary diagnosis in 35%, the text 42%. The abstract says that at least one abnormal finding gave “42 versus 15%” delirium, but it is not clear whether the percentages refer to delirium among those with and without findings, or findings among those with and without delirium.
  • Watson 2008, figures and covariates: the text says that “mortality for the whole cohort was 26% (32 of 125)”, but 32 is the number who died in intensive care (18 + 14); hospital mortality was 42 of 125 (34%) and 6-month mortality 54 of 125 (43%). The abstract lists seven covariates, while the footnotes to tables 2 and 3 additionally give admission diagnosis (sepsis or ARDS).
  • Lobo and Lamperti ch. 12, units: the normal values for microdialysis are given as pyruvate 120 mM, glutamate 10 mM and glycerol 20–50 mM, while glucose and lactate are given as 2 mM. Pyruvate, glutamate and glycerol in the interstitium are usually measured in micromoles per litre, so the unit is probably wrong for these three.
  • Vlisides 2017, figure reference: the results section on directed connectivity (dPLI) refers to fig. 4B, while the dPLI topographies are in fig. 5B. Table 1 gives “absolute power” in dB with values near zero (for example gamma 0.02 dB), which does not match the scale in the spectrograms; the unit in the table is probably not dB as stated.
  • Leslie 2009, table versus text: the text says that the EEG comparison involved 34 dreamers and 116 non-dreamers, while the heading of table 6 gives n = 75 in each group (the same figures as propofol/desflurane in table 7). Table 2 gives movement as 9 (45%) and 37 (68%), but 9 of 150 is 6% and 37 of 150 is 25%, so the denominator is unclear.
  • Russell and Wang 2001, error in the text: the closing conclusion says that the authors “found explicit or implicit memory”, while the results and abstract show that they found none. It is probably an error where the word “no” is missing. Table 1 gives a mean age of 46.4 years with a range of 35–45 years in the vegetable group, which cannot be right. The authors write that 7 + 5 of 52 patients woke up, and call it 21%, but 12 of 52 is 23%, and 21% corresponds to 11 of 52. Nordström 1997 is given as 5 of 2500 in the introduction and as 1000 patients in the discussion.
  • EEG and ICP, conflicting findings: McNamara 2003 found no EEG changes during acute ICP peaks, while Sheikh 2022 describes slowing and attenuated fast activity that often preceded clinical deterioration. Sample, method and EEG duration differ. Neither case series nor small studies can settle the matter.
  • Balanza 2022, figures in the text: the abstract states that respiratory depression occurs at about 1700 times lower concentration than sedation, while the results give 1750 (CI 839–2854) and the figure legend 1754. The text says that minute ventilation fell 51.4% (CI 30.9–80.4) before reaction time increased, while the figure legend says it fell to 51% (CI 31–79). “Fell by” and “fell to” are not the same.
  • Sheorajpanday 2009, p-value: the abstract gives p = 0.0003 for the difference in pdBSI between infarction and TIA or controls, while the results section and figure 5 give p = 0.001 (Kruskal–Wallis). Table 4 gives n = 40 for the first group, even though the study has 41 patients.
  • Cornelissen 2018, timing of frontal alpha dominance: the abstract gives about 6 months, the discussion about 7 months, the results section 7–9 months, and the legend to figure 3 that it begins to appear at 8 months and peaks at 15–20 months. Different electrode pairs (F3–O1) and definitions may underlie this. Similarly, the abstract states that frontal slow oscillation is coherent until 6 months, while the results section says about 8 months.
  • Cornelissen 2015 versus 2018: the 2015 study found a small but significant frontal alpha dominance at 4–6 months (FPz versus Oz), while 2018 puts the first signs at 6–9 months (F3 versus O1). The difference may be due to electrode choice and age grouping.
  • Peak in EEG power in children: Akeju 2015 states that power increases until about 6 years and declines until about 21 years. Other sources (cited in reviews) give about 6–8 years, and one source gives about 8 years. Different frequency bands, agents and age groups may underlie this.
  • Thresholds, Foreman and Claassen: fast activity disappears at CBF 25–35, slow activity increases at 17–18, and the EEG is silent at 10–12. Figure 3 in van Putten and Hofmeijer (who refer to them) puts the increase in slow activity at about 15. van Putten and Hofmeijer themselves put membrane changes below 10. All give only approximate ranges, and they overlap.
  • Energy use: Lobo states that 75–80% of the brain's oxygen consumption goes to restoring the membrane potential. van Putten and Hofmeijer give about 40% for resting membrane and action potentials and about 35% for synaptic transmission in the cortex. Guay 2025 states that action potentials, synaptic transmission and membrane potential account for at least 75% of ATP use in the cortex. The total thus agrees well, and the difference concerns what counts as “membrane work”.
  • EEG-guided shunting, figures for stroke rate: the text gives 1.6% with selective shunting guided by EEG and 4.8% with selective shunting guided by TCD. The study shows only a numerical difference and does not document that TCD is worse, and the authors themselves point out that there is no clinical evidence that TCD is more reliable than EEG.
  • Burst suppression, different explanations: Georgii raises hypotension-induced hypoperfusion as a possible mechanism, while Lobo ch. 5 describes cortical hyperexcitability and a metabolic theory. Neither is proven.
